regions.name: Southeast coast
regions.teaser: Robusta from Mananjary down to Farafangana; one French company had over half a million trees around Mananjary in the 1950s

regions.name: East and northeast coast
regions.teaser: Robusta around Toamasina (Tamatave) and Antalaha

regions.name: Sambirano
regions.teaser: Northwest Robusta around Ambanja and Nosy Be, by the Sambirano river

regions.name: Central highlands
regions.teaser: Smallholder Arabica, near Lake Alaotra and in Itasy, Amoron'i Mania and Haute Matsiatra, where one exporter buys from farms of 15–50 trees

harvest.text: Robusta picking starts in June and July (PDG). FAO's 2000 profile gave May or June to October, and one new exporter's first season ran June to August (Sprudge, 2025).

cup.text: Madagascar Coffee Company finds its Arabica fairly sweet, with citrus on lighter roasts, and says natural processing brings out acidity in its Robusta, with a chocolate-covered-cherry effect (Sprudge, 2025). PDG says Malagasy Robusta has long been known for a smooth mouthfeel and less of the classic Robusta taste.
cup.prized: Q graders (the industry's certified tasters) scored one farm's 2019/20 Arabica at 83 and 84 points; its grower calls it a clean cup with body (PDG).
cup.watch: The Robusta trees average about 70 years old, which lowers yields and invites disease, and one exporter says the island has no dry mill, the plant that hulls and sorts green coffee for export (PDG; Sprudge, 2025). Washed coffee exists only in small, experimental lots.

story.text: The Merina kingdom worked with planters from nearby Réunion to build a coffee industry around the highland capital; coastal plantations followed.
Coffee passed vanilla among the colony's exports, nearly all of it shipped duty-free to France.
Production peaked at an estimated 1.1 million bags; in 1988 the coffee trade was opened to private exporters.
Exports fell from tens of thousands of tonnes to 495 tonnes.
The government drew up a 2026–2036 revival program with an indicative budget of about $150 million; its first phase (2027–2031) targets 46,800 tonnes a year on 45,000 hectares.

sections.title: Wild coffee
body: About 65 of the world's roughly 130 known coffee species grow in Madagascar, against 48 in the rest of Africa, and Kew botanists Aaron Davis and Franck Rakotonasolo described six more from the north in 2021. These wild coffees, grouped as Mascarocoffea, mostly have little or no caffeine and taste too bitter to farm, a Malagasy researcher told Sprudge, but breeders cross them with farmed coffee; the researcher estimates 70% of the native species are endangered.
Ratelo, an Arabica now on trial, brings in genes from a cross of Coffea eugenioides and Robusta.

cup.text: Coffeeness describes Mexican coffee as smooth, balanced and silky, with a base of dark cocoa and milk chocolate and notes of nuts, caramel, spice and sometimes citrus or stone fruit. Sweet Maria's calls it typically light-bodied and mild, with subtle flavors.
cup.why: Region matters: Sweet Maria's says the cup varies widely from region to region.
cup.prized: High-grown lots: Sweet Maria's says the best come from farms at 1,800 m (5,900 ft) and up, often from old Typica plants with a clean, classic profile.
cup.watch: Bulk lots are often poorly picked and processed, with taints from under-ripe cherries, says Sweet Maria's.

records.name: Myanmar
records.summary: Shan State smallholders and Mandalay estates, known for clean naturals.
records.lede: Myanmar's coffee comes mainly from Shan State, where smallholders grow Arabica on plots of a hectare or less, and from Mandalay Region, where larger estates around Pyin Oo Lwin wash much of their crop. A quality push that began in the mid-2010s taught farmers to sort and process for specialty buyers, and cup scores rose from the low 70s to the mid 80s within a few years. Buyers single out its clean, sun-dried naturals.

facts.label: where the coffee grows (3,300–4,900 ft)
of coffee exported a year to neighboring markets, led by China (2026 estimate)
cup scores after the quality push
first coffee, planted by missionaries at Myeik and Dawei

regions.name: Shan State (Ywangan)
regions.teaser: Smallholders, often with 10–20 trees beside food crops. Cherries go to a central mill or are sun-dried on raised beds

regions.name: Mandalay (Pyin Oo Lwin)
regions.teaser: Larger estates, up to about 400 acres (160 ha), that wash most of their coffee

regions.name: Kayin State
regions.teaser: Robusta, grown here since about 1885

harvest.text: Picked from late November or December to March, in the dry season, which makes sun-drying easier; exports run from April to October.

grows.species: mostly Arabica in the highlands, with Robusta lower down

story.text: Missionaries plant the first coffee at Myeik and Dawei; Robusta growing in Kayin State begins around the same time.
Catholic missionaries bring Arabica to Shan State.
The government, with the UN, promotes coffee to replace opium poppy, and in 1986 imports several tons of seed to build a national program.
A USAID-funded project run by Winrock International and the Coffee Quality Institute trains Ywangan farmers in farming, sorting and processing, and helps fund wet and dry mills.
After the military takeover, a Swiss-backed effort to register Ywangan as a geographical indication goes on hold.

cup.text: Processing is what sets Myanmar apart, says the trading platform Algrano: producers make very clean naturals that former Coffee Quality Institute staff compare to Panama's. Royal Coffee New York tasted grape, tangerine, caramel and red apple in a Ywangan lot of SL28 and Catuai.
cup.why: The harvest falls in the dry, sunny season, and Sucafina says that dry heat suits naturals, coffee dried in the whole cherry.
cup.watch: Logistics. Roads, processing plants and port capacity lag behind, and since 2021 military rule has stalled efforts such as registering Ywangan as a protected origin name.

sections.title: Before the quality push
body: Farmers used to hand-pulp their cherries and sell the beans unsorted at village "five-day markets", and traders often moved them on to China and Thailand. Local cherry prices rose from 300 kyat per viss (1.63 kg) in 2014 to 3,700 kyat in 2023.

records.name: Malawi
records.summary: A small, estate-led crop of washed Arabica, Geisha included.
records.lede: Malawi grows a small crop of washed Arabica and some Robusta, and unlike most origins, most of it comes from estates; a few thousand smallholders farm the northern and central hills. Geisha is grown widely here, and one roaster describes floral cups with stone fruit, sweet citrus and a milk-chocolate finish.

facts.label: of the crop grown on estates
smallholders grow the rest, per Sucafina
among coffee exporters (ICO, 2022–24 average)
altitude, estates lowest (2,950–8,200 ft)

regions.name: Northern hills
regions.teaser: Smallholder co-ops in Misuku, Phoka, Viphya and the Nkhata Bay highlands, where shaded coffee is grown

regions.name: Thyolo and Mulanje
regions.teaser: The south, where commercial estates began; most grow unshaded coffee

harvest.text: Picked from April to September (Cafe Imports) or into October (Sucafina). It usually reaches importing countries between November and February.

cup.text: Achilles Coffee Roasters describes medium acidity and body with mild sweetness and, next to Kenyan coffee, florals, stone fruit and sweet citrus with a clean milk-chocolate finish.
cup.prized: Specialty growers are setting apart their Geisha, SL28 and Bourbon-type lots, says Cafe Imports.
cup.watch: Catimor, widely grown, is hardy but usually cups lower, and Cafe Imports says it has had to cancel contracts over scores and defects.

story.text: Missionaries brought the first coffee, which one roaster says came from Edinburgh's Royal Botanic Garden; sources date it from the 1880s (Sucafina) to 1891 (Achilles).
Independence; land redistribution and cooperatives later made coffee more workable for small growers.
Coffee wilt disease nearly wiped out smallholder coffee.
Malawi began hosting a site of the world's largest Arabica variety trial; its first harvest, at Mzuzu in 2022, let local cuppers taste 29 varieties.

sections.title: An unusual mix of trees
body: After a wilt disease devastated the first Arabica, a researcher from Ethiopia brought in Geisha and Agaro, says Achilles. Catimor 129, selected in Malawi for release in 2006 and sometimes called Nyika there, is common here and in Zambia and Zimbabwe.

records.name: Malaysia
records.summary: A small, mostly Liberica crop from Johor, Sabah and Sarawak.
records.lede: Malaysia grows only about 2,900 t of coffee a year, and most of it (87% in 2024) is Liberica, a species that makes up only about 1% of the world's coffee. Most comes from Johor, Sabah and Sarawak, and the country imports about two-thirds of the coffee it uses. Small producers are now trying specialty processing on Johor Liberica and growing highland Arabica in Sabah.

facts.label: of coffee in 2024, from 2,924 ha
of the 2024 crop was Liberica; Robusta 10%, Arabica 3%
of its coffee needs met at home (2024)
Sabah's highland Arabica farms (4,300 ft+)

regions.name: Johor
regions.teaser: The long-time heart of Malaysian Liberica, grown in coastal Batu Pahat villages such as Bagan and Senggarang. About two-thirds of the 2018 crop

regions.name: Sabah
regions.teaser: Highland Arabica around Ranau, mostly Catimor, sold as Sabarica; Tenom once had about 1,000 ha of Robusta

regions.name: Sarawak
regions.teaser: One of the three main coffee states in 2024

grows.species: mostly Liberica, with some Robusta and a little Arabica

cup.text: Johor roaster Adam Esham of House of Kendal describes his Liberica as candy-sweet with a round, silky mouthfeel: natural-process lots lean wine-like with strong jackfruit notes, and honey-process lots toward hazelnut and chocolate.
cup.watch: Liberica's reputation. Little high-quality Liberica reaches the market, so many drinkers think of it as poor coffee, and the same roaster says much of its flavor is lost if it is processed and roasted like Arabica or Robusta.

story.text: Malaysia grows about 25,000 t of coffee a year on average.
Coffee area shrinks about 13% a year and output about 16% a year, as oil palm and other crops win out and labor costs rise.
Output is down to 3,369 t, mostly from Johor and Sabah.
Output is 2,861 t; replanting uses the government's Liberica clones MKL5, MKL6 and MKL7, with MKL-8 to MKL-10 in testing.

sections.title: About USDA's figure
body: USDA's world coffee tables list Malaysia at about 1.5 million 60-kg bags (about 90,000 t) for 2026/27, all as Robusta. That is roughly 30 times the 2,861 t that Malaysia's agriculture minister gave for 2024, of which 87% was Liberica. This page uses the ministry's figures. Malaysia also imported 126,062 t of coffee beans in 2024.

cup.text: Perfect Daily Grind's 2021 guide describes the typical Nicaraguan cup as having a bright, citric acidity and a smooth body, with floral, citrus or chocolate notes.
cup.why: Altitude matters: producers quoted in the guide say higher farms give more complex cups, while lower ones struggle more with disease and drying.

records.name: Nepal
records.summary: A tiny, mostly washed mid-hills crop, grown since 1938.
records.lede: Nepal grows only about 640 t of green coffee a year (2024/25), spread across some 45 districts, mostly in Bagmati, Koshi and Gandaki provinces. Most of it is washed Bourbon, Typica and Caturra from largely organic farms. The planted area has more than doubled in a decade, but yields per hectare have fallen.

facts.label: of green coffee in 2024/25, from 5,501 ha planted
average yield in 2024/25, down from about 225 in 2013/14
districts reporting coffee (2024/25)
a hermit, Hira Giri, plants the first seeds in Gulmi

regions.name: Bagmati (Kavre, Nuwakot)
regions.teaser: The biggest producing province in 2024/25, about 290 t. Kavre (121 t) and Nuwakot (about 90 t) are the top two districts

regions.name: Koshi (Ilam)
regions.teaser: The east, with the most coffee area (about 1,700 ha); Ilam grew 83 t in 2024/25, near tea country

regions.name: Gandaki (Syangja)
regions.teaser: Mid-hill districts such as Syangja, Kaski, Lamjung and Tanahu; about 156 t in 2024/25

regions.name: Lumbini (Gulmi, Arghakhanchi, Palpa)
regions.teaser: Where Nepali coffee began in 1938, and home of the Coffee Development Centre since 1984

cup.text: Nepali coffees tend toward bright acidity and a medium body, with notes from floral and citrus to chocolate and spice depending on region and process, says exporter Himalaya Coffee Company in a sponsored Perfect Daily Grind article.
cup.watch: Roast level. Beans roasted darker, as they are for export, turn strong, bitter and burnt-tasting, The Kathmandu Post noted in 2019; the home market asks for lighter roasts.

sections.title: How high it grows
body: Sources disagree. A research review puts Nepal's suitable coffee land at about 600–1,350 m (2,000–4,400 ft) in the mid-hills, and a plot study sampled farms at 525–1,275 m. An exporter quoted by Perfect Daily Grind says most farms sit at 1,000–2,100 m (3,300–6,900 ft).

sections.title: About these figures
body: Production numbers come from Nepal's agriculture ministry, as compiled in a 2026 preprint that has not yet been peer-reviewed. The taste notes come from Himalaya Coffee Company, an exporter that sponsored the article they appeared in, so treat them as company-reported.

harvest.text: Ripe red cherries are picked in November.

story.text: Hira Giri, a hermit from Burma, brings coffee seeds to Aapchaur in Gulmi district.
Commercial growing takes off: a commercial nursery opens in 1981, the first processing mill in 1983, and Gulmi's Coffee Development Centre in 1984.
Nepal makes its first recorded green-coffee export, dry-processed beans to Japan.
Donor programs push washed processing and organic certification, and a National Coffee Policy follows in 2004.
Nepal ratifies membership of the International Coffee Organization.

cup.text: Panama's fame rests on Gesha, which World Coffee Research describes as having delicate floral, jasmine and peach-like aromas; Ozone Coffee adds bergamot and a tea-like texture in Boquete lots. Coffeeness describes its other regions more softly: caramel, chocolate and nut in Volcán, and milk chocolate and brown sugar in Renacimiento.

feel.acidity: bright in Gesha; mellow in Renacimiento

cup.why: Sucafina credits bajareque, a fine mist blown over the mountains, which cools the farms and slows ripening so the cherries build more sugar and aromatic oils.
cup.prized: Gesha's floral clarity, which first set an auction record at Best of Panama in 2004.
cup.watch: Gesha needs altitude: Sucafina reports that at lower elevations it gave very poor-tasting coffee.

cup.text: Sweet Maria's describes good Peruvian lots as clean washed coffees led by brightness, with moderate fruit or floral hints and good sweetness: Central American brightness in a South American flavor package. German retailer Roastmarket says Peruvian coffee mostly tastes low in acid, with a flat profile, a simple but strong body and subtle cocoa and nut notes, and US roaster Colipse calls it clean and citrus-accented.

feel.acidity: bright in top lots, often low in everyday ones

cup.why: Sweet Maria's credits the growing conditions, from altitude to soils and climate: the best Peruvian coffees grow very high, often above 1,800 m (5,900 ft), mostly on old Typica plants.
cup.prized: Clean, bright, sweet washed coffees from very high farms. In the Cup of Excellence, every top-three lot from 2023 to 2025 came from Cajamarca or Cusco and was washed, most of them Geisha.
cup.watch: Sweet Maria's warns that poor picking and processing, hot coastal processing plants and the long trip overland can ruin a coffee, that sweetness and fruit can fade a few months after arrival, and that some lots have a blunted acidity.

records.name: Philippines
records.summary: Four coffee species, from Mindanao Robusta to Batangas barako.
records.lede: The Philippines is one of the few countries that grows all four commercial coffee species: Robusta, Arabica, Liberica (sold locally as barako) and Excelsa. Robusta is most of the crop, much of it from Mindanao, while small Arabica farms on Mt Apo and in the Cordillera mountains are building a specialty name. The country grows far less than it drinks and imports most of its coffee.

facts.label: 60-kg bags forecast for 2026/27 (about 28,500 t)
of output was Robusta in 2020; Arabica was 16.7%
of the coffee Filipinos drink is imported (2024)
Mt Apo's Arabica farms (4,600–5,600 ft)

regions.name: Sultan Kudarat
regions.teaser: The top coffee province: in 2021 it grew about 86% of SOCCSKSARGEN's crop, and that region grew about 36% of the country's

regions.name: Mt Apo (Davao del Sur)
regions.teaser: Smallholder Arabica on steep slopes around Bansalan. Its farms took the top three Arabica places in the 2021 national competition

regions.name: Benguet and the Cordillera
regions.teaser: Shade-grown Arabica in the northern mountains, such as Agnep Heritage Farms in Benguet at 1,620 m (5,300 ft); Sagada also places in competitions

regions.name: Batangas and Cavite
regions.teaser: Home of barako (Liberica). Lipa is where coffee was first planted, in the 1740s

regions.name: Ilocos Sur
regions.teaser: Robusta: its farmers took the top five Robusta places in the 2021 national competition

harvest.text: The general harvest runs from October to March.

grows.species: mostly Robusta, with Arabica, Liberica and Excelsa

cup.text: Davao baristas describe Mt Apo Arabica as bright, fruity and nutty, with lemon, cacao and nut notes, says the magkape coffee zine (2025). The winning Arabica in the 2021 Philippine Coffee Quality Competition, a natural Catimor from Bansalan at 1,560 m, scored 85.86 with peach, guava, chocolate, apricot and almond.
cup.prized: Mountain Arabica from Mt Apo and the Cordillera, and barako, which the Philippine Coffee Board calls a robust, powerful cup.
cup.watch: Scale and consistency: in 2020 farms averaged only about 0.54 t of dried cherry per hectare, and most farmers work 1–2 ha.

story.text: A Spanish Franciscan friar is said to plant the Philippines' first coffee tree at Lipa, Batangas. Barako (Liberica) came later: it reached Southeast Asia in the 1800s.
The Philippines becomes one of the world's biggest coffee exporters, shipping from Batangas and Cavite; PCAARRD ranks it fourth in 1880.
Coffee leaf rust, a fungal leaf disease, reaches the islands in 1889, and with pests and Brazil's oversupply the boom collapses in the 1890s.
Farms at the foot of Mt Apo take the top three Arabica places in the national Philippine Coffee Quality Competition.

sections.title: Barako
body: Barako is the Philippine name for Liberica, grown mainly in Batangas and Cavite. Its fragrance is often compared to aniseed, and many Filipino coffee drinkers prefer it to Arabica. Low production has put it on Slow Food's Ark of Taste, a catalogue of endangered heritage foods.

sections.title: About the numbers
body: Philippine figures vary by source and by unit. The 2022 industry roadmap counted about 60,600 t of dried cherry from about 113,000 ha in 2020; USDA counts green coffee in 60-kg bags. Either way, the country grows only about 15–30% of the coffee it drinks, depending on whose figures you use.

records.name: Papua New Guinea
records.summary: Highland smallholder coffee descended from Blue Mountain seed.
records.lede: Smallholders grow at least 85% of Papua New Guinea's coffee, most of them growing Arabica above 1,500 m (4,900 ft). The main regions are in the highlands, and most highland plants trace back to the 1930s Blue Mountain plantation at Wau, spread over many years from a station in the Aiyua Valley.

facts.label: 60-kg bags forecast for 2026/27 (980,000 in 2023/24)
grown by smallholders
where most smallholders grow Arabica (4,900 ft+)
first official record of coffee here

regions.name: Eastern Highlands
regions.teaser: Capital Goroka. Over many years, the Aiyua Valley station here spread Blue Mountain stock through the highlands

regions.name: Western Highlands
regions.teaser: A key region, around the provincial capital, Mount Hagen

regions.name: Jiwaka
regions.teaser: A key highland region on the importer Sucafina's list

regions.name: Morobe
regions.teaser: Home of Wau, where the colonial government planted Arabica in 1928, on the farm later named Blue Mountain Coffee

harvest.text: Main crop from May to September, with a small fly crop (a second, lighter picking) in January and February.

grows.species: Arabica, grown mostly by highland smallholders

story.text: A colonial government report gives the first official record of coffee.
The Variarata plantation, which had 20,000 Arabica trees by 1897, began exporting to Australia.
The colonial government planted Arabica at a Department of Agriculture station in Wau; its 1931 buyer, Carl Wilde, renamed it Blue Mountain Coffee.
Most highland plants today are genetically linked to the Blue Mountain plantation's trees of this decade, later spread across the highlands through the Aiyua Valley station.
Coffee land grew from 147 to 4,800 hectares.

sections.title: How it's processed
body: Many smallholders pulp their cherry with small drum pulpers or by hand, ferment it for about 36 hours, then wash off the mucilage (the sticky fruit layer left on the seed). The parchment is dried to about 10.5% moisture on raised beds or tarps, or in mechanical dryers, of which the Asaro dryer is the most popular. Some farmers sell cherry instead of parchment.

records.name: Puerto Rico
records.summary: Sixth-largest producer in 1896; now grows under a tenth of its coffee.
records.lede: In the 1800s Puerto Rico was one of the world's leading coffee origins, sixth-largest in 1896, says Coffee Review. Mountain towns such as Adjuntas, Yauco and Lares still grow it, about 32,000 quintales in 2024/25, but that was under 8% of what the island used; the rest was imported. Since Hurricane María in 2017, groups including World Coffee Research have set out to help rebuild the industry, while a shortage of pickers leaves coffee on the trees.

facts.label: grown in fiscal 2024/25 (Department of Agriculture)
of the coffee the island used in 2024/25 was grown there; about 389,000 quintales were imported
largest coffee producer in the world in 1896
pickers short, the Department of Agriculture estimated in 2021

regions.name: Yauco
regions.teaser: One of the oldest coffee areas, and home of Yauco Selecto, which Coffee Review in 1998 called often a splendid coffee

regions.name: Adjuntas
regions.teaser: Still the island's main coffee-producing town

regions.name: Jayuya
regions.teaser: Farms in the Jayuya valley sit at 1,100–1,200 m, and Jayuya Valley has its own origin seal

regions.name: Utuado
regions.teaser: The leading coffee area before 1898, and the island's third-largest producer in 2002

regions.name: Lares
regions.teaser: One of the main coffee municipalities, with Yauco, Adjuntas, San Sebastián and Las Marías

regions.name: Maricao
regions.teaser: With Indiera, among the oldest coffee areas; it boomed with coffee in the 1800s

harvest.text: Picked from August on the lower farms to January in the highest, says the University of Puerto Rico's extension service.

cup.text: Coffee Review says the best Puerto Rican lots show the Caribbean style: soft but powerful, with a fragrant, fruit-toned sweetness. Its tasters describe Caribbean coffees in general as full, rounded and balanced, with understated acidity.
cup.watch: Processing and drying faults. Many lesser lots have carried a faint mustiness, and in a 2010 tasting all three Puerto Rico samples had mild drying taints and scored 85–87.

story.text: Coffee is first planted in Puerto Rico.
Puerto Rico ranks sixth among the world's coffee producers.
The island passes from Spain to the United States; sugar cane becomes the focus and coffee declines.
The island's Agricultural Experiment Station releases Limaní, a rust-resistant variety selected from a Brazilian population.
Hurricane María hits; World Coffee Research, TechnoServe and others begin helping rebuild the industry.

sections.title: Right now
body: Farmers are paid a minimum of $18 an almud (a measure of about 28 pounds of coffee cherry), a price set in 2017. In August 2026 the Secretary of Agriculture backed a review, with proposals of $20 to $23. He says the island averages about 34,000 quintales but could pick about 100,000 if there were enough hands, because unpicked coffee falls to the ground and is lost.

sections.title: Where the rest comes from
body: Most coffee drunk on the island is imported, and much of the local crop is blended with it, the Secretary of Agriculture says. In 2023, 52% of the Dominican Republic's coffee exports went to Puerto Rico.

cup.text: Visit Rwanda, the national tourism board, describes a silky, creamy body with lemon, orange blossom and a caramel aftertaste, and Sweet Maria's often finds black tea and lemon in its Rwandan lots. Melbourne Coffee Merchants tastes floral, bright coffees in the north and jammy, syrupy ones in the south.
cup.watch: The potato taste defect, a raw-potato smell that swamps the cup, turns up in coffees from the Great Lakes, Rwanda's among them; it is linked to bacteria spread by the Antestia bug.

records.name: Saudi Arabia
records.summary: Terraced Jazan mountain farms growing Khawlani coffee for centuries.
records.lede: Saudi Arabia grows a small amount of Arabica on terraced farms in its southwestern mountains, mostly in Jazan Province. Khawlani tribes there have grown it for more than 300 years, and in 2022 UNESCO added their growing and processing know-how to its list of the world's intangible cultural heritage. The government is now investing to grow far more of it.

facts.label: where coffee suits the southern highlands (2,600–6,550 ft)
coffee trees in the southwest in 2022
of 43 Jazan farm samples graded specialty (80+ points) in an FAO study; top score 86
UNESCO lists Khawlani coffee know-how as intangible heritage

regions.name: Jazan
regions.teaser: The heart of it: about 1,985 of the country's 2,535 coffee farms (2022), in mountain districts such as Al-Dayer, Fayfa and Al-Aridah

regions.name: Asir
regions.teaser: The second-biggest area: about 300 farms (2022)

regions.name: Al Baha
regions.teaser: The third: about 250 farms (2022), plus a planned Coffee Development City for about 300,000 more trees

harvest.text: Picked mostly from October to January; FAO researchers found December 2021 to be the main picking season in Jazan. Trees flower from late March and the cherries take about six months to ripen. Saudipedia, by contrast, says picking usually begins in spring.

cup.text: Arabian Coffee Institute co-founder Almohanad Almarwai lists raisins, dates, dried fruit, dark chocolate, cardamom and cinnamon among Saudi coffee's flavor notes, and in a 2022 Jeddah cupping (the industry's standard tasting) of coffees from seven countries that he led, Saudi Khawlani stood out for dried fruit, dates, chocolate and caramel. The retailer Bateel describes its natural Jazan coffee as dark chocolate and caramel with a touch of grapefruit.
cup.watch: Water and old trees. Rain is unpredictable and steep slopes are hard to irrigate, old trees yield little and show defects, and in 2022 a single small mill served Jazan and was often swamped with unhulled coffee.

story.text: Khawlani tribes were growing coffee in these mountains: UNESCO and Saudipedia both put it at about 300 years or more, and some local accounts claim far longer.
After the government launched coffee festivals in Jazan, about half a dozen local landowners began growing coffee commercially.

The Year of Saudi Coffee: the Public Investment Fund launched the Saudi Coffee Company, planning $320 million over 10 years and 900,000 more Arabica trees, and UNESCO inscribed the Khawlani tradition.

sections.title: Growing it
body: Seeds are sown in soil-filled mesh bags and kept in shade for three to four months, then planted out on terraces that hold water and soil. Trees first fruit after two to three years. Cherries are picked by hand and dried, then hulled by rolling a stone cylinder over the dried fruit on a large flat stone, which frees the bean while limiting cracks.

sections.title: About the numbers
body: Published figures disagree widely. Saudipedia, a government-run encyclopedia, put output at about 2,400 t a year from 398,000 trees on 2,535 farms (2022). The same year, the Christian Science Monitor reported about 300 t from about 400,000 trees, and Perfect Daily Grind estimated about 300 t for 2020, with about 400,000 trees on 600 farms by the end of 2021 able to give about 800 t. Targets differ too: 2,500 t by 2032 in one report, about 5,000 t a year in another. Treat any single production number with care.

records.name: South Sudan
records.summary: A wild home of Arabica, and the source of Rume Sudan.
records.lede: South Sudan's Boma Plateau holds wild Arabica that a 2021 genetic study found distinct from Ethiopia's, confirming the country as one of the species' centers of origin. Seed collected there in 1941 is the likely ancestor of the Rume Sudan variety. Farmed coffee is a recent restart: washed Robusta from Yei became the country's first coffee export in 2015.

facts.label: where Boma's wild Arabica mostly grows (3,950–7,200 ft)
seed gathered at Rume, likely parent of Rume Sudan
wild Arabica here by IUCN criteria; Critically Endangered once climate change is counted
first coffee export: washed Robusta from Yei

regions.name: Boma Plateau
regions.teaser: Wild Arabica in the Rumit and Ngelecho forests of Upper Boma, Jonglei; villagers plant it too

regions.name: Yei
regions.teaser: Smallholder Robusta, washed at wet mills the farmers set up, and first sold by Nespresso in 2015

grows.species: Wild and village-grown Arabica on the Boma Plateau; farmed Robusta around Yei

story.text: Botanist A. Chevalier made the first record of Arabica on the Boma Plateau in 1929; J. G. Myers confirmed wild trees in its forests in 1938.
A. S. Thomas collected seed and sent it to East African research stations; it is the likely source of the Rume Sudan and Barbuk Sudan varieties.
A team including Kew's Aaron Davis and WCR founder Tim Schilling found wild Arabica again, in poor health; they collected only leaves, not seed.
Robusta from Yei, sold by Nespresso as Suluja ti South Sudan ("beginning of South Sudan" in Kakwa), became the country's first coffee export.
Genetic tests on the 2012 samples confirmed Boma as a center of origin for Arabica; fighting since 2013 has kept researchers from going back.

sections.title: Where Rume Sudan comes from
body: Rume is a spot on the Boma Plateau about 2–3 miles south of Barbuk, at about 1,250 m (4,100 ft), and it was already largely cleared for maize when Thomas visited in 1941. His seed went to breeding stations in Kenya and Tanganyika, and the CATIE genebank received Rume Sudan and Barbuk Sudan from Kenya in 1953.

In the 2021 tests, only one of the Rume Sudan samples from CATIE carried a genetic marker found only in South Sudan's wild coffee. The authors think it unlikely any Arabica still grows at Rume itself; the variety lives on at a few specialty farms, such as in Colombia.

sections.title: Under threat
body: The wild trees grow about 88 km from the nearest wild Arabica in Ethiopia. The region has lost forest for about 70 years, and the civil war that began in 2013 displaced up to 4 million people; in 2021 WCR warned that the few plants seen in 2012 may already be gone.

records.name: Sierra Leone
records.summary: Natural Robusta country, where wild stenophylla was found again in 2018.
records.lede: Sierra Leone grows mostly Robusta on small farms in the east and south, and most of it is dried whole in the cherry. Coffee was a bigger export than cocoa before the 1991–2002 civil war, when most farms were abandoned, and output has never recovered. The country is also home to stenophylla, a wild coffee once exported from Freetown, which Kew scientists found again in 2018.

facts.label: a year in the 1960s–80s
forecast for 2021/22, a third less than the year before (Index Mundi, 60 kg bags)
average coffee farm, per the ICO
of the world average price reaches farmers (2023 estimate)

regions.name: Eastern Province
regions.teaser: Kenema, Kailahun and Kono, where most of the coffee grows

regions.name: The south and other districts
regions.teaser: Bo, Pujehun and Moyamba, plus Koinadugu and Tonkolili; wild stenophylla survives in Moyamba's Kasewe Hills

harvest.text: Picked by hand from December to March and dried on patios. Cherries picked once the rains build in late March often can't dry down to the 10–12% moisture that export needs (PDG).

grows.species: Robusta, with pockets of Liberica and wild stenophylla

story.text: Stenophylla, known locally as Highland coffee, was exported from Freetown; French buyers reportedly rated it with top Arabica.
The British introduced Robusta, which became a bigger export than cocoa before the civil war.
Civil war; most coffee farms were abandoned, and most trees standing today were planted before it.
An EU-funded program pruned and fertilized abandoned farms, with some success, though volumes stayed low.
In December, Kew's Aaron Davis and NRI's Jeremy Haggar found wild stenophylla again: first a single plant, then a healthy population in a forest farther east.

sections.title: The lost coffee
body: Stenophylla grows wild in hot lowlands at about 400 m (1,300 ft) and tolerates more heat than Arabica. A sample from partners in Sierra Leone, cupped in London in 2020, scored 80.25, a specialty score on the Arabica scale, and seedlings were to be planted in Sierra Leone and on Réunion from 2021 to test it as a crop (CIRAD). It yields poorly, one reason it never became a world crop (Lahai et al., 2023).

sections.title: Selling it
body: Up to 80% of the crop is exported, Walid Bahsoon told PDG in 2023, and some goes unofficially across the borders to Liberia and Guinea. Coffee is not known for quality here, partly because of drying problems.

records.name: El Salvador
records.summary: Bourbon, Pacas and Pacamara from the land of volcanoes.
records.lede: El Salvador is Central America's smallest country, and its coffee grows in volcanic soil across six regions; the western Apaneca-Ilamatepec range alone gave 53% of the 2022–23 crop. Bourbon is the main variety, followed by two born here: Pacas, a natural Bourbon mutation, and Pacamara, a very large-beaned cross of Pacas and Maragogipe.

regions.name: Apaneca-Ilamatepec
regions.teaser: The western range, around the Santa Ana volcano. 53% of the 2022–23 crop, and the country's first denomination of origin, a protected origin name

regions.name: Santa Ana
regions.teaser: The largest and most historic coffee area, inside the Apaneca-Ilamatepec range. Pacas was found on a farm here in 1949

regions.name: El Bálsamo-Quezaltepec
regions.teaser: The central belt, taking in the San Salvador volcano. 26% of the 2022–23 crop

regions.name: Tecapa-Chinameca
regions.teaser: The third-largest range: 10% of the 2022–23 crop and 11% of producers

regions.name: Alotepeque-Metapán
regions.teaser: A high zone known for coffee of very high quality, says Coffee Hunter

regions.name: Chalatenango
regions.teaser: A microclimate suited to Pacamara. Cafe Imports has sold blended peaberry lots from its growers

harvest.text: Picked from about November to April (Coffee Hunter says October to March). New-crop coffee typically reaches importers from May to July.

cup.text: Coffee Review calls traditional Salvadoran coffee generally sweet, smooth and clean. Its Bourbon and Pacas lots tend toward quiet florals, stone fruit, berry and gentle citrus such as tangerine, sometimes with chocolate.
cup.why: Altitude: Coffee Review says Strictly High Grown lots, from above 1,200 m, may be brighter and fuller-bodied than High Grown ones.
cup.prized: Pacamara. Coffee Review finds all-Pacamara lots deep, savory-sweet and often floral, Coffee Hunter adds tropical fruit and a syrupy body, and the variety has scored 90 to 93.52 points in Cup of Excellence, a national competition for top lots.
cup.watch: Mónica Herrera of COAUSOLES, a Salvadoran cooperative, told Perfect Daily Grind that many producers are choosing lower-quality hybrids that need less financing.

story.text: Pacas, a dwarf mutation of Bourbon, is found on the Pacas family's farm in Santa Ana.
The Salvadoran Institute for Coffee Research begins the experiments that produce Pacamara.
Civil war disrupts the coffee industry; in the early 1970s the country had been among the world's top four or five producers.
A leaf-rust epidemic hits Central America, and Salvadoran production falls about 60% between the 2012–13 and 2013–14 crops.

sections.title: Right now
body: USDA forecasts 542,000 60-kg bags for 2026/27, down 7.5% from 586,000, mainly because of El Niño weather and structural problems such as ageing farms. Heavy rain in December 2025 had already knocked ripe cherries off the trees early. A large share of plantations are more than 25 years old, and the Instituto Salvadoreño del Café estimates the country needs about 30 million rust-resistant plants a year for a decade to renew them.

sections.title: The varieties
body: Bourbon is the backbone: Coffee Hunter puts it at about 60% of production, and Coffee Review says it was about 70% before the 2012–13 rust epidemic, counting a local selection called Tekisic. Pacas, a compact Bourbon mutation, makes up about 25% of the crop, says World Coffee Research.

Pacamara crosses Pacas with Maragogipe. It has very large beans and low yields, and like Pacas it is very susceptible to leaf rust, a fungal disease of the leaves. Coffee Review says 10–40% of its seedlings revert to one parent.

sections.title: On the bag
body: SHG, Strictly High Grown, means grown above 1,200 m (3,900 ft); HG, High Grown, means 900–1,200 m (3,000–3,900 ft); CS, Central Standard, is lower still. These are altitude grades, not a measure of quality or traceability.

records.name: Thailand
records.summary: Southern Robusta, plus northern hill Arabica rooted in opium replacement.
records.lede: Thailand grows two coffees. Robusta, most of the crop, comes from the southern provinces around Chumphon and has traditionally been grown for industrial coffee such as instant. Arabica grows in the northern highlands, where King Rama IX's Royal Project promoted it from the 1970s as a replacement for opium, and growers and university researchers there now experiment with processing, from carbonic maceration (fermenting whole cherries in a sealed, carbon-dioxide-rich tank) to low-temperature drying.

regions.name: Chumphon
regions.teaser: The south's Robusta heartland and the biggest coffee province: about 11,500 t a year

regions.name: Ranong
regions.teaser: The second-biggest producer, about 4,700 t a year, in the southern Robusta belt

regions.name: Chiang Rai
regions.teaser: Northern Arabica: Doi Chang, Doi Wawee and Doi Pang Khon, open hillsides that once grew opium. About 3,400 t a year

regions.name: Chiang Mai
regions.teaser: Northern Arabica; Thailand's organic coffee farming started here in 2011

regions.name: Nan
regions.teaser: Northern Arabica, about 3,800 t a year

regions.name: Tak
regions.teaser: Remote Karen villages such as Po Te Jo, whose coffee placed fifth in a national competition

harvest.text: Northern Arabica farmers traditionally picked in November, a cool, dry month, but rain now often runs into the harvest, and mold from wet harvests can cut prices by 30–70%.

grows.species: Robusta in the south, Arabica in the north

story.text: Through King Rama IX's Royal Project, Arabica becomes a livelihood for northern hill communities in place of opium.
Thailand begins exporting coffee.
Organic coffee farming begins in Chiang Mai, later spreading to Chiang Rai, Mae Hong Son, Lampang and Tak.
Doi Tung and Doi Chang coffee are registered in the EU as protected geographical indications (PGI), a protected origin name.
Low-temperature, low-humidity drying is first used, and a coffee dried this way wins first and third place at the 2019 Thai Specialty Coffee Awards.

cup.text: Sweet Maria's, which has cupped northern Arabica from Chiang Mai over the years, finds it generally mild, with good body and moderate to low acidity, and says quality has been improving. Coffee Review gave a Doi Chaang Arabica 92 points in 2014 for almond, cacao nib, sweet lime and honeysuckle-like florals with a gently crisp acidity; a darker 2013 Doi Chang roast showed cedar, raisin, dark chocolate and cardamom.
cup.prized: Process-led northern lots. Writing for the Böll Foundation, an adviser to northern growers says careful, science-based fermentation since 2016 has challenged the old belief that Catimor can't reach specialty grade.
cup.watch: Weather and pests at harvest. Mold from late rains and coffee borer beetle damage can slash what farmers are paid.

sections.title: About the numbers
body: Thai figures are patchy. USDA puts the whole crop at about 0.9 million 60-kg bags for 2026/27 and lists it only as Robusta, although the north grows Arabica. A 2021 Nation report gave yearly output for five provinces: Chumphon, the biggest, about 11,500 t, Ranong 4,700 t, Nan 3,800 t, Chiang Rai 3,400 t and Chiang Mai 2,300 t.

records.name: Timor-Leste
records.summary: Where the Timor Hybrid was found; coffee is the top non-oil export.
records.lede: Timor-Leste, the eastern half of the island of Timor, is where the Timor Hybrid appeared in the 1920s: a natural cross of Arabica and Robusta whose rust resistance went into Catimor and other modern varieties. Coffee is the country's most valuable export after oil, and a third of its people rely on it as their main income.

regions.name: Ermera
regions.teaser: Includes Letefoho, which supplies most of Sucafina's Timor coffee

regions.name: Aileu
regions.teaser: One of the key regions on the importer Sucafina's list

regions.name: Ainaro
regions.teaser: One of the key regions on the importer Sucafina's list

harvest.text: Picked from May to September.

grows.species: Mostly Arabica, with a little Robusta grown lower down

story.text: Coffee is believed to have first been grown on Timor in the 17th century.
Portugal won control of the island's eastern half; coffee already made up at least half the value of its exports.
The Timor Hybrid, a natural Arabica × Robusta cross, appeared on its own on the island; its Robusta genes made it resistant to leaf rust.
Portugal's coffee rust research center (CIFC) received Timor Hybrid seed and picked two highly rust-resistant plants for breeding; Timor Hybrid lines were later crossed with Caturra to make Catimor.
Timor-Leste became independent. Portugal had effectively abandoned the colony after its 1974 revolution, and Indonesia annexed it in 1976.

records.name: Taiwan
records.summary: Tiny, costly farms; Alishan Geshas now win Cup of Excellence.
records.lede: Taiwan grows a little over 1,000 t of coffee a year on about 1,200 ha, mostly on one-hectare family farms whose owners often roast and sell the coffee themselves. Labor is expensive, so the coffee is costly and nearly all of it is drunk at home. Since Taiwan's first Cup of Excellence in 2024, its best lots, mostly Geshas from Chiayi County, home of Alishan, have scored above 90 points.

regions.name: Alishan (Chiayi)
regions.teaser: Misty high slopes. Most of the 2025 Cup of Excellence winners, including the top three, came from Chiayi County

regions.name: Yunlin (Gukeng)
regions.teaser: Where coffee from Hawaiian seedlings was first planted under Japanese rule. Gukeng is known as Taiwan's coffee capital

regions.name: Nantou
regions.teaser: Mountain microclimates; a Nantou SL34 placed fourth in the 2025 Cup of Excellence

regions.name: Pingtung
regions.teaser: Forested mountains around Taiwu village, where growing has picked up in recent years

harvest.text: Picked from November to May.

cup.text: Cup of Excellence jurors in 2025 described an Alishan washed Gesha (90.84 points) with jasmine, black tea, peach, apricot and bergamot, and an Alishan honey Gesha with apricot, orange, jasmine and brown sugar. Coffee from Yunlin is often described as low in acidity with nut and citrus notes.
cup.why: Paradise Roasters, which buys from Alishan, credits its cool temperatures, mist and cloud cover with slowing ripening, which it links to sweetness and aroma.
cup.prized: Competition Geshas and SL34s: a natural-process Gesha (dried in the whole cherry) sold for US$500.50 a pound at Taiwan's first private auction, in 2021.
cup.watch: Price. High labor costs and tiny farms make Taiwanese coffee expensive, and one Taiwanese buyer estimates about 98% of it is drunk in Taiwan.

story.text: A British company brings the first few Arabica plants to Taiwan.
Under Japanese rule, a trial at what is now the Hengchun Tropical Botanical Garden shows Arabica suits Taiwan; coffee is grown as a luxury crop for Japan.
Higher prices revive interest, and the government imports rust-resistant varieties from Hawaii.
After the Jiji earthquake, a One Town, One Product policy helps make Gukeng, in Yunlin, Taiwan's coffee capital.
Taiwan hosts its first Cup of Excellence, and four coffees score over 90 points.

sections.title: Growing it
body: Most Taiwanese coffee is washed. Farmers at lower elevations use natural processing (drying the whole cherry) to build sweetness, and honey processing is spreading. SL34, from Kenya, has become popular for its yield and cup quality, and many farmers are planting it over older varieties.

records.name: Tanzania
records.summary: Bourbon-type Arabica from Kilimanjaro and the south, known for peaberry.
records.lede: Tanzania grows Arabica and Robusta in roughly equal amounts, by USDA's 2025/26 figures, and over 90% of it comes from smallholders. Its Arabica, mostly Bourbon-type trees, grows on Kilimanjaro and Mount Meru in the north and, now mostly, in the southern highlands around Mbeya and Mbinga. It is the origin most identified with peaberry, the round single bean.

facts.label: grown in 2025/26, USDA estimate (60 kg bags)
Robusta in 2025/26 (700,000 bags)
smallholders, who grow over 90% of it
Arabica altitude (3,300–8,200 ft)

regions.name: Kilimanjaro
regions.teaser: The north, on Mount Kilimanjaro's slopes; sold as Kilimanjaro or Moshi. Northern cups run brighter, sweeter and more intense

regions.name: Arusha and Ngorongoro
regions.teaser: Mount Meru and the Karatu–Ngorongoro area; with Kilimanjaro and Mbeya, home to most of the estates

regions.name: Mbeya and Mbozi
regions.teaser: The south-west. With Ruvuma, now an estimated 75–85% of the crop; by reputation softer, perhaps more floral

regions.name: Ruvuma (Mbinga)
regions.teaser: The south, usually sold as Mbinga or Ruvuma. Soft and floral by reputation, like Mbeya

regions.name: Kigoma
regions.teaser: Some very good Arabica grows near the town of Kigoma, though getting it out has been hard

harvest.text: Sources differ. Sucafina gives May to November in one place and July to December in another; a Starbucks origin sheet gives May to September in the north and July to September in the south. All agree on July to September.

grows.species: Arabica and Robusta, about half each (2025/26)

cup.text: Coffee Review compares the best Tanzanian coffee to Kenya's, usually less intense and more balanced, and almost always sweetly tart, with honey, orange-like citrus, cacao nib and dark fruit such as plum or black cherry.

feel.body: deep and rich; peaberry lots often lighter

cup.why: Coffee Review notes the trees are mostly Bourbon variations, and that the best lots come from central mills using Kenya-style washing: a second soak, then drying on raised tables.
cup.prized: Peaberry. Every origin has some, but Tanzania is the one most identified with the PB grade.
cup.watch: Supply has been uneven: Coffee Review notes a recent big drop in volume from hotter, drier weather, and says the auction never lifted quality the way Kenya's did. The potato taste defect shows up here less often than in Rwanda or Burundi, says World Coffee Research.

story.text: The Haya people reportedly brought coffee from Abyssinia (today's Ethiopia); their traditional coffee, amwani, was a Robusta.
The Kilimanjaro Native Cooperative Union was founded, Africa's earliest cooperative.
A Scott Labs officer toured Tanganyika, today's Tanzania, and took a drought-resistant coffee to Kenya; SL28 was selected from it in 1935.
A socialist government broke up the colonial estates, and in 1976 it banned cooperatives outright.
Reforms let private traders buy cherry from farmers and process it.

sections.title: Peaberry and grades
body: Tanzanian Arabica is graded AA (the largest, most uniform beans), then A and AB, while PB is the peaberry grade: the round seed that forms when a cherry grows one seed instead of the usual two. Peaberries are usually 3–30% of a farm's crop, and Coffee Review finds them often lighter-bodied and more delicate than flat beans.

sections.title: How it's sold
body: Coffee goes to auction or straight to buyers. The modern auction took shape in the 1980s, with roots in British colonial rule, and Moshi was long the north's only milling and sales hub. Exports leave through Dar es Salaam and Tanga.

records.name: Uganda
records.summary: Robusta's native home, with washed Arabica from Mount Elgon.
records.lede: Uganda is the native home of Robusta, and about 1.8 million households grow coffee there. In 2025/26 about 84% of its crop was Robusta. Its specialty Arabica comes mostly from Mount Elgon on the Kenyan border, sold as Bugisu, and from the Rwenzori Mountains on the Congo border.

facts.label: grown in 2025/26, USDA estimate (60 kg bags)
Robusta in 2025/26; the rest is Arabica
households grow coffee (World Coffee Research)
where its Arabica grows (4,250–7,550 ft)

regions.name: Mount Elgon (Bugisu)
regions.teaser: The east, on the Kenyan border. Most specialty Arabica, sold as Bugisu or Sipi Falls; typically washed, and organic farming is the norm

regions.name: Rwenzori Mountains
regions.teaser: The south-west, on the Congo border. Volcanic soil; naturals are most common, washed lots too

regions.name: West Nile
regions.teaser: The north-west. Usually washed, and known for citrus

regions.name: Central Uganda
regions.teaser: The Robusta heartland on the central plateau, where it once grew wild by Lake Victoria; now spreading north

harvest.text: Uganda straddles the equator, so picking runs most of the year. Sucafina puts the Arabica main crop north of the equator, where Mount Elgon is, in September and October, with a smaller second crop (the fly crop) from January to April. Perfect Daily Grind says Mount Elgon's lower farms pick June to December and higher ones July to February. Robusta's large crop in the south-west and west comes May to August.

cup.text: Coffee Review finds Bugisu coffee from Mount Elgon tends toward sweet, savory depth with dark chocolate and aromatic wood. Bugisu is also known for fruity, winey cups, and more often tastes sweet and citrusy with raisin and fig.

feel.acidity: low-toned in farm-processed lots, brighter in station-washed ones

cup.why: Processing makes a big difference: Coffee Review says coffee washed at central mills cups brighter and cleaner than coffee processed on the farm.
cup.prized: Sucafina says Bugisu is in high demand for its winey, fruity cups.
cup.watch: Farm-processed lots can taste rustic, with malty, musty or earthy notes (Coffee Review). The Great Lakes potato taste defect also turns up in Ugandan coffee, says World Coffee Research.

story.text: Robusta grew wild along Lake Victoria's northern shore, and the Baganda grew it in household gardens.
European and Asian settlers had set up the first Arabica plantations.
Exports peaked at around 3.5 million bags.
Coffee wilt disease killed nearly half the trees, and output fell as low as 2 million bags a year.
In May, World Coffee Research reports, Uganda passed Ethiopia as Africa's top coffee exporter, with exports worth over US$2 billion.

sections.title: Right now
body: USDA expects a 2026/27 crop of 7.16 million bags, up 0.9%, and exports of 6.83 million. The Uganda Coffee Development Authority has been folded into the agriculture ministry, which now runs regulation, extension and quality control, and officials plan a gradual move from exporting green coffee toward roasted and soluble coffee.
Uganda's own figures run higher than USDA's: the ministry counted 7.93 million bags exported in the year to August 2025, worth US$2.27 billion.

sections.title: Words on the bag
body: Home-processed naturals, cherry dried unsorted on the ground, are sold as Drugar (Dry Ugandan Arabica); Sucafina calls Wugar the semi-washed version of Drugar. The agriculture ministry's daily price sheet lists Arabica grades like Bugisu AA, Wugar and Drugar, and Robusta by bean size, such as Screen 18 (about 7.2 mm).

records.name: Venezuela
records.summary: Andean coffee beside Colombia, far smaller than a century ago.
records.lede: Venezuela once ranked close to Colombia in coffee, and in 1919 only Brazil exported more. Oil wealth, price controls from 2003 and the later economic crisis shrank the crop, and most of it is now drunk at home. The best-known coffees come from the Andes in the west: Táchira, Mérida and Trujillo.

regions.name: Táchira
regions.teaser: By the Colombian border. Coffee Review says its coffees resemble Colombia's: rich acidity, medium body, sometimes fruity. The Monte Claro variety was bred here

regions.name: Mérida
regions.teaser: Andean coffee with fair to good body and a mild, pleasant sweetness, says Coffee Review

regions.name: Trujillo
regions.teaser: The third Andean state whose coffee is traded as 'Maracaibo', after the port it ships through

regions.name: Caripe
regions.teaser: From the eastern mountains near the Caribbean, in Monagas. Coffee Review calls it soft and gentle, like the island coffees

harvest.text: Picked from September to January; it typically reaches buyers from May to October, says Cafe Imports.

grows.species: Arabica in the highlands, Robusta in the lowlands

cup.text: Coffee Review splits it by place: Táchira tends to resemble Colombian coffee, with rich acidity, medium body and sometimes fruit; Mérida is milder and gently sweet; Caripe, from the east, is soft and gentle like the Caribbean island coffees.
cup.prized: The top grade is Lavado Fino, 'fine washed'. In 2023 Reuters reported a Monte Claro scoring 90.11 to take first place among 186 samples at an expo in Caracas.

story.text: Coffee arrives; Cafe Imports credits Gervasio Rubio in Táchira, while other accounts name the Jesuit José Gumilla, in 1732.
Venezuela becomes the world's third-largest coffee exporter.
Exports reach 82,382 tonnes; only Brazil exports more.
Price limits meant to fight inflation make coffee hard to grow at a profit, and production falls sharply.
The first EICEV coffee expo and producer competition, and the country's first barista competition, are held.

sections.title: How big is the crop?
body: Estimates disagree. USDA's July 2026 report lists 500,000 bags of 60 kg for every year from 2021/22 to 2026/27, with no note explaining the unchanging figure. Reuters put 2022 output at about 383,000 bags.

Fedeagro, the farmers' federation, counts in quintales (sacks). It estimated 0.9–1 million for 2023/24 and 1.2 million for 2024/25, up from a low of about 350,000 in 2020, and forecasts 1.8 million for 2026/27; it says 1.4 million quintales would be more than a million bags. Official figures cited in 2024 were higher still: 3.6 million quintales for 2022.

sections.title: Monte Claro
body: Venezuela's agricultural research institute, INIA, spent about 40 years developing Monte Claro in Táchira: an Arabica variety that tolerates leaf rust, registered in 2013.

records.name: Vietnam
records.summary: The world's top Robusta supplier, from the Central Highlands.
records.lede: Vietnam is the world's second-biggest coffee producer and its top Robusta supplier. Nearly all of the crop is Robusta from the Central Highlands, much of it sun-dried as naturals on small family farms. A little Arabica grows around Đà Lạt and in the northwest.

Robusta (31.4M of 32.5M bags in 2026/27)

regions.name: Central Highlands
regions.teaser: Đắk Lắk, Gia Lai, Lâm Đồng, Đắk Nông and Kon Tum: the Robusta heartland, with 92% of the coffee land in 2021

regions.name: Đà Lạt and Cầu Đất
regions.teaser: Lâm Đồng province, where the French brought coffee to the mountains. Home to much of Vietnam's Arabica

regions.name: Sơn La and Điện Biên
regions.teaser: The northwest. Arabica, picked October to January; one Sơn La natural grew at 800–1,100 m (2,600–3,600 ft)

harvest.text: The season opens in early October. Sucafina gives November to January for the Central Highlands and October to January for the north. Some late-ripening Robusta types are picked in January or February, after the rains.

story.text: Coffee arrived with the French, and the first trees planted were Arabica.
Robusta and Excelsa arrived.
Buôn Ma Thuột, in Đắk Lắk, was chosen as the center for Robusta; by 1922 it was covered in plantations.
The Đổi Mới reforms opened the economy and allowed private land use, and coffee planting took off in the 1990s.

sections.title: Right now
body: Exports earned a record US$8.4 billion in the 2024–25 season, the national coffee association VICOFA reported. Farmers say fertilizer and fuel costs rose about 30% and labor 33% in a year, and about 30% of the coffee land has trees 20 years old or more that need replanting.

records.name: Yemen
records.summary: Terraced mountain naturals, grown for more than 500 years.
records.lede: Yemen has grown coffee on terraced, semi-arid mountainsides for more than 500 years, and its port of Mocha was once the world's main coffee market. Most of the crop is natural-processed: the cherry dries whole, often on village rooftops. Its trees include Yemenia, a genetic group found only in Yemen.

facts.label: of continuous commercial coffee growing, says Coffee Review

regions.name: Haraz
regions.teaser: Mountains west of Sana'a, also sold as Harazi or Haraaz. Steep terraces and stone villages

regions.name: Bani Matar
regions.teaser: A very high district just southwest of Sana'a; its coffee is sold as Matari

regions.name: Haymah
regions.teaser: West of Sana'a, just north of Bani Matar

regions.name: Bani Ismail
regions.teaser: North of Haraz. Ismaili is also a local name for a tree with small, round beans

regions.name: Dhamar
regions.teaser: Mountains south of Sana'a, sold as Dhamari or Anisi. Home of the Women Farmers of Dhamar group

regions.name: Sa'dah
regions.teaser: The far northwest, toward the Saudi border; recent conflict has disrupted growing here, says Coffee Review

harvest.text: Picked from October to December. Trees are usually picked about three times, the last pass stripping whatever is left, and the cherry then dries for about two weeks, often on rooftops because villages have no room for patios.

cup.text: Coffee Review's tasters often find dried fig, black cherry, clove and dark chocolate, with a winey acidity. Sweet Maria's describes flavors from candied fruit through wine to dark chocolate, and a wild, almost gamey note in the aftertaste.

feel.body: medium to full, often creamy or syrupy

cup.prized: Clean, sweet naturals. At Qima's 2020 blind cupping, one judge called the Yemenia coffees the cleanest and by far the sweetest natural he'd had in a long time.
cup.watch: Small, irregular beans with the physical defects typical of Yemen, partly because the dried husk is traditionally knocked off with a millstone.

story.text: Sufi communities are said to have begun growing coffee in Yemen's highlands.
Legend says the saint Baba Budan carried seven seeds from Mocha to India, starting coffee there.
Qima Coffee and researcher Christophe Montagnon announced Yemenia, a genetic group of Arabica found only in Yemen.
A survey of 148 farms found that local tree names don't match genetics; where a tree grew predicted its group far better.

sections.title: Names on the bag
body: Most Yemeni bags name a place. Matari means Bani Matar, Harazi means Haraz, and Ismaili can mean Bani Ismail. Sanani usually means a blend from several areas west of Sana'a.

Bags may also name a local tree type, such as Udaini, Dawairi, Tufahi or Jaadi. A 2022 study of 148 farms found these names had no real link to genetics: Udaini, the most common name, turned up in all three genetic groups.

sections.title: Getting it out
body: War has made moving coffee hard. In 2020 one roaster described many checkpoints on the road, some charging fees, and long delays shipping from Aden. The same year, World Coffee Research warned that Yemen's coffee production faced possible collapse from war and economic stagnation.

records.name: Zambia
records.summary: Estate-grown washed Arabica from the far north.
records.lede: Zambia grows only Arabica, nearly all of it in the north along the Muchinga escarpment, and most of it on a handful of large estates rather than small farms. Exports peaked in the mid-2000s, collapsed, and have been climbing back. The coffee is mostly washed, and buyers describe clean cups with sweet, often citrusy acidity.

facts.label: the one species Zambia's Coffee Act allows for commercial growing
of the crop grown on estates, says the growers' association chair (2021)
exports at the 2004/05 peak, then in 2015
where most coffee grows (4,250–5,250 ft)

regions.name: The north
regions.teaser: Kasama, Mbala, Nakonde and Isoka along the Muchinga escarpment: nearly all the crop, and the big Kasama estates

regions.name: Lusaka and the south
regions.teaser: A few estates near Lusaka, Serenje and Mazabuka

harvest.text: Picked from May to August (PDG) or into September (Algrano), in the long dry season, which makes sun-drying easier.

cup.text: The African Fine Coffees Association calls Zambian coffee full-bodied with sweet, mild acidity, and importer Covoya describes its lots as mostly citrus with berry and melon. Algrano hears clean, balanced washed cups that range from citrus and fruit to chocolate and caramel.
cup.prized: Pulped naturals (skin removed, the sticky fruit layer left on to dry) add sweetness to the acidity and tend to be the best Zambian coffee, says ZCGA chair Teija Lublinkhof; a few experimental SL28 micro-lots have scored as high as 89.
cup.watch: Zambia has no flavor identity buyers recognize, the way they do Kenya's or Ethiopia's, says Algrano.

story.text: Settler farmers were already growing coffee around Mbala.
The World Bank funded coffee projects, the Kasama estates among them, to move the economy beyond copper.
Zambia began exporting coffee commercially.
Exports peaked at 6,654 tonnes; after funding dried up and a 2005/06 drought, many smallholders pulled out their trees and exports fell to 180 tonnes by 2015.
Olam bought the assets of the Kasama Coffee Company, in receivership since 2008, and renamed it Northern Coffee Corporation.

sections.title: Estates and outgrowers
body: Olam's Northern Coffee Corporation runs five estates (Kateshi, Ngoli, Luombe, Isanya and Nsunzu) in Kasama, Mbala and Mungwi districts, with about 2,171 ha under coffee, and buys from more than 3,000 small outgrowers (ZANIS, 2022). PDG put its share of exportable coffee at about 97% in 2021.
Exports recovered to almost 2,000 tonnes in 2019. Zambia is landlocked, so northern coffee travels overland to Dar es Salaam in Tanzania to be shipped.

records.name: Zimbabwe
records.summary: Eastern Highlands Arabica, slowly rebuilding after the farm seizures.
records.lede: Zimbabwe grows Arabica in the Eastern Highlands along the Mozambique border, mainly in Manicaland's Chipinge, Chimanimani and Mutasa districts. In the early 1990s it produced more than 15,000 tonnes a year; after farm seizures began in 2000, output fell to a few hundred tonnes, and smallholders are now slowly bringing it back.

facts.label: a year in the early 1990s, from more than 20,000 farmers
a year by 2023, from two estates and about 450 small farms
of the crop lost by the early 2000s
Honde Valley to Chipinge (2,800–4,500 ft)

regions.name: Chipinge
regions.teaser: Most of the crop and the most suitable land; Catimor is popular here for rust resistance and yield

regions.name: Chimanimani
regions.teaser: Second to Chipinge in land suited to Arabica

regions.name: Honde Valley
regions.teaser: Rain all year, tea and coffee estates, and the base of Nespresso's revival program

regions.name: Mutare and the Vumba
regions.teaser: Mutare district, Vumba Mountains included; the smallest suitable area of the three

harvest.text: PDG gives May to September and Sweet Maria's June to November; both cover June to September. Most rain falls from November to March.

cup.text: Sweet Maria's calls Zimbabwe a balanced "drinking coffee" with body, chocolate-like flavors and moderate acidity, and finds Chipinge lots aromatic and slightly spicy. PDG adds bright, berry-like or citric acidity, with chocolate and wine notes.
cup.prized: At its best, says Sweet Maria's, fine acidity set against complex roasty, almost savory notes.
cup.watch: Some lots have tasted wild or unclean, or earthy and a little leathery, says Sweet Maria's.

story.text: Travellers brought coffee in, but plant disease destroyed most of the small plantations in the 1920s.
After a resurgence from 1958, a commercial industry took hold.
More than 20,000 farmers grew over 15,000 tonnes a year.
Forced evictions of commercial farmers began; with low prices and bad weather, about 97% of the crop was lost.
Nespresso and the NGO TechnoServe began training Honde Valley smallholders, and Nespresso pays them premium prices.

sections.title: Rebuilding
body: In 2023 the Nespresso program paid about $8 a kilo, close to double what local buyers paid, to some 450 Honde Valley smallholders. A 2018 government plan aimed for 10,000 tonnes by 2024; in 2023 the head of the Coffee Research Institute in Chipinge said it was still too early to tell whether that would be met.
On bags, Zimbabwe's top AA grade is often marked "Code 53", says Sweet Maria's.

records.name: Anaerobic

cup.common: Turned-up fruit, often tropical, with a winey or tangy, yogurt-like edge and a fuller, sweeter feel.
cup.text: Reviewers report intensity above all: a fuller mouthfeel, often more sweetness, fruit like passion fruit and mango, and a tangy, lactic note like yogurt or fresh cheese. Anaerobic washed lots came out leaner and brighter than anaerobic naturals.
cup.why: With air shut out, yeasts, which tend to make fruity, boozy notes, are partly held back, lactic acid bacteria do more of the work, and everything slows down, so ferments run for days. The longer the coffee stays sealed, the stronger the effect, though variety, ripeness and drying still shape the cup.
cup.prized: Intensity, sweetness and a full mouthfeel with the fruit still clean. In one review site's 2021 tasting of 43 anaerobic coffees, 19 scored 93 or higher.
cup.watch: A runaway ferment tastes sharp, vinegary, solvent-like or savory; a big temperature rise in the tank is the warning sign. Even when it works, too much intensity can hide the coffee's own character, one roaster warns.

byCoffee.text: In Coffee Review's 2021 tasting, anaerobic natural Wush Wush lots were silky and floral with a yogurt-like lactic tang, some with a savory or cedar-like edge.

Producers here took up sealed tanks in the late 2010s. In the same tasting, a Castillo given a sealed phase went tart and tropical (passion fruit, mango), and an anaerobic natural Pink Bourbon was light and tropical (lychee, jasmine).
Mills ferment sealed for several days, aiming at the fruit-forward style buyers in North America and Europe want; one 2019 Costa Rican anaerobic tasted of raw chocolate and cinnamon.
In a trial on Conilon (a Brazilian Robusta type), five days sealed with a chosen yeast raised the cup score by more than 3 points.

steps.title: Seal it in
steps.text: Whole cherries or pulped coffee go into tanks or bags; valves let carbon dioxide out without letting air back in.

steps.title: Ferment sealed
steps.text: Microbes use up the oxygen and work slowly. Some producers track sugar (Brix), pH or temperature and stop at a set point; there's no single recipe.
steps.hours: about 1–6 days; about 96 h at one Costa Rican farm

steps.title: Finish and dry
steps.text: It's then dried as a natural, honey or washed coffee.

records.layers: Depends on the base method: the whole cherry for anaerobic naturals, mucilage and parchment for anaerobic honeys, and parchment only once an anaerobic washed coffee is washed.

story.text: Saša Šestić won the World Barista Championship with a Colombian coffee described as carbonic macerated, drawing wide attention to sealed-tank ferments.
A Costa Rican anaerobic won bronze at the Golden Bean North America competition, and Coffee Review's editor wrote that, judged by standards of ten years earlier, many such coffees might seem flawed.
In Coffee Review's tasting of 43 anaerobic coffees, 19 scored 93 or higher.
Coffee Review's new Kenneth Davids Cup barred anaerobic coffees from its Traditional Washed category.

records.name: Carbonic maceration

cup.common: Big, juicy fruit and intense sweetness, with a syrupy texture and wine-like acidity, roasters say.
cup.text: Roasters describe explosive fruit, a syrupy texture, intense sweetness and wine-like acidity. In one review site's tasting, carbonic lots were more restrained: bright and layered, with only a soft hint of fruity funk.
cup.why: Added carbon dioxide pushes out more oxygen than a plain sealed tank, and with the cherries left whole, one roaster says the fruit breaks down from the inside out. The method comes from Beaujolais winemaking; we found no controlled study of how closely coffee follows the wine version.
cup.prized: Big, clean fruit and sweetness. A carbonic Sudan Rume from Colombia won the 2015 World Barista Championship.
cup.watch: Pushed too far, it becomes overwhelming or unstable. Labels are loose too: one roaster says the 2015 winner was depulped first, unlike wine's whole-fruit method.

byCoffee.text: The 2015 world title came with a carbonic Sudan Rume from Colombia. In a 2021 tasting, a carbonic lot from Nariño showed quiet chocolate, citrus and flowers with only a soft hint of fruity funk.
In the same tasting, a Colombian Gesha fermented under pressurized CO2 and dried in the whole fruit stayed bright, layered and complex, with a very subtle funk.
One roaster's carbonic Kenyan, sealed with added CO2 and then slow-dried 25–35 days in thick layers, showed blackberry, lime-like acidity and hibiscus rather than herbal or savory notes.

steps.title: Load whole cherries
steps.text: Ripe cherries, usually whole, go into a sealed tank.

steps.title: Flush with CO2
steps.text: Carbon dioxide is added to push the oxygen out, and temperature and yeast activity are watched as it ferments.
steps.hours: days; sealed ferments generally run about 1–6

steps.title: Dry slowly
steps.text: The cherries usually dry whole, in thick layers in one example; times vary.

records.layers: Usually everything: whole cherries (skin, fruit flesh, mucilage and parchment) go through the CO2 tank and dry that way. Some versions depulp first.

story.text: Fermenting whole fruit in CO2-filled tanks became a staple of Beaujolais winemaking for Gamay grapes.
Specialty coffee producers began experimenting with sealed tanks and controlled fermentation.
Saša Šestić won the World Barista Championship with a carbonic-macerated Sudan Rume from Colombia.
Producers in Colombia, Costa Rica and elsewhere took up sealed tanks and extended ferments.

records.name: Co-fermented

cup.common: The cup can taste noticeably of what went in, such as pineapple or ginger, on top of the coffee.
cup.text: It can taste clearly of the addition: a coffee co-fermented with pineapple would taste noticeably of pineapple, says one trade article, and one Colombian Gesha made with mossto and hops tasted of fresh ginger, lime and hops, says an importer.
cup.why: Part of the flavor comes from the added ingredient itself, though one project's data suggest only about 3% of the added fruit ends up in the cup. Some additions mostly steer the ferment instead: mossto (juice and microbes from an earlier batch) is used to speed it up and control it, and cinnamon is sometimes added to regulate its pace more than for flavor.
cup.prized: Results that still taste distinctly like coffee, with its own flavors turned up. At best they score very high: Coffee Review named a Kona coffee fermented with oranges its top coffee of 2024, at 98 points.
cup.watch: Critics call it adulteration that masks the coffee and can taste synthetic, and artificially flavored imitations tend to taste one-dimensional. In the US, labels don't have to list what went in, which matters for allergies.

byCoffee.text: In Quindío, one producer's lots use mossto, hops, ginger or chili, and an importer says they taste of the additions while still tasting like coffee.
Hula Daddy's Orange Kahiko, fermented in the whole fruit with oranges grown on the same farm, was Coffee Review's top coffee of 2024 at 98.
Best of Panama excluded infused coffees in 2024 and disqualified four lots it said were altered with additives, citing the need to protect Panama coffee's identity.

steps.title: Add the extras
steps.text: Fruit, spices, hops or mossto go in with the coffee pulp or whole fruit.

steps.title: Ferment together
steps.text: They ferment along with the coffee, sometimes sealed away from air, as in one Colombian chili-and-mossto lot.

steps.title: Finish before green
steps.text: Everything has to go in before the coffee is dry-milled into green beans; adding anything later is barred at the World Barista Championship.

records.layers: Depends on the base method: the additions go in with pulped coffee or with whole fruit.

story.text: Rumors of an 'infusion' method began to circulate in specialty coffee.
The SCA changed World Barista Championship rules to allow additives as long as they go in before the green-coffee stage.
Best of Panama excluded infused coffees, while Coffee Review named an orange co-fermented Kona its top coffee of the year.
Coffee Review's new Kenneth Davids Cup allowed co-ferments only in its Experimental category and barred infused and flavored coffees.

records.name: Cold fermentation
records.summary: A ferment kept cool to slow it down and stretch it out.
records.lede: The coffee ferments in chilled or temperature-controlled tanks, so the microbes work more slowly and the ferment can run longer before it goes wrong. Coffee Review described a Colombian Gesha whose whole cherries spent three days in refrigerated tanks. There's no agreed temperature or recipe; it's a choice producers make inside other methods.

facts.label: a Colombian Gesha's refrigerated whole-cherry ferment
how long one agronomist says he can ferment below 20 °C (68 °F)
a Panama estate's tank target (59–68 °F)
one champion's range for complex acidity (39–46 °F)

steps.title: Chill the tank
steps.text: Whole cherries or pulped coffee go into refrigerated or temperature-controlled tanks.

steps.title: Ferment slowly
steps.text: Kept cool, the ferment runs longer than it would in a warm open tank.

steps.title: Keep it even
steps.text: Producers hold the temperature steady, since uneven temperature inside a tank can cause off-flavors.

records.layers: Whatever the base method leaves on: the whole fruit when cherries are chilled whole, or just the sticky mucilage on the parchment when the coffee is pulped first.

cup.common: Producers and reviewers link it to cleaner, sweeter cups with more complex acidity, but the evidence is a handful of farm trials and tastings.
cup.text: Coffee Review found that three refrigerated days brought out the deeply sweet yet brisk, savory side of a Colombian Gesha. A Panamanian estate says its 15–20 °C tanks give a sweeter lactic ferment and a cleaner washed coffee.
cup.why: Temperature sets the speed of fermentation. In one champion barista's trials, a 24-hour dry ferment at 16 °C (61 °F) tasted balanced while 26 °C (79 °F) gave an alcoholic acidity, and another producer says lower temperatures hold back fungi that can cause unwanted flavors.
cup.prized: A slower, steadier ferment that can be stopped at the right moment instead of racing ahead in warm weather.
cup.watch: It takes chilled or adapted tanks (one Panama estate brought in beer tanks), and the taste claims come from producers' own trials; a champion barista who recommended cold ferments for acidity said in 2017 that coffee had little fermentation research.

byCoffee.text: In Coffee Review's tasting, three days of refrigerated whole-cherry fermentation emphasized the sweet, brisk and savory side of a Colombian Gesha from Finca Monteblanco.
Carmen Estate says holding its tanks at 15–20 °C gives cleaner washed coffees with more sweetness and complexity.

spectrum.label: Alcoholic acidity if it runs warm

story.text: Saša Šestić told Perfect Daily Grind that fermenting at 4–8 °C favors complex acidity and 18–20 °C favors sweetness.
Coffee Review rated the Old Soul Co. Colombia Monteblanco Gesha Cold Fermentation, from producer Rodrigo Sánchez, 93 points.
Carmen Estate in Panama adapted beer tanks to hold its ferments at 15–20 °C.

records.name: Extended fermentation

cup.common: A stronger version of whatever the ferment brings: more pronounced fruit, tang or funk than the same coffee fermented briefly.
cup.text: It doesn't add one particular flavor. In sealed tanks, one review site notes, the longer the coffee stays in, the stronger the effect; a Colombian Gesha chilled for three days came across deeply sweet, brisk and savory.
cup.why: Microbes keep turning the fruit's sugars and acids into other acids, alcohol and aroma compounds for as long as they have fuel and moisture, so more time means more of what they make. Sealing or chilling the tank slows them down, which is what lets a ferment run for days.
cup.prized: More sweetness and depth with the coffee still clean; one leading Colombian lactic producer says its best lots ferment past 80 hours.
cup.watch: Pushed too far it turns vinegary or overwhelming, and too much intensity can mask the coffee's own character.

byCoffee.text: Kenyan mills already ferment long by washed standards (overnight, then up to 36 more hours) before a 12–48 hour soak. The soak holds the coffee safely until drying space opens and may make batches more consistent.
A Colombian Gesha (Monteblanco) fermented whole for three days in refrigerated tanks scored 93 with Coffee Review in 2019, which found it deeply sweet, brisk and savory.
One slow-dried natural from Elida Estate, six days sealed and 60 days on the patio, showed lots of chocolate, a huge mouthfeel and a tart, lactic acidity reviewers likened to fresh goat cheese.

spectrum.label: Ferment that drowns out the coffee

steps.title: Slow it down
steps.text: Sealing out air or chilling the tank slows the microbes so the ferment can run longer.

steps.title: Ferment for days
steps.text: The ferment runs well past the usual 12–72 hours of a washed coffee; there's no standard length.
steps.hours: examples: about 72 h chilled, 80+ h lactic, 96 h sealed, up to about 6 days

steps.title: Stop and dry
steps.text: The producer ends it, sometimes when the sugar level (Brix) falls to a target, then washes or dries the coffee.
