records.layers: Depends on the base method it's added to: the whole cherry, the mucilage and parchment, or parchment only.

story.text: A Colombian Gesha fermented whole for three days in refrigerated tanks scored 93 with Coffee Review.
La Palma y El Tucán, a leading Colombian lactic producer, reported its best results from ferments beyond 80 hours.
Coffee Review's new Kenneth Davids Cup kept extended or deliberately flavor-changing ferments out of its Traditional Washed category.

records.name: Fermented
records.summary: Microbes eating the fruit's sugars, from picking until it dries.
records.lede: Fermentation is microbes, mostly yeasts and bacteria, breaking the coffee fruit's sugars down into acids and alcohols. It starts soon after picking and happens in washed, honey and natural coffees alike, so the word “fermented” on its own doesn't say what the producer did. Producers steer it with time, temperature, oxygen and sometimes added microbes, and that's where most new process names come from.

facts.label: typical tank ferment for a washed coffee
sealed ferments in experimental lots
where one Brazilian farm stops its ferments
that fermentation has raised, or lowered, a coffee's score in one champion's work

steps.title: Pick the fruit
steps.text: Fermentation begins once the cherry is picked, because the fruit holds both sugar and water for microbes to use.

steps.title: Ferment in tank or fruit
steps.text: In a washed coffee the pulped seeds ferment in tanks; in a natural the whole fruit ferments during the first days of drying.
steps.hours: 12–72 h in tanks · first days of drying

steps.title: Watch and stop it
steps.text: Careful producers track temperature, pH (acidity) and Brix (sugar) and end the ferment when it reaches their target.

steps.title: Dry it down
steps.text: Drying continues until the beans are down to about 11–12% moisture.

records.layers: Depends on the base method: in a washed coffee only the sticky mucilage on the parchment ferments; in a natural the whole fruit ferments around the seed while it dries.

cup.common: In traditional washed coffee its effect on taste was long ignored; in today's experimental lots reviewers often find extra sweetness and fruit, with a sour, yogurt- or sour-beer-like edge.
cup.text: A well-run ferment can lift sweetness, acidity and body and add fruit, caramel or chocolate notes, says one Brazilian farm. One long-running review site finds experimental ferments usually sweet but often sour, like plain yogurt or sour beer.
cup.why: Yeasts such as Saccharomyces cerevisiae and bacteria such as Lactobacillus turn the fruit's sugars into acids, alcohols and aroma compounds, and some of these show up in the green beans. Temperature sets how fast it all happens.
cup.prized: Control: a ferment that's tracked and stopped on time. One producer warns that good fermentation draws out what the coffee already has, but can't add quality that wasn't grown in the field.
cup.watch: Gone too far, it tastes of vinegar, rotten fruit, sour milk or wine gone bad, and over-fermented beans can look reddish and smell of rotting fruit. It can also leave black or “stinker” beans, and one study found that stopping a ferment at a lower pH went with lower cupping scores. One champion barista says fermentation has raised, and also lowered, a coffee's score by as much as eight cupping points (cupping is the industry's standard tasting).

story.text: Saša Šestić won the World Barista Championship with a carbonic-macerated Sudan Rume, a coffee fermented in tanks flushed with carbon dioxide.
Šestić told Perfect Daily Grind that most processing inconsistencies come from fermentation, and that the coffee industry had done little research on it.
Coffee Review's editor wrote that, judged by the standards of ten years earlier, many of the new fermented coffees might seem flawed.
A trade article noted there were still no industry standards for naming processing methods and little agreement on what the names mean.

sections.title: On the bag
body: “Fermented” alone is vague. Words like “anoxic” or “acetic” have appeared on bags as producers look for new ways to shape flavor and raise cup scores, and one roaster, the head of WatchHouse, argues that printing exact hours and temperatures only adds to the confusion.

sections.title: How producers steer it
body: Temperature and time are the big two: one agronomist says that below 20 °C (68 °F) he can let a ferment run up to 36 hours, while at higher temperatures problems can show up in the cup after 24. Others seal the tank to cut oxygen or add a chosen yeast or bacterium.

records.name: Honey

cup.common: More sweetness and body than washed, with rounder acidity, but less fruit and ferment than a natural.
cup.text: One long-running review site found honeys rounder in acidity than washed coffees, with less citrus and more chocolate and sweetness. An importer adds caramel, nutty and sometimes jammy, stewed-fruit notes.
cup.why: The mucilage stays on while the beans dry, so microbes keep fermenting it until the seed is down to about 11% moisture; in lab tests, pulped naturals' sugar levels fall between washed and natural beans. Drying matters too: one veteran reviewer suspects most of the differences between the honey lots he tasted came from how they were dried.
cup.prized: Sweetness and a syrupy body with more clarity than a natural: well-made honeys taste less powerful than naturals but clearer and more defined.
cup.watch: The sticky beans can mold or spoil if they aren't turned often, and drying too slowly invites over-fermentation. The green beans often look uneven, which puts some roasters off.

byCoffee.text: Honey is usually said to have started here. Small private micro-mills (over 150 since 2000) have led the country's processing experiments, and strict wastewater rules make full washing costly. Mills use the color names differently.
Brazil's pulped natural keeps nearly all the fruit flesh on; one roaster describes it as nutty and chocolatey with low acidity.
Like natural, honey tends to add fruit, sweetness and ferment to Gesha, where washing leans floral and citrus, one roaster says.

steps.title: Pulp off the skin
steps.text: The skin and fruit flesh come off, leaving some or all of the sticky mucilage on the parchment.

steps.title: Choose how much stays
steps.text: Some mills scrub part of the mucilage off by machine; others leave it all on and change the drying to get the different colors.

steps.title: Dry, turning often
steps.text: The sticky beans are raked several times an hour at first, then turned daily, and keep fermenting until about 11% moisture. Darker honeys dry longer; times vary by mill and weather.
steps.hours: about 1–3 weeks: one roaster lists 6–8 days for white honey up to 15–20+ for black; one importer says 18–25 days on average

records.layers: Mucilage (some or all of it) and parchment. The skin and fruit flesh are removed before drying.

story.text: Limited commercial volumes of honey-processed coffee first appeared, according to a Brazil-based exporter; one roaster dates Brazil's related pulped natural to the 1970s.
Costa Rica's micro-mill wave began with La Candelilla; more than 150 small mills followed.
An earthquake damaged Costa Rica's water infrastructure; one roaster says modern honey is often traced to it and credits the Chacón family's Las Lajas mill.
Coffee Review still called honey relatively new, tasting lots from El Salvador, Costa Rica and Nicaragua.

records.name: Kenyan double ferment
records.summary: Ferment, wash, then soak under clean water before drying.
records.lede: Kenya's factories (its washing stations) pulp the cherries, ferment the sticky coffee in tanks, wash it down channels, and then hold the clean parchment under fresh water before it goes onto raised drying beds. The whole ferment-and-wash cycle can run past 72 hours. It's credited with Kenya's very clean, bright cups, though a Cafe Imports researcher quoted in Barista Magazine thinks the country's varieties likely contribute significantly.

facts.label: the second ferment in lower tanks, after a night in the first tank
the soak in clean water
how long the whole ferment-and-wash cycle can run
drying on raised beds

steps.title: Sort, pulp and grade
steps.text: Cherries are sorted for unripe or insect-bitten fruit, pulped, and the parchment is graded into separate tanks.

steps.title: Ferment in tanks
steps.text: The pulped coffee ferments overnight and often longer, sometimes in two stages with a stir or a move between tanks.

steps.title: Wash in channels
steps.text: The coffee is pushed down a channel, which scrubs off the last of the sticky fruit.

steps.title: Soak under clean water
steps.text: The clean parchment sits under fresh water, changed so that little or no fermentation happens, and stays longer when the drying beds are full.

steps.title: Dry on raised beds
steps.text: It then dries on raised beds to about 11.5–12% moisture.

records.layers: Only the parchment: skin and fruit come off at the pulper, and the sticky mucilage is fermented and washed away before the soak.

cup.common: A bright, very clean cup with citrus and blackcurrant-like acidity.
cup.text: Sweet Maria's calls Kenya one of the brightest, cleanest cups in the world, with citrus, blackcurrant and berry acidity balanced by syrupy, sometimes wine-like sweetness. Another importer adds grapefruit-like citrus and occasional savory, tomato-like notes, and one grinder maker's guide mentions black tea and florals.
cup.why: Nobody has pinned it down. A Cafe Imports researcher suggests the soak might even out temperature and microbes, trigger reactions in the still-living seed or leach compounds out of it, but presents these only as possibilities. One roaster claims the soak builds amino acids behind the citrus acidity; we found no study testing that.
cup.prized: Cleanliness and consistency. The many handling steps also give extra chances to find and remove defects.
cup.watch: The soak is partly a way to store wet coffee in busy weeks, so its length depends on bed space, and copying the method elsewhere won't necessarily make a coffee taste Kenyan.

byCoffee.text: Bright, clean citrus-and-blackcurrant cups, though a Cafe Imports researcher quoted in Barista Magazine thinks Kenya's varieties likely contribute significantly to that profile.

It's hard to predict how the Kenyan process would taste on other coffees, says Cafe Imports' Taya Brown; in Guatemala, a whole-cherry pre-ferment followed by a normal tank ferment could also be called “double fermented”, though it's a different process.

sections.title: Why the soak
body: It helps when the drying beds are full: washed parchment can wait under water, kept cool and away from insects, until there's space. It adds another point to pick out defects, and may make batches more consistent.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Bags may say “double fermentation”, “Kenyan process” or “double washed”. A Cafe Imports researcher quoted in Barista Magazine calls “double fermentation” a bit misleading, since the second wet step is mostly a soak, and the term can mean different processes.

records.name: Koji
records.summary: Cherries dusted with the mold behind sake and miso.
records.lede: Koji is Aspergillus oryzae, a mold used for centuries in Asian food and drink; in Japan it's used to make sake and miso. Producers spread its spores on coffee cherries, and its enzymes break starches down into sugars that later fermentation can use. Only a handful of farms do it, and the results so far are the developers' own tastings.

facts.label: spores per kilo of cherries
price of spores, in 2022
score gain one producer claims
a koji coffee at the World Barista Championship

steps.title: Prepare the starter
steps.text: Producers use bought spores, or a cheaper “rice koji”: part-steamed rice inoculated with spores and then ground up.

steps.title: Dust the cherries
steps.text: About 2 grams of spores go onto each kilo of cherries; early trials on green coffee instead gave strong umami flavors most drinkers disliked.

steps.title: Grow it in the shade
steps.text: The cherries are spread in a shaded area while the mold grows, with close attention to time and temperature.

steps.title: Ferment and dry
steps.text: The coffee then carries on through its process; El Vergel's first trial was a koji natural set against a plain natural of the same Red Bourbon.

records.layers: The whole cherry: in the trials described, spores went onto the fruit, which was then processed as a natural.

cup.common: More body and a creamier, rounder mouthfeel than the same coffee without koji, say the people who developed it.
cup.text: In a blind comparison run in Japan, the US, the Netherlands and Finland, the koji sample scored higher, with more body, a longer aftertaste and more refined acidity, according to one of its developers. El Vergel's head of processing says the main change is body: soft becomes creamy and well rounded.
cup.why: Koji's enzymes break big starches into sugars that microbes can ferment, and it makes amino acids and glutamates (the savory, umami kind); one developer says it also produces esters and aldehydes that boost fruity aromas. El Vergel thinks it enhances what's already there more than it creates new flavors.
cup.prized: Extra body and aftertaste, and perhaps a point or two on a coffee that's already good.
cup.watch: Applied to green coffee it tasted strongly of umami. One developer says farms making 82–83 point coffee will gain more from selective picking, sorting and clean tanks, and in 2022 the safety and choice of strains for wider use were still being confirmed.

byCoffee.text: El Vergel has used koji on Geisha, Bourbon, Caturra and Java, and says Java responded especially well.

story.text: Kaapo Paavolainen, Finland's 2021 barista champion, used a koji coffee at the World Barista Championship in Milan.
Its developers had published what they called the first formal koji coffee process, open-source in English and Spanish, while El Vergel sold its koji lots only as pre-orders.

sections.title: Who's behind it
body: Coffee consultant Christopher Feran; Kaapo Paavolainen of One Day Coffee in Finland; Elias Bayter of El Vergel Estate in Colombia; and Koichi Higuchi of Higuchi Matsunosuke Shoten, an Osaka maker of koji starters whose expertise was sought for the early trials.

records.name: Lactic

cup.common: A creamier cup with a yogurt-like tang and more sweetness.
cup.text: Producers describe a creamier, velvety body, more sweetness, and chocolate and butter notes; reviewers often find the lactic tang fused with fruit.

feel.acidity: tangy; brighter in some pulped lots

cup.why: Sealed away from air, lactic acid bacteria (the yogurt kind) gain ground over yeasts and turn the mucilage's sugars into lactic acid; a salt brine of about 2–3% helps because these bacteria tolerate salt better than most competitors. One producer says the falling pH also sets off enzyme reactions that shape flavor, and that up to 90% of the glucose and fructose is gone compared with a natural.
cup.prized: Body and sweetness with chocolate. One consultant calls it a cleaner, lower-risk route than other experimental ferments, though one that sets a coffee apart more than it improves it.
cup.watch: It takes skill and trial and error; fungi can cause off-flavors, one reason producers keep tanks cool. One producer warns it may not suit drinkers of traditional coffee.

byCoffee.text: La Palma y El Tucán, in Cundinamarca, has championed the style; its producer reports more sweetness, chocolate and butter, with the best results from ferments past 80 hours. The 2019 World Barista Champion used a Sidra from the farm.
Adding the lactic bacterium Leuconostoc mesenteroides to sealed-tank Conilon (a Brazilian Robusta) gave a cup with caramel, fruit and spice notes.

steps.title: Pulp the cherries
steps.text: Many lactic lots are pulped first, though some start from whole or even dried cherries.

steps.title: Seal and add a starter
steps.text: The coffee is sealed away from air with a lactic starter culture or a salt brine of about 2–3%.

steps.title: Ferment, watching pH and heat
steps.text: Producers track pH and temperature and keep the tanks cool to hold back fungi. Lengths vary by producer.
steps.hours: 80+ h for one leading producer's best lots

records.layers: Often the mucilage and parchment, when the coffee is pulped before the sealed ferment; some lactic lots start from whole cherries.

story.text: Coffee Review described oxygen-limited ferments that hold back yeasts and favor lactic acid bacteria, sometimes called lactic acid fermentation.
Jooyeon Jeon won the World Barista Championship using a Sidra from La Palma y El Tucán, a farm that champions lactic fermentation.
A coffee consultant called lactic fermentation a cleaner, safer alternative for producers using other methods, though one that sets a coffee apart more than it improves it.
A research review reported that adding Leuconostoc mesenteroides to sealed Conilon ferments gave caramel, fruit and spice notes.

records.name: Mechanical drying
records.summary: Warm, moving air in a machine dries the coffee faster and evenly.
records.lede: Instead of the sun, a machine moves warm air through the coffee; a guardiola, for example, is a horizontal rotating drum. Temperature and humidity are easier to control, so drying is faster and more uniform, and it stops the spontaneous fermentation that sun-dried coffee goes through. Often the coffee is partly dried in the sun first and the machine finishes it.

facts.label: suggested top temperature for parchment (104 °F)
suggested top temperature for naturals (113 °F)
machine drying of some Colombian experimental lots
target moisture

steps.title: Pre-dry (often)
steps.text: Coffee is often partly dried in the sun first, or pre-dried in an overhead silo.

steps.title: Load the dryer
steps.text: It goes into a guardiola or another rotary dryer with a perforated drum, which turns the coffee in a steady flow of warm air.

steps.title: Hold the heat steady
steps.text: Producers are advised to hold the temperature steady through parts of the drying and keep it below about 40 °C (104 °F) for parchment or 45 °C (113 °F) for naturals.

steps.title: Stop at target
steps.text: Drying ends at about 11–12% moisture.
steps.hours: about a day for El Paraíso's lots

records.layers: Any: washed parchment, parchment with its mucilage, or whole cherries can go through dryers, a 2024 review says, though one importer says naturals can't be machine-dried the way washed coffees are.

cup.common: When gentle, a clean, consistent finish; too hot or rushed, it costs quality.
cup.text: A 2024 review credits machines with faster, more uniform drying. Finca El Paraíso says its low-temperature, dehumidifying dryers protect aromatic compounds and help the coffee store without defects, while one importer calls flash-drying coffee to cut its moisture terrible for the cup.
cup.why: Controlled heat and humidity dry the coffee more evenly, and fast drying halts the fermentation that would otherwise carry on in the fruit or mucilage.
cup.prized: Consistency, and drying on schedule in wet weather or when patios and beds are full; at the peak of harvest, some Central American mills fire their dryers with wood.
cup.watch: Too much heat costs quality (one guide's limits are 40 °C for parchment and 45 °C for naturals), and rotary dryers were long linked with commodity-grade coffee. Dryers also cost money many small producers don't have, so some sell their coffee wet instead.

byCoffee.text: Finca El Paraíso machine-dries its thermal-shock lots for about a day at 34–42 °C (93–108 °F); another lot had 12 hours in a dryer and then about 15 days in a parabolic (covered) dryer.
With rain likely during harvest, coffee often starts in the sun and is finished in a Guardiola.
Mechanical drying prevents the spontaneous fermentation that whole fruit goes through while it sun-dries, a 2024 review notes.

spectrum.label: Heat damage from drying too hot or too fast

sections.title: Drying in the dark
body: Finca Hartmann in Panama dries coffee in drawers in a dark room, using a large dehumidifier and fans rather than sun or high heat. Its owner sees it as an option for small producers who lack space for traditional drying or money for rotary dryers.

records.name: Monsooned
records.summary: Indian natural coffee aged for months in the monsoon wind.
records.lede: Natural (dry-processed) Indian coffee is spread out in well-ventilated warehouses on the Malabar Coast through the June–September monsoon, soaking up the moist sea wind for 12 to 16 weeks. The beans swell to nearly double their size, turn pale straw-yellow and lose much of their acidity. It recreates the taste coffee used to pick up on six-month voyages by sail to Europe, and both the Arabica and Robusta versions are protected names in India.

facts.label: in the monsoon wind
the southwest monsoon season
bean size after monsooning
registered as a Geographical Indication in India

steps.title: Start with a natural
steps.text: Only top-grade, dry-processed coffee, dried on the estate to about 11% moisture and then hulled and graded, is used.

steps.title: Spread on warehouse floors
steps.text: The beans are spread 10–15 cm (4–6 in) deep on the cement floors of well-ventilated warehouses and raked about every 3 hours.

steps.title: Bag loosely and stack
steps.text: They're packed half-full into unstitched jute bags, stacked so the wind can pass, and emptied and rebagged once a week.

steps.title: Wait out the monsoon
steps.text: The coffee is done when the beans have swollen and turned pale yellow, the color of straw.

steps.title: Sort and fumigate
steps.text: Beans that didn't monsoon, black beans and broken ones are picked out, and the coffee is fumigated, graded and packed for export.

records.layers: None of the fruit: monsooning starts after the dried cherry has been hulled and graded, so it's the bare green bean that meets the wind.

cup.common: Heavy, mellow and low in acidity, with an earthy, aged character.
cup.text: India's Coffee Board describes good body, mild acidity, sweetness and a mellow taste with a distinctive aged, musty flavor. One importer finds it spicy, earthy and smoky with sweet tobacco and a creamy body; another writer notes spice and almonds.
cup.why: The beans soak up water, from about 9% to 13–15% moisture, and get much lighter for their size (density drops from about 1.24 to 0.86–1.00 g/ml in the Arabica). Microbe counts rise several-fold, sugars fall slightly and soluble solids rise slightly.
cup.prized: Body and low acidity: it's a sought-after part of espresso blends, especially Scandinavian and German ones, and one importer says it adds a rich crema.
cup.watch: Above about 14% moisture, mold grows fast, and the coffee is prone to weevils, which is why warehouses rake, rebag and sort constantly. The Coffee Board notes that attempts elsewhere on the mainland didn't produce the flavor.

byCoffee.text: On the Coffee Board's sensory scale, monsooned Arabica scores 3.5–4.0 for acidity and 6.0–7.0 for body.
Monsooned Robusta scores lower still for acidity (1.5–2.5) and a little higher for body (6.5–7.5).

spectrum.label: Musty, aged flavor that fans seek out

story.text: Indian coffee went to Europe on wooden sailing ships around the Cape of Good Hope, about six months at sea, and arrived pale, swollen and musty-tasting, a character European buyers came to like.
Steamships and the Suez Canal cut the trip to about a month, the flavor disappeared, and Malabar Coast exporters devised monsooning to bring it back.
Cecil Gifford wrote about monsooning Robusta in the journal Indian Coffee, the earliest of the records the Coffee Board cites.
A Coffee Board member reported on bringing monsooned coffee back after the war.
Monsooned Malabar Arabica and Monsooned Malabar Robusta were registered as Geographical Indications, with certificates dated 28 March 2008 and the Coffee Board as applicant.

sections.title: Where it's made
body: The protected name covers monsooning on the Malabar Coast, from Mangalore in Karnataka to Kozhikode (Calicut) in Kerala. The Arabica comes from estates in Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and the Araku Valley, and the monsooned beans are graded by size as AAA, AA, A and Triage.

sections.title: Who buys it
body: One big exporter, Aspinwall, processed more than 3,500 tonnes in 2018, and buyers have included Nespresso, Benecke and Grecof.

records.name: Mossto
records.summary: Juice from fermenting cherries, reused to start the next batch.
records.lede: Mosto is Spanish for fresh fruit juice, the “must” of winemaking. In coffee it's the liquid that collects as cherries ferment, full of yeasts, bacteria, sugars and acids, which is saved and added to a new batch as a starter, a trick known as backslopping. Recipes vary a lot: some use only the coffee's own juice, while others add yeast, sugar or other fruit.

facts.label: of the cherry weight comes off as mosto
when the mosto is often collected
ferment time in the Bolivian washed method
batches before the mosto needs refreshing

steps.title: Ferment a first batch
steps.text: Coffee ferments in a closed tank and releases liquid, the mosto, whose pH and microbes are watched.

steps.title: Collect the mosto
steps.text: The liquid is drawn off, often around the 72-hour mark, when microbial activity is strongest.

steps.title: Start the next batch
steps.text: Freshly pulped coffee goes into a new tank with the mosto added, so the yeasts and bacteria go straight to work on the mucilage.

steps.title: Rinse and dry
steps.text: In the washed version, the coffee is rinsed and dried like any washed coffee.

records.layers: In the washed method, only the sticky mucilage on the parchment ferments with the mosto before it's rinsed off. Mossto naturals keep the whole cherry on through fermentation and drying.

cup.common: Riper, juicier fruit than a plain washed coffee while keeping the washed coffee's clarity, say roasters who sell it.
cup.text: One roaster describes stone fruit, fruit cordial and grape-like sweetness with bright, complex acidity, and gives one lot's notes as cherry cordial, white grape and tangerine. A Sumatran mossto natural was sold with berry and citrus notes and a juicy body.
cup.why: The mosto carries a ready-made crowd of the yeasts and bacteria that thrived in the last batch, so the new ferment gets going quickly. Colombian producer Edwin Noreña calls it a catalyst that speeds up, controls and enhances fermentation.
cup.prized: Complexity without bringing in anything from outside, when the starter is made only from the coffee's own fruit.
cup.watch: Reused liquid can carry unwanted microbes into the next batch, and the leftover liquid can harm streams if it isn't treated. Some “mossto” lots are also fermented with added yeast, sugar or other fruit, so read the details.

byCoffee.text: Edwin Noreña's mossto Caturra, whose starter also had added yeast, glucose and other juices and which fermented with fruit pulp and nuts, was sold with notes of peach candy, rosewater and passion fruit.
A cooperative's experimental mossto natural scored 86 points, with berry and citrus fruit and a silky mouthfeel.

spectrum.label: Juicy, ripe fruit with washed clarity
Spoilage carried over in reused liquid

story.text: In Panama, Wilford Lamastus was using a similar idea, pouring the red juice from the bottom of his fermentation tanks into tanks of fresh coffee, lots he labels “Dose”.
An importer's review of co-fermentation quoted Edwin Noreña calling mossto a catalyst for fermentation.
Mossto lots were reaching beyond Latin America, such as a Sumatran cooperative's mossto natural.

sections.title: Who started it
body: No single inventor is named. One roaster says the washed mosto method is widely credited to the Rodríguez family's Agricafe in Caranavi, Bolivia, which uses it on small single-day microlots, and that Costa Rican micro-mills helped spread the technique.

sections.title: Is it a co-ferment?
body: Made only from the same coffee's fruit, it adds nothing from outside, which is how one roaster frames it. But some producers build the starter with added yeast, glucose or other juices and ferment alongside fruit pulp, which moves it toward a co-ferment.

records.name: Natural

cup.common: Ripe or dried fruit (berries, stone fruit, prune-like notes) and a heavier body than the same coffee washed.
cup.text: Berry, stone-fruit or dried-fruit notes and a heavier body than the same coffee washed. It can turn wine-like or brandy-like; when the fruit rots, the cup goes bad.
cup.why: Yeasts and bacteria ferment the fruit around the seed during the first days of drying, and some of what they make, especially fruity-smelling esters, seems to get into the seed and survive roasting. Studies don't support the idea that fruit sugar soaks into the bean: naturals keep more of their own simple sugars because the pulp holds back germination, while sucrose, over 90% of the bean's sugar, hardly changes. Drying speed matters too: long drying pushes toward wine or whisky notes, and drying that's too short can leave the flavors muted.
cup.prized: Clean, distinct fruit with little or no ferment. Coffee Review found the ferment virtually undetectable in the cleanest Ethiopian naturals, and at the 2019 Best of Panama auction the winning naturals sold for much more than the washed winners.
cup.watch: With the whole fruit on, it can over-ferment, mold or rot, especially when it dries too slowly or the cherries are under- or overripe. Then a bitter, rotten edge appears, most of all as the cup cools.

byCoffee.text: Well-made ones are known for sweet berry fruit (blueberry and strawberry in fine lots), sometimes floral with a honey-like sweetness; some carry a mild brandy- or whiskey-like edge.

Brazil has long dried most of its Arabica this way (90% in a 1987 estimate), mostly on patios. One importer describes pulpy, coffee-cherry fruit rather than Ethiopian blueberry, with dark chocolate, toasted nuts and caramel, lower acidity and a heavy body.
Natural and honey Geshas tend to bring more fruit, sweetness and ferment into the cup, while washed ones lean floral and citrus, one roaster says.

Practically all of the world's Robusta is dried in the fruit. In a trial cited by a 2024 review of Robusta-type fermentation, adding a chosen yeast to naturals raised the cup score by about 1.5 points and cut mold by about 90%.

steps.title: Ferment in the fruit
steps.text: Ripe whole cherries are spread on patios or raised beds, and yeasts and bacteria feed on the fruit, mostly in the first days. Ripe fruit matters most here.

steps.title: Dry slowly
steps.text: The cherries are turned until the seed is down to about 11–12% water. Weather sets the pace, so times vary widely.
steps.hours: about 10–30 days; 60+ days for deliberately slow-dried lots

steps.title: Rest
steps.text: The dried cherries rest before milling.
steps.hours: 30 days or more at one Panama estate

steps.title: Hull
steps.text: A dry mill removes the dried skin, fruit and parchment.

records.layers: Everything: skin, fruit flesh, mucilage and parchment all stay on the seed until it's dry.

story.text: Southern Ethiopia dried all of its coffee in the whole fruit, a very old practice, until washing arrived.
Starbucks first brought the cleaner 'new natural' style to North American retail; Coffee Review calls the style more an update and revival of the old method than an innovation.
Coffee Review's report 'Brandy and Surprises' covered the new naturals: careful small-batch versions of drying in the whole fruit.
At the Best of Panama auction, the winning naturals sold for much higher prices than the washed winners.

records.name: Patio-dried
records.summary: Spread out on concrete or asphalt in the sun, and turned.
records.lede: The coffee is spread thinly in the sun on a large open floor, often concrete or asphalt, and turned so it dries evenly. How well it goes depends on the weather: rain, heat, humidity and sunshine all shape the result. In rainy regions producers often start on the patio and finish in a mechanical dryer.

facts.label: average patio drying at one Panama farm
sun drying a washed coffee
sun drying a natural or honey
layer of whole cherries when sun-drying a natural (4 in)

steps.title: Spread it out
steps.text: Cherries or parchment are spread thinly across a concrete or asphalt patio.

steps.title: Turn it often
steps.text: It's turned regularly; coffee that isn't turned dries unevenly and can overheat in strong sun.

steps.title: Mind the weather
steps.text: Coffee doesn't dry at night or in the early morning and rain can harm it, so some mills build covered patios.

steps.title: Finish
steps.text: Drying ends at about 11–12% moisture, sometimes in a mechanical dryer when rain threatens.

records.layers: Any: parchment for washed and honey coffees, the whole cherry for naturals, and in Indonesia the bare wet-hulled bean.

cup.common: No signature taste; the result depends on the weather and on how clean and well run the patio is.
cup.text: A 2024 review notes that the quality of sun-dried coffee depends on rainfall, temperature, humidity and sunshine, and one importer singles out very clean patios as a mark of the best mills.
cup.why: The fruit keeps fermenting in the first days of drying, so coffee that dries too slowly in damp weather can ferment out of control, while coffee left unturned in hot sun dries unevenly and can overheat.
cup.prized: Clean, well-turned patios; one importer's partner mills in Indonesia are building covered patios to lengthen drying.
cup.watch: Rain can delay drying or harm quality, and on open floors birds and animals can damage or contaminate the coffee.

byCoffee.text: Bare beans dry fast on tarps or patios, which one importer warns can be harsh and uneven without the parchment's protection.
Because rain can fall unexpectedly during harvest, coffee often starts in the sun and is finished in a Guardiola dryer.

spectrum.label: Over-fermented when it dries too slowly

records.name: Raised beds
records.summary: Mesh tables off the ground, so air moves around the coffee.
records.lede: The coffee dries on mesh-topped tables raised off the ground. Air circulates around it, it stays clear of dirt and contamination from the ground, and workers can spread it thin and turn it. Raised beds are used at Kenyan and Ethiopian washing stations and for many specialty lots elsewhere; one Panama farm uses them mostly for slow-dried lots.

facts.label: washed Kenyan parchment
honeys to naturals at one mill
slow-dried lots at one Panama farm
moisture when it's done

steps.title: Spread it thin
steps.text: Parchment or whole cherries are spread thinly across the mesh.

steps.title: Turn it often
steps.text: Workers turn it regularly so it dries evenly.

steps.title: Sun, shade or cover
steps.text: Beds can stand in full sun, under shade, in polytunnels or in greenhouses.

steps.title: Dry to target
steps.text: Drying ends at about 10–12% moisture.

records.layers: Depends on the base method: clean parchment for washed coffees, parchment with its sticky mucilage for honeys, the whole cherry for naturals.

cup.common: No flavor of its own; beds are chosen for clean, even drying.
cup.text: Esmeralda says raised beds let air circulate for clean, evenly dried coffee, and one importer pictures small, covered raised beds as ideal for higher cup quality.
cup.why: Air moves more easily around coffee on a bed, the coffee stays away from contamination on the ground, and thin, well-turned layers dry evenly. Coffee that isn't turned properly is left unevenly exposed to heat and airflow.
cup.prized: Clean, even drying; one Panama farm uses its beds mostly for slow-dried lots.
cup.watch: Bed space runs short at the peak of harvest: Kenyan mills keep washed coffee soaking until beds free up, and many small producers can't afford beds or dryers and sell their coffee wet.

byCoffee.text: Washed parchment moves from the soak to raised drying screens and dries in about 7–15 days.
Cherries go onto raised beds straight from the tree, and drying in the fruit strongly shapes their flavor, says Sweet Maria's.
The Lamastus family's anaerobic slow-dry (ASD) lots, from estates such as Elida, dry on raised, shaded beds.

records.name: Slow dry
records.summary: Drying stretched over weeks, often on shaded beds, for even drying.
records.lede: Drying is slowed on purpose, using raised beds, shade, covers or even dark, dehumidified rooms, so the coffee loses water over weeks instead of days. Hacienda La Esmeralda in Panama uses raised beds for slow-dried lots that average 29 days, against 7–9 days on its patios. One importer says coffee dried slowly and evenly lasts longer, but too slow brings its own trouble.

facts.label: slow-dried lots on raised beds at one Panama farm
drying for an anaerobic slow-dry (ASD) natural
ordinary sun drying for a washed coffee, for comparison
past this, slow parchment drying hurts the cup, one importer says

steps.title: Ferment first (often)
steps.text: Many slow-dry lots start with a sealed ferment; Elida Estate's ASD naturals spend about five or six days sealed in tanks or bags.

steps.title: Spread thin, in shade
steps.text: The coffee goes onto raised beds, often shaded, or onto covered patios, spread thinly and turned.

steps.title: Lose water slowly
steps.text: Drying runs for weeks rather than days, down to about 10–12% moisture.

steps.title: Rest before milling
steps.text: Esmeralda then bags its dried coffee for at least 30 days to let it stabilize.

records.layers: Any, but the best-known slow-dried coffees are naturals and anaerobic naturals, dried with the whole fruit still on.

cup.common: No single flavor of its own; producers use it for clean, even drying, and one importer says slow, even drying helps coffee keep its quality longer.
cup.text: Esmeralda says its raised beds let air circulate for clean, evenly dried coffee. Coffee Review scored two of Elida Estate's anaerobic slow-dry naturals 93 and 94.
cup.why: The parchment shell and a gentle pace buffer the bean against harsh, uneven drying, and very fast drying is bad for coffee. In a lab study, beans dried with nightly pauses, like sun drying, took about eight days instead of five but ended with much the same sugars, so the authors concluded sugars can't explain quality differences between the two.
cup.prized: Even drying and a coffee that holds its quality. A Geisha natural dried in a dark room won best natural Geisha at Best of Panama 2020.
cup.watch: Too slow is a problem too: coffee that doesn't dry quickly enough can ferment out of control or grow mold, and one importer says parchment drying for more than 30 days shows problems in the cup.

byCoffee.text: Elida Estate's ASD Catuaí natural spent six days sealed and 60 days drying, and scored 94 at Coffee Review.
Finca Hartmann's dark-room drying produced the Black Jaguar natural Geisha from Guarumo farm, best natural Geisha at Best of Panama 2020.

spectrum.label: Over-fermented or moldy if it stays wet too long

story.text: Ratibor Hartmann of Finca Hartmann in Panama began drying coffee in drawers in a dark room with a dehumidifier and fans; by 2021 he'd been experimenting for almost ten years.
A dark-room-dried natural Geisha won best natural Geisha at the Best of Panama competition.
Coffee Review described anaerobic slow-dry naturals as drying 60 days or more and credited Wilford Lamastus of Elida Estate with popularizing them.

sections.title: A balancing act
body: Dry too slowly and the coffee can ferment out of control or mold; dry too fast and it suffers too: coffee left unturned in hot sun can overheat, and one importer calls very fast drying of bare beans harsh and uneven. The parchment shell itself slows drying and shields the bean from strong sun and day–night temperature swings.

records.name: Thermal shock
records.summary: A warm rinse, then a cold one, after a long ferment.
records.lede: After a long, controlled fermentation, the coffee is rinsed in warm water and then straight away in cold water. Perfect Daily Grind credits it to Diego Bermúdez of Finca El Paraíso in Cauca, Colombia. Producers say the swing “opens” the beans to take in aroma and then “seals” it in, but the roaster that explains this theory says research is still needed.

facts.label: the warm rinse (104 °F)
the cold rinse (54 °F)
El Paraíso's altitude (6,330–6,430 ft)
El Paraíso's Cup of Excellence top-10 finish

steps.title: Sanitize the cherries
steps.text: Ripe cherries are washed in ozonated water, sometimes with UV light, to cut down wild microbes.

steps.title: Sealed ferment
steps.text: Whole cherries ferment in sealed steel tanks, in some lots flushed with CO2 and seeded with yeasts selected from wild samples.

steps.title: Pulp and ferment again
steps.text: The cherries are pulped and the coffee ferments again with its mucilage.

steps.title: Warm rinse
steps.text: The coffee is rinsed in, or heated in its juices to, about 40–50 °C (104–122 °F).

steps.title: Cold rinse
steps.text: It then goes straight into cold water at about 10–12 °C (50–54 °F), which producers say stops the fermentation.

steps.title: Controlled drying
steps.text: El Paraíso lots then dry in machines at gentle heat, about 34–42 °C (93–108 °F), down to 10–11% moisture.

records.layers: It varies. In El Paraíso's double-ferment lots the shock comes after pulping, on parchment still coated in mucilage; other lots shock the whole cherries, before pulping or before a sealed ferment.

cup.common: Very intense, perfumed fruit, sometimes so intense that people suspect something was added.
cup.text: Roasters list notes like freeze-dried strawberry, cotton candy and violet, or citrus, orange blossom, peach, mango, passion fruit and lychee. One roaster's education director says the processing has an intensive impact on flavor.
cup.why: Unproven. The producers' working theory is that heat opens the beans' pores so they take in esters (fruity aroma compounds) from the fermentation juice, and cold closes them again; the quick swing may also halt enzymes, as blanching does to vegetables. The roaster that explains this says scientific research is still needed.
cup.prized: Big, clear aromatics, and roasters credit the step with a clean, consistent cup and with stopping fermentation before it goes too far.
cup.watch: The intensity led many to suspect that one El Paraíso release was infused with additives; the roaster selling it says the flavor came only from processing. Because the shock is one step among sanitizing, added yeast, sealed ferments and machine drying, it's hard to know how much of the flavor it causes.

byCoffee.text: Diego Bermúdez's double-washed thermal-shock Castillo was sold with notes of citrus, orange blossom, peach, mango, passion fruit, honey, lychee, strawberry, raspberry and plum.

story.text: The Bermúdez family started Finca El Paraíso in Piendamó, Cauca.
El Paraíso won a regional competition, its way into specialty coffee.
Diego Samuel Bermúdez placed 10th in Colombia's Cup of Excellence with a washed Bourbon that scored 89.76.
He placed 24th with an anaerobic washed Castillo, and won the body and exotic categories of the coffee federation's Colombia, Land of Diversity contest.
Trade writers were describing thermal shock as his creation: a rinse at about 40 °C, then one at about 12 °C.

sections.title: Who invented it
body: Perfect Daily Grind credits Diego Bermúdez. One roaster's education director credits him together with Wilton Benítez, and describes both sanitizing cherries and adding yeast strains selected from wild samples. Bermúdez co-founded a processing company, INDESTEC, with his brother and cousin, and the family now runs several more farms.

sections.title: Recipes differ
body: Lots sold as thermal shock don't follow one recipe. One roaster's listing describes washing whole cherries in 50 °C (122 °F) water, sealing them for 80 hours at 35 °C (95 °F) and spraying on a Saccharomyces cerevisiae yeast; another producer shocks before pulping in a washed process.

records.name: Washed

cup.common: A clean, bright cup with clear acidity, where the coffee's origin and variety come through plainly.
cup.text: Importers describe washed coffees as clean and crisp, with caramel-like sweetness and pronounced acidity. A 2015 research review found wet-processed coffees more aromatic and acidic, and less bitter, burnt or woody, than dry-processed ones.
cup.why: The fruit comes off first, so microbes work on the sticky mucilage for 12–72 hours in a tank instead of for weeks around the seed, and the parchment dries in roughly one to two weeks. The seed changes too: lab studies find washed beans start germination-like activity within about a day of pulping, using up simple sugars (they end with roughly 5–10 times less glucose and fructose than naturals) and building amino acids, raw material for flavor in the roast.
cup.prized: Clarity: a cup in which place and variety are easy to taste. Kenya's best washed lots, for example, are prized for bright acidity with citrus, blackcurrant and berry.
cup.watch: A ferment left too long turns sour and alcoholic and can leave over-fermented 'stinker' beans. Separately, washed coffees left underdeveloped in the roast can taste sour or thin.

byCoffee.text: Kenyan mills ferment overnight, then up to 36 more hours, wash, and soak the parchment in clean water for 12–48 hours before drying. The best lots are known for bright citrus, blackcurrant and berry acidity, sometimes leaning winey.
Washed Ethiopians can have sparkling, citrusy acidity, with florals and sweet spice in the aroma, says one importer; the same coffees dried in the fruit lean toward berry and dried fruit.
Washing can bring out the variety's floral and citrus side, one roaster says; natural and honey Geshas can carry more fruit, sweetness and ferment.

Washing stations (the first private one opened in 2001, and over 200 since) are credited with greatly improving Rwanda's coffee. One importer's washed lots run floral and clear, with bright lemon acidity.

spectrum.label: Tangy, lactic from a long or sealed ferment

steps.title: Sort and pulp
steps.text: Cherries are floated to skim off unripe and overripe fruit, then a machine strips the skin and fruit flesh.

steps.title: Ferment in tanks
steps.text: The sticky mucilage left on the parchment ferments as microbes break it down. Dry tanks are usually done within a day; tanks under water can take longer. It varies with climate, water and microbes.

steps.title: Wash (and soak)
steps.text: The loosened mucilage is rinsed off. In Kenya the clean parchment then soaks under fresh water before drying.

steps.title: Dry the parchment
steps.text: Parchment dries on patios, raised beds or in machines until the seed is about 11–12% water. Weather and method change the time a lot.
steps.hours: about 6–15 days in the sun; about 29 on one estate's slow-drying raised beds; 18–36 h in a mechanical dryer

steps.title: Rest, then hull
steps.text: The dry parchment rests before a dry mill strips it off.
steps.hours: 30 days or more at one Panama estate

records.layers: Parchment only. The skin, fruit flesh and mucilage are all off before drying, so the seed dries in its papery parchment shell.

story.text: Washed processing reached southern Ethiopia, which until then had dried all its coffee in the fruit.
Rwanda's first private washing station opened in Huye, run by the Maraba cooperative; more than 200 followed.
Coffee Review's new Kenneth Davids Cup set up a Traditional Washed category that excludes anaerobic, carbonic, inoculated, extended and co-fermented coffees.

records.name: Wet-hulled

cup.common: A heavy, low-acid cup with earthy, herbal and savory notes, often with dark chocolate.
cup.text: Importers describe earthy, herbal and savory flavors with dark chocolate and nuts. At its best, one adds, the earthiness is clean and humus-like, with raw-sugar or molasses sweetness.
cup.why: The parchment is stripped while the bean is still about 25–50% water, and the bare seed then dries fast, exposed to the weather; importers tie the signature flavor to this processing, not just to the islands. Sumatran lots that are hulled dry instead come out brighter and lighter in body.
cup.prized: Clean earthiness with a little green herb or moss, real sweetness, and even, slow drying on clean patios.
cup.watch: Bare, damp beans pick up dirt and humidity easily: watch for dirt-like or rubbery flavors, vegetal bitterness, crushed beans and harsh, uneven drying. Dark roasting can hide such defects.

byCoffee.text: Wet-hulling is traditional here: smallholders sell damp parchment within hours of washing, partly because cloudy, rainy weather makes slow drying in parchment hard. One importer names Aceh and the Lake Toba area, including Lintong, among its sources.
Traditionally wet-hulled too, though some estates, such as Toarco's Pedemeran plantation, have used washed processing.
Its old estates in East Java (Jampit, Blawan, Kayumas) have historically fully washed their coffee instead.

steps.title: Pulp and ferment
steps.text: Smallholders pulp the cherries and ferment them overnight in bags, tubs or tanks.

steps.title: Wash, dry briefly
steps.text: The mucilage is washed off and the parchment dries for just a few hours, then is sold while still around half water.

steps.title: Hull while damp
steps.text: The mill may dry it a little more, then strips the parchment at about 25–50% moisture (sources differ), far wetter than the 10–12% at which most coffee is hulled.

steps.title: Dry the bare beans
steps.text: The bare green beans dry on tarps or patios; at the port they're often flash-dried to 11–12% before export.
steps.hours: about 12–15 days (one importer); picking to shipping can take under a month

records.layers: Parchment for a short while, then nothing. The skin and mucilage come off first, the parchment is stripped while the bean is still damp, and the bare seed finishes drying.

records.name: Yeast-inoculated
records.summary: A chosen yeast strain is added to steer the ferment.
records.lede: Instead of relying on whatever microbes are on the fruit, the producer adds a starter culture, usually a known yeast strain. The added yeast tends to crowd out the wild ones, which makes the ferment more predictable. Research is young and mostly small trials, so the flavor claims are still largely producers' and suppliers' own.

facts.label: the species behind one major supplier's coffee yeasts
more yeast than a wild ferment, in a 2021 trial
producers sent yeast kits by one Brazilian project in 2020
yeast dose on cherries in one roaster-listed lot

steps.title: Clean the cherries
steps.text: Some producers wash cherries in ozonated water, sometimes with UV light, so fewer wild microbes compete.

steps.title: Add the yeast
steps.text: A measured dose of a known strain goes onto the cherries or into the tank of pulped coffee.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.text: The added yeast multiplies and, in one trial, used up the sugars faster and more completely than wild microbes did.
steps.hours: 36 h in one washed trial · up to 120 h in sealed ones

steps.title: Finish and dry
steps.text: The coffee is then washed or dried; trials have inoculated both pulped (washed) and whole-fruit (natural) coffee.

records.layers: Either: trials have inoculated pulped coffee with its mucilage in a washed ferment, and whole fruit in natural and sealed ferments.

cup.common: Usually a cleaner, more predictable version of the base process rather than one signature flavor; each strain is sold for a different effect.
cup.text: One yeast supplier markets a strain for fruit and mouthfeel and another for brightness and citrus. In Brazilian robusta trials, one added yeast brought fruity, almond, chocolate and nutty notes that consumers could pick out.
cup.why: The added yeast takes over: in a 2021 Australian trial it reached about 100 times the yeast count of a wild ferment, used the sugars faster and more completely, and left two to three times more glycerol, alcohols, esters and acids in the green beans.
cup.prized: Consistency: ferments left to chance can be hard to predict, and starter cultures promise more control. In one agronomist's trials, added yeasts outcompeted the native microbes and gave cleaner cups.
cup.watch: The taste gains are small or unproven: in that 2021 trial most differences weren't statistically significant. A producer in one Brazilian project says lots from different varieties, altitudes and processes all ended up with similar sensory profiles.

byCoffee.text: In Brazilian trials on Conilon (Brazilian robusta), one added yeast raised cupping scores by more than a point, and another raised them by over 3 points in a 120-hour sealed ferment.
In a 2021 Australian trial on Bourbon, a mix of two yeasts gave the top score, 82.0, against 80.3 for the uninoculated ferment.
A Syngenta–Nucoffee project with Brazil's Federal University of Lavras uses yeasts isolated from coffee itself and reports more than 1,000 lots scoring 80–90 points.

story.text: Brazilian studies in 2014 and 2015 were among the few early trials of adding yeast to coffee's wet ferment, a 2021 paper notes.
In an article Lallemand sponsored, an agronomist trialling its LalCafé yeasts (all Saccharomyces cerevisiae) reported more consistent ferments and cleaner cups.
A Brazilian project sent 383 kits of coffee-derived yeasts to 323 producers, after more than 20 years of research on over 3,000 microbes.
An Australian trial found inoculated yeasts dominated the ferment and doubled or tripled key compounds in the beans, though most taste differences weren't significant.

sections.title: Not the same as co-fermenting
body: Inoculation adds microbes, usually a known yeast; co-fermenting adds fruit, spices or other ingredients. US rules don't require co-fermentation additives to be listed, and one importer calls clear disclosure of processes and additives best practice.

records.name: Campo das Vertentes
records.summary: A mild Minas highland: very sweet, with chocolate and nuts
records.lede: A protected coffee origin (Indicação de Procedência) in Minas Gerais with a mild climate: cool, rainy summers and, in its higher parts, very cold winters. Its protected name covers green, roasted and ground coffee.

facts.label: protected origin name (Indicação de Procedência)
summers, with very cold winters up high

cup.text: Brazilian Farmers' guide to the protected names describes it as very sweet, with a balanced body and hints of chocolate and nuts.

story.text: In the 2007 Minas Gerais state quality contest, samples from here clustered in the early rounds but had mostly dropped out by the later ones.
Its producers joined 12 other protected Brazilian coffee regions in a marketing agreement with BSCA, the Brazilian Specialty Coffee Association.

records.name: Cerrado Mineiro
records.summary: Flat, mechanized savanna farms and Brazil's first protected coffee origin
records.lede: A high, flat savanna plateau in western Minas Gerais, where coffee grows at 800–1,300 m (2,600–4,300 ft) on mostly large, highly mechanized farms. In 2005 it became Brazil's first protected coffee origin, and in 2013 its first Denominação de Origem, the tier under which Brazil's patent office requires the coffee to show set traits of flavor and aroma.

facts.label: municipalities in the protected area
coffee producers (2025)
growing altitude (2,600–4,300 ft)
of Minas Gerais's coffee

harvest.text: Picked from May to September, in the dry season; the low humidity at harvest lowers the risk of unwanted fermentation.

cup.text: The region's official profile, as Senar/MG cites it from Brazil's agriculture ministry, runs from caramel to nut aromas, with delicately citric acidity and a chocolate flavor. Embrapa-linked researchers add a moderate body and a long, sweet finish.
cup.why: Distinct seasons help: rain falls mostly from October to March, so the harvest comes in dry weather. Brazilian Farmers' guide to the protected names also credits uniform ripening and a concentrated harvest.

story.text: Farmers found that liming the acidic savanna soil, to balance its pH, made large-scale farming possible.
Growers filed their first request for a protected origin name.
It became Brazil's first geographical indication for coffee.
It became Brazil's first coffee Denominação de Origem.
Heat, dry spells, frost and scarce, uneven rain cut the harvest 13.8%, to 4.6 million 60-kg bags (Conab).

sections.title: Growing it
body: Coffee here grows in full sun on flat land, and a 2007 Coffee & Conservation review called it the most mechanized coffee growing in the world, with little hand picking. Because the dry season is long, most farms irrigate at least part of their coffee, often with center-pivot sprinklers.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Look for “Região do Cerrado Mineiro” and its origin seal. In 2025 about 1,300 of the region's producers were cleared to use the seal, on 102,000 of its 234,000 hectares of coffee.
Patrocínio, home of the growers' federation, is the region's hub. Other towns you may see include Monte Carmelo, Carmo do Paranaíba, Araguari and Coromandel.

records.name: Espírito Santo
records.summary: Brazil's Conilon (Robusta) heartland, with mountain Arabica up high
records.lede: Brazil's Robusta heartland: about 70% of the country's Robusta, called Conilon here, grows in this state, which also grows Arabica in its mountains. Its protected coffee names include Conilon from Espírito Santo, Montanhas do Espírito Santo and Caparaó, which it shares with Minas Gerais.

facts.label: of Brazil's Robusta (2026/27 forecast)
Conilon grown here since
where its Conilon grows (up to 2,000 ft)
mountain Arabica, Montanhas do Espírito Santo (1,600–4,600 ft)

harvest.text: By late May 2026, Espírito Santo's Conilon harvest was 15–25% done, ahead of most Minas Gerais Arabica (Cepea).

cup.text: For Conilon, Brazilian Farmers' guide to the protected names says lower farms give a full body with chocolate and almond, and higher ones floral and fruity notes. Mountain Arabica from Montanhas do Espírito Santo is described with bright acidity and a chocolate and sugarcane aroma; StoneX adds sweetness and aromatic complexity.

feel.acidity: low in Conilon; bright in mountain Arabica

cup.why: Altitude sorts the cup here: for both Conilon and mountain Arabica, the protected-name descriptions tie fruitier, more floral or more unusual notes to higher farms.
cup.watch: Lower Montanhas lots can turn woody, cereal-like and astringent, and Conilon in general tends to be more bitter and less aromatic than Arabica.

story.text: Conilon growing began in the state.
Montanhas do Espírito Santo and Caparaó each gained Denominação de Origem status.
Cool, wet weather trimmed Robusta yields even as Brazil headed for a record crop.

sections.title: Two coffees, one state
body: Most of the state's coffee is Conilon, a Brazilian type of Coffea canephora, the species behind Robusta. Its mountains grow Arabica, mostly on small family farms: StoneX counts 16 municipalities above 400 m in Montanhas do Espírito Santo, and says the misty, humid climate leads growers to washed or semi-washed processing.
Caparaó, a mountain area shared with Minas Gerais, has many small family farms, and its coffee is picked by hand.

records.name: Mantiqueira de Minas
records.summary: Mountain coffee that often ranks in Brazil's Cup of Excellence top ten
records.lede: The Minas Gerais side of the Serra da Mantiqueira mountains, part of the wider Sul de Minas region, with coffee at about 1,000–1,400 m (3,300–4,600 ft). Its name comes from the Tupi word Amantikir, “crying mountains,” for its many springs, and its coffees often finish in the top ten of Brazil's Cup of Excellence.

facts.label: growing altitude (3,300–4,600 ft)
protected origin name (Indicação de Procedência)
upgraded to Denominação de Origem

harvest.text: Picked from May to September.

cup.text: Brazilian Farmers' guide to the protected names sums it up as sweet with slightly citric acidity. A SAGA lot of red and yellow Bourbon from five smallholders was described with citrus, floral and fruity notes, a creamy, dense body and a long finish (BeanScene, 2021).
cup.why: StoneX credits hot days and cold nights, which slow ripening and, it says, make the coffee sweeter and more aromatic. Embrapa researchers point to mild temperatures plus dry spells while the cherries ripen and are picked.
cup.prized: Competition lots: Melbourne Coffee Merchants notes its coffees often finish in Cup of Excellence's top ten.

story.text: In a Minas Gerais state quality contest, Carmo de Minas was the hot spot for finalist samples, both naturals and pulped naturals.
It won a protected origin name based on its tradition and reputation.
The name was upgraded to a Denominação de Origem.
São Gonçalo do Sapucaí hosted the first festival of Mantiqueira de Minas specialty coffees.

sections.title: Towns and farms
body: Carmo de Minas is the name you'll see most; Barista Hustle calls it a microregion of Mantiqueira. One farm there, Pé de Cedro, has 25 of its 35 hectares in coffee at 1,000–1,200 m; one of its lots was a natural Yellow Catucaí.
A specialty coffee tourism route runs through Carmo de Minas and São Lourenço.

records.name: Matas de Minas
records.summary: Hilly, once-forested southeast Minas: small family farms, citrus and caramel
records.lede: The hilly southeast of Minas Gerais, around the city of Manhuaçu, on land once covered by Atlantic rainforest. Coffee grows at about 600–1,200 m (2,000–3,900 ft), mostly on small family farms, and it is the state's second-biggest coffee region.

facts.label: municipalities
of its ~51,000 coffee farms are under 20 ha (2022)
growing altitude (2,000–3,900 ft)
protected origin name (Indicação de Procedência)

harvest.text: Picked from April to September.

cup.text: A Federal University of Viçosa study of state contest lots from 2016, 2017 and 2019 found citrus aromas, medium sweetness with caramel and fruity flavors, pronounced acidity, a full body and a long finish. Itatiaia adds a chocolatey aroma, and StoneX describes a medium to full body and high sweetness.
cup.why: Altitude seems to help: in that study, higher farms tended to score higher, though the authors call it a trend, not a firm result.
cup.prized: Contest lots: in those contests naturals averaged above 84 points and pulped coffees above 83, with tops of 90.80 and 91.58.
cup.watch: Damp air. In the 2007 state contest many early entries came from here but few reached the late rounds, which researchers linked partly to fermentation risk from humidity and to small family farms on slopes.

story.text: Its plantations drove much of the growth of Brazil's coffee industry.
A regional origin seal was created.
Late in the year it won a protected origin name (Indicação de Procedência).
In the Florada Premiada contest it had more washed Arabica lots selected than any other region.

sections.title: Small farms on slopes
body: Most growers are families with small plantings of 3–20 hectares, and about 71% of the region's coffee land sits on slopes, according to the Viçosa study. Royal Coffee describes rolling, uneven terrain suited to small and medium farms.
Coffee towns here include Manhuaçu, Araponga, Espera Feliz, Caratinga and São João do Manhuaçu.

records.name: Alta Mogiana
records.summary: São Paulo hill country near Franca: creamy, chocolatey and nutty
records.lede: Hill country in northern São Paulo state along the Minas Gerais border, around Franca, with coffee at about 900–1,280 m (2,950–4,200 ft). It has been tied to coffee for over a century and has held a protected origin name (Indicação de Procedência) since 2013.

facts.label: growing altitude (2,950–4,200 ft)
protected origin name (Indicação de Procedência)
municipalities in São Paulo and in Minas Gerais

harvest.text: Picked from May to August.

cup.text: Brazilian Farmers' guide to the protected names describes a velvety, creamy body, a strong fruity aroma, soft chocolate and nut notes and medium, balanced acidity. A 2021 SAGA lot added caramel and a hint of toasted almond.
cup.why: Revista Cultivar (2009) credits its altitude and climate with slow, even ripening; Barista Hustle notes its cool climate and high elevations.

story.text: Coffee arrived with the spread of the railways.
Low prices, frost and plant-health problems discouraged many growers and sharply cut the coffee area.
Across 25 Mogiana municipalities, coffee land roughly doubled to 111,000 hectares while sugarcane nearly quadrupled to 234,700, an Embrapa satellite study found.
Alta Mogiana gained its protected origin name.

sections.title: Coffee holds the hills
body: Sugarcane has spread fast in northeastern São Paulo, but it is hard to harvest by machine on slopes steeper than 12%, so coffee keeps the hilly ground. The Embrapa study also credits professional growers with strong technical support.
Franca hosted the region's 2009 coffee quality contest. Other Alta Mogiana towns include Pedregulho, Altinópolis, Batatais and Cristais Paulista.

records.name: Oeste da Bahia
records.summary: Bahia's Cerrado plateau: mechanized, high-yield coffee above 700 m
records.lede: Coffee in western Bahia grows above 700 m (2,300 ft), mostly in the Cerrado, the tropical savanna of central Brazil. StoneX describes Bahia's coffee as fully mechanized, with warm temperatures and some of the country's highest yields, and dates it to the 1970s, which makes Bahia Brazil's newest coffee region.

facts.label: growing altitude (2,300 ft+)
protected origin name (Indicação de Procedência)
when coffee began in Bahia

cup.text: Brazilian Farmers' guide to the protected names describes a pleasant flavor and fragrance, a slightly fruity, floral aroma, excellent sweetness and good acidity.

story.text: Coffee growing began in Bahia.
Oeste da Bahia gained a protected origin name.

records.name: Rondônia
records.summary: Amazon Robusta, holder of the first canephora Denominação de Origem
records.lede: A western Amazon state on the Bolivian border where nearly all the coffee is Coffea canephora, the species behind Robusta, grown mostly on small family farms. Its coffee is known as Robustas Amazônicos (Amazonian Robustas), and in 2021 its Matas de Rondônia area won the world's first Denominação de Origem for this species.

facts.label: world's first Denominação de Origem for canephora coffee
municipalities in the Matas de Rondônia DO
growing altitude (600–1,300 ft)
families farming coffee (2024)

harvest.text: Rondônia usually starts and finishes picking before Brazil's other regions: by late May 2026 it was 50% to over 60% done (Cepea).

cup.text: Embrapa researcher Enrique Alves describes mild sweetness and acidity, a velvety body and a lasting aftertaste, with notes of nuts, chocolate and dried fruit; any bitterness tends toward cacao nib. Brazilian Farmers' guide to the protected names adds woody, spicy and herbal notes.
cup.why: Embrapa says the character comes from more than four decades of genetics, environment and farming working together, as growers selected crosses between canephora's two botanical groups, Conilon and Robusta.
cup.prized: Clean, sweet lots judged on the Fine Robusta tasting protocol, where Embrapa sets its quality bar for clones at over 80 points.
cup.watch: Canephora in general tends to be fuller-bodied but more bitter, less aromatic and less acidic than Arabica, and careless drying, with too much heat or mold, hurts the cup.

story.text: The first Arabica demonstration field, of Mundo Novo, was probably planted near what is now Ji-Paraná, as settlers arrived.
Conilon and Robusta were brought to new farm settlements.
Embrapa released BRS Ouro Preto, a multi-clone Conilon cultivar for the western Amazon.
Matas de Rondônia won its Denominação de Origem in June.
About 92% of the state's coffee land was planted with Robusta amazônico (IBGE figures).

sections.title: What Robusta means here
body: Arabica and Robusta are two different coffee species. Robusta's proper name is Coffea canephora, and Brazil grows two main botanical groups of it, Conilon and Robusta. Rondônia's farmers have crossed and selected the two over the years, and those plants make up about 80% of the coffee in Matas de Rondônia, whose Denominação de Origem covers 15 municipalities, including Cacoal, Alta Floresta d'Oeste, Rolim de Moura and São Miguel do Guaporé.

Canephora has long been seen as the lesser species because it tends to be more bitter and less acidic than Arabica. Careful picking, controlled fermentation and better drying are changing that: Embrapa uses a Fine Robusta tasting protocol, and in a 2022 national contest Matas de Rondônia had more canephora lots selected than any other region. Embrapa also measures less caffeine in these coffees, 1.4–1.8%, than in standard Conilon.

sections.title: Indigenous growers
body: Aruá and Tupari families in the Rio Branco Indigenous Land have grown coffee in their villages for about 15 years. In 2018 they began training with Embrapa, picking only ripe cherries and drying them on raised beds; one of their lots was described with caramel, malt and nuts, a silky body and a sweet finish.

records.name: Sul de Minas
records.summary: Southern Minas, where most of the state's Arabica grows
records.lede: The south and southwest of Minas Gerais, where coffee grows at about 800–1,400 m (2,600–4,600 ft), mostly on small farms. It grows most of Minas Gerais's Arabica: in 2016 it produced 37% of all Brazil's coffee.

facts.label: of Brazil's coffee output in 2016
growing altitude (2,600–4,600 ft)
first coffee farms
of coffee in 2016

harvest.text: Picked from April to September. Rain slowed the 2026 harvest: by late May only about 10% was in, according to Cepea.

cup.text: Embrapa-linked researchers describe a medium body, citric acidity and a sweet finish, and StoneX notes high acidity and sweetness. Itatiaia says the mountain coffees add fruit, caramel, chocolate and almond, while southwest lots lean floral and citrus.

story.text: The first coffee was planted in Aiuruoca, Jacuí and Baependi, in the Sapucaí and Grande river valleys.
Railroads, after decades of poor transport, set off a new coffee boom.
State investment and incentives, and growing cooperatives, built up the sector.
The region had 52% of Minas Gerais's coffee land and produced 37% of Brazil's coffee.

sections.title: Where it's traded
body: Varginha is the region's logistics and export hub, home to many exporters and warehouses. It, Guaxupé and Três Pontas rank among Brazil's top ten towns for coffee storage, and Alfenas and Muzambinho host big coffee companies' facilities.
The region is also home to Cooxupé, which StoneX calls the world's largest coffee cooperative.

records.name: Antioquia
records.summary: Colombia's second-biggest producer, and home of Urrao's Chiroso.
records.lede: Antioquia, the department around Medellín, is Colombia's second-largest coffee producer, at about 2.1 million bags a year, grown at roughly 1,300–2,200 m. Migrating antioqueño growers helped carry coffee to other parts of the country. For specialty buyers its best-known name is Urrao, where the Chiroso variety grows.

facts.label: where coffee grows (4,300–7,200 ft)
of Colombia's coffee, about 2.1 million bags a year (2020)
coffee-growing families, farming 1.55 ha each on average (2022 figure)
planted with coffee in 2021

harvest.text: Main crop September–December and mitaca (the smaller second crop) April–June, says Barista Hustle. The growers' federation likewise counts Antioquia's first-half picking as its mitaca.

cup.text: Antioquia has no protected regional profile of its own. Its best-known specialty coffee, Chiroso, tends to be described as aromatic, floral, bright and tea-like (Sweet Maria's); Sey Coffee found bright citrus, orange-oil aromatics, jasmine and a sweet, tea-like finish in an Urrao lot and compared it to Ethiopian coffees.

story.text: Records mention coffee plants in Antioquia, grown as medicine.
Growers make the first attempt at commercial coffee.
Production grows fast in the first half of the century.
In November, a family farm at 1,950 m in Urrao harvests its first Chiroso.

sections.title: Urrao and Chiroso
body: Chiroso, named after a rural Colombian word for something long or stretched out, grows around Urrao. Despite the bag name Bourbon Chiroso, genetic work links it to Ethiopian landraces.

Most Antioquia growers process their coffee on the farm and sell it as parchment (dried, still in its papery hull) through cooperatives. Cenicafé's regional Castillo line for Antioquia is Castillo El Rosario, and one of its trial sites was the El Rosario station in Venecia, Antioquia.

records.name: Cauca
records.summary: Sunny southwestern mountains: bright, clean coffee with caramel aromas.
records.lede: Cauca is a southwestern department of high mountains and volcanic soils, where Indigenous, Afro-descendant and mestizo families grow coffee at about 1,400–2,100 m. Its protected regional profile credits long hours of sun and steady weather all year, with the mountains shielding farms from Pacific wind and damp. Inzá and Piendamó are coffee towns whose names appear on specialty lots; Piendamó is home to Diego Bermúdez's Finca El Paraíso, known for thermal-shock lots (fermented coffee rinsed in hot, then cold water).

facts.label: where coffee grows (4,600–6,900 ft)
protected regional origin name granted
lots entered in the Best Coffee of Cauca contest (2025)
record price there, for a Piendamó grower's lot (2025)

harvest.text: Main crop April–July and mitaca (the smaller second crop) November–January, says Barista Hustle; Juan Valdez puts the main crop a little earlier, March–June. Either way, Cauca picks most of its coffee in the first half of the year, as Nariño does.

cup.text: Cauca's protected regional profile describes high acidity, a medium body and a clean, soft cup with sweet and floral notes over strong caramel aromas; Juan Valdez likens its sweetness to a basket of fruit. Sweet Maria's tasted panela (unrefined cane sugar), brown sugar, raisin and cinnamon in an Inzá lot that arrived in 2025.
cup.why: The regional profile credits long hours of sunshine, steady weather all year and high mountains that block wind and humidity from the Pacific.

story.text: In August, Café de Cauca becomes a protected regional origin name, months after Nariño's.
A Castillo lot from Cauca places third at Colombia's Cup of Excellence.
The Best Coffee of Cauca contest draws 223 lots and sends 16 to auction; a Piendamó grower's lot sets a record US$42 a pound.

sections.title: Towns on the bag
body: Inzá lots come from farms at about 1,400 m to over 2,000 m, where growers traditionally ferment and wash in the same tank, then dry the coffee in covered rooms for two weeks or more. Piendamó is home to Diego Bermúdez's Finca El Paraíso and produced the 2025 contest record; one roaster lists a thermal-shock lot from El Tambo, about 28 km from the capital Popayán. Intelligentsia buys Pink Bourbon from Finca Juan Martín in the Sotará area.

records.name: The Coffee Axis
records.summary: Caldas, Risaralda and Quindío: Colombia's old coffee heartland, medium-bodied and bright.
records.lede: The Coffee Axis (Eje Cafetero) is Colombia's central coffee belt: Caldas, Risaralda and Quindío, with Barista Hustle also counting northern Tolima and northern Valle del Cauca. Old Caldas, which then took in Risaralda and Quindío, was the country's biggest producer in the early 1900s, but production has since shifted southwest toward Huila, Cauca and Nariño. Its coffee cultural landscape is a UNESCO World Heritage site.

facts.label: where coffee grows across the three (3,900–7,200 ft)
grown in old Caldas in 1932
of coffee in Caldas in 2021, down from 220,000 in 1960
plants per hectare in Quindío, the most intensively farmed department (2019)

harvest.text: Caldas picks its main crop August–December and Risaralda September–December, each with a small mitaca (second crop) in April–May. Quindío picks all year: its north peaks September–December and its south March–May, and in 2021 the growers' federation said half of its municipalities were in their main crop in the first half of the year.

cup.text: Juan Valdez, the growers' federation's brand, describes a strong coffee with character: a pronounced aroma, pronounced acidity and a medium body. The Coffee Axis has no protected regional profile of its own.

story.text: The first commercial coffee plantations go in, in what is now Caldas.
Caldas is carved out of Cauca and Antioquia, taking in today's Risaralda and Quindío.
Old Caldas grows more than a million bags of coffee.
Quindío and Risaralda split off from Caldas as departments of their own.
Caldas has about 60,000 hectares of coffee, after decades of decline.

sections.title: The three departments
body: Caldas, with its capital Manizales, has the widest altitude range and the heaviest rain, 2,100–5,500 mm a year. Risaralda, on a plateau between the central and western ranges of the Andes, has about 19,000 coffee-growing families (2022 figure). Quindío is the most technified, meaning densely planted and intensively farmed.

Cenicafé's regional Castillo lines here include Castillo Naranjal (for Caldas, Quindío, Risaralda and Valle), Castillo El Rosario and Castillo Paraguaicito; a 2006 Cenicafé study grew Castillo lines at the Maracay station in Quimbaya, Quindío.

records.name: Huila
records.summary: Colombia's biggest coffee department: sweet, balanced, with caramel notes.
records.lede: Huila is a department in Colombia's southwest where coffee grows between about 1,000 and 2,200 m, often under heavy cloud. It is now the country's largest coffee producer, and a 2015 study put about a third of its coffee at specialty grade, the quality tier specialty roasters buy. Its lots and Nariño's regularly lead Colombia's Cup of Excellence, the best-known national quality competition.

facts.label: where coffee grows (3,300–7,200 ft)
of its coffee graded specialty, in a 2015 study
of sun a day under the cloud cover
protected regional origin name granted

harvest.text: Barista Hustle gives August–December for the main crop and March–June for the mitaca, the smaller second crop. That is the pattern in the south, around San Agustín. Northern Huila runs the other way round, with its main crop in the first half of the year, so farms only 100 km apart can be in different harvests.

cup.text: Huila's protected regional profile describes a balanced, sweet cup with a medium-to-full body and an intense fruity, caramel-like aroma. Juan Valdez, the growers' federation's own brand, adds herbal notes to the fruit.
cup.why: The regional profile points to cloud that cuts direct sun to about 3.5 hours a day and to steady daytime temperatures; Juan Valdez says the cloud shields the cherries from intense sun so they ripen in a balanced, sweet way.
cup.prized: Huila and Nariño lots regularly top Colombia's Cup of Excellence, says Barista Hustle.

story.text: Coffee is first planted in Huila.
Huila's 4,471 coffee farms grow about 48,000 bags a year, around 1.5% of Colombia's crop.
Cheap land draws smallholder families as big farms are split up and sold; some bring know-how from the Coffee Axis.
Café de Huila becomes a protected regional origin name.
The Huila Coffee 2025 competition draws 156 lots, and a Pitalito grower's lot sets a record of US$65 a pound.

sections.title: Towns and varieties
