body: Pitalito and Acevedo are the towns most tied to the Papayo variety, with farms in Bruselas, near Pitalito, and in Oporapa. Workshop Coffee based its 2013 buying trip in San Agustín, at the department's southern tip.
Huila is also where Pink Bourbon was first identified and where Bourbon Ají comes from, says the importer Sucafina.

records.name: Nariño
records.summary: Colombia's high far south: bright, citric and sweet.
records.lede: Nariño, in Colombia's far south, grows its coffee high: about half of its farms are above 1,800 m. Over roughly 30 years it has gone from nearly unknown among specialty buyers to perhaps the best quality reputation in the country, says Barista Hustle. In 2011 it became the first Colombian region with its own protected origin name.

facts.label: where coffee grows (4,300–7,500 ft)
of its farms lie above 1,800 m (5,900 ft)
Colombia's first regional protected origin name
bags a year, about a fifth of Huila's (2022 figures)

harvest.text: Barista Hustle gives a single picking season, May–September. The growers' federation counts Nariño's first-half picking as its main crop, as it does Cauca's.

cup.text: Nariño's protected regional profile describes high acidity, a medium body, sweet notes and a clean, soft cup with a very pronounced aroma; Juan Valdez adds citric notes. Barista Hustle sums it up as notable acidity, sweetness and complex flavour.
cup.why: Cool temperatures slow ripening, which both the regional profile and Juan Valdez link to more sugar in the bean. The farms sit near the equator under strong, direct sun, on volcanic soils.
cup.prized: Nariño lots regularly top Colombia's Cup of Excellence, says Barista Hustle.

story.text: In February, Café de Nariño becomes Colombia's first protected regional origin name.
In January, StoneX reports the Nariño coffee committee expecting first-half output about 30% above a year earlier.

sections.title: Where it grows
body: The coffee lands center on Pasto, the department capital, with the Galeras volcano above it. Nariño grows far less than Huila, about 600,000 bags a year against roughly five times that.

records.name: Santander
records.summary: Shade-grown under native forest; balanced, herbal and lightly citric.
records.lede: Santander is where Colombian coffee first took hold: in the 1800s it flourished here and in neighbouring Norte de Santander, before Antioquia and the rest of the country took the lead. Much of it now grows under the shade of native forest, which keeps temperatures even, and it gained its protected origin name in 2014. A 2022 review says it has the highest share of rust-resistant varieties of any department.

facts.label: protected regional origin name granted
grown under trees, much of it native forest
of improved seed requested in 2025, the most of any department

harvest.text: In the first half of 2021 the growers' federation listed only a small part of Santander as picking, in its mitaca (the smaller second crop). The federation's 1932 coffee census put Santander's harvest at August–October with no second crop; we found no newer month-by-month figure.

cup.text: Santander's protected regional profile describes a clean, balanced cup with a medium-to-full body, medium acidity, and sweet, herbal and fruity flavours with a light citrus edge. Juan Valdez also stresses its pronounced aroma and herbal notes.
cup.why: Shade keeps temperatures even, says the regional profile; Juan Valdez adds that the forest protects the coffee from high heat.

story.text: Coffee flourishes first in Santander, Norte de Santander and Cundinamarca.
These early departments lose ground as production grows in Antioquia and spreads across the country.
Café de Santander becomes a protected regional origin name.
The growers' federation opens a regional coffee hub here in November, a COP 4.22 billion investment, and pilots carbon credits for smallholders' agroforestry farms (farms that mix coffee with trees).

records.name: Sierra Nevada
records.summary: Shaded coffee on a coastal mountain range: chocolate and nuts.
records.lede: The Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta is an isolated mountain range on Colombia's Caribbean coast, with peaks of about 5,700 m (18,700 ft) only 42 km from the sea. Coffee grows at about 500–1,900 m, much of it shaded by remaining forest, and many growers are Indigenous Arhuaco families. Its protected origin name, granted in 2017, covers 33 municipalities in Magdalena, Cesar and La Guajira.

facts.label: where coffee grows (1,600–6,200 ft)
municipalities in three departments under its protected name
of growers are Arhuaco, says Colombia's tourism site
the year it became a UNESCO biosphere reserve

harvest.text: One long picking season, September–February, says Barista Hustle, with no mitaca (second crop) listed. The growers' federation's 1932 census also recorded a single harvest in Magdalena, November–January.

cup.text: The protected regional profile describes a clean, balanced cup with an even, medium-to-full body, medium acidity, chocolate-like flavours and a sweet, nutty aroma. Juan Valdez puts it as hazelnut with lingering chocolate.
cup.why: The regional profile points to strong light, low rainfall, high humidity and coffee grown entirely in shade.

story.text: Forest clearing begins to cut the range's water supply; two rivers have since dried up completely.
UNESCO makes the Sierra Nevada a biosphere reserve.
Café de la Sierra Nevada becomes a protected regional origin name, covering coffee areas in Magdalena, Cesar and La Guajira.

sections.title: Who grows it
body: Colombia's tourism site says about 70% of the growers are Arhuaco, an Indigenous people, and Barista Hustle says more than a tenth of the area's population lives in Indigenous reserves. Growers use the remaining native forest as shade for their coffee, which helps protect that forest.

The protected name also takes in some coffee areas outside the range itself, in the eastern Andes near the Venezuelan border. Cenicafé bred a regional Castillo line for these departments, Castillo Pueblo Bello.

records.name: Tolima
records.summary: Third-biggest coffee department: citrus and fruit, with lively acidity.
records.lede: Tolima is Colombia's third-largest coffee producer, with coffee at about 1,000–2,000 m. Its north belongs to the Coffee Axis, while its southern municipalities, around Planadas, have become the most important for specialty buyers. A warm climate gives it two flowerings a year, and it gained its protected origin name in 2017.

facts.label: where coffee grows (3,300–6,600 ft)
Colombia's third-largest coffee department
record at the Tolima international coffee fair (2025)
protected regional origin name granted

harvest.text: Barista Hustle gives March–June for the main crop and October–December for the mitaca, the smaller second crop. The growers' federation counts central and southern Tolima's first-half picking as the main crop. The regional profile credits a warm climate with two flowerings a year.

cup.text: Tolima's protected regional profile describes medium-high acidity, a clean, soft, balanced cup, sweet flavours and citrus and fruit; Barista Hustle reads it as fairly high acidity and body with many fruity and citrusy flavours. Juan Valdez calls it smooth and balanced, sweet from the aroma on.

story.text: The first coffee trees are planted in Tolima.
Café de Tolima becomes a protected regional origin name.
At the third Tolima international coffee fair, 20 of 642 lots go to auction and one sets a record US$72 a pound.

sections.title: Where it grows
body: Planadas, in the far south, is the third-largest coffee municipality in all of Colombia. The Nevado del Tolima volcano rises in the north. A 2015 study of hundreds of samples from Tolima, Huila, Cauca, Nariño and Norte de Santander found Tolima's the least like the others.
Cenicafé, the federation's research centre, selected a regional Castillo line for Tolima, Castillo La Trinidad.

records.name: Brunca
records.summary: Early-ripening Pérez Zeledón and Coto Brus; mild to citrus-sweet cups.
records.lede: Brunca covers the coffee cantons of Pérez Zeledón, Coto Brus and Buenos Aires, and made about 20% of Costa Rica's crop in 2019/20. It ripens early, so the national harvest starts here, and in 2025 ICAFE split it into two regions named Pérez Zeledón and Coto Brus.

facts.label: of Costa Rica's crop in 2019/20
where it grows (2,000–5,600 ft)
top score in the honey and natural category at the 2025 Taza de la Excelencia, a Pérez Zeledón Gesha
split into Pérez Zeledón and Coto Brus regions

harvest.text: Picked from August to February. ICAFE counts Brunca as the early-ripening zone where Costa Rica's harvest begins.

cup.text: 1Zpresso's guide says Brunca varies widely: lower farms tend toward smoother cups, higher ones toward more sweetness, complex citrus and jasmine-like aromatics. Café Britt describes complex citrus ranging from very mild to very sweet, and Royal Coffee calls the profile milder and full-bodied.
cup.why: Altitude: farms run from 600 to 1,700 m (2,000–5,600 ft), and 1Zpresso links the sweeter, more citric cups to the higher ones.
cup.prized: Gesha lots from Pérez Zeledón won first place in both the washed category and the honey and natural category at the 2025 Taza de la Excelencia.

story.text: ICAFE described Brunca, with Coto Brus and Pérez Zeledón, as the early-ripening zone where the country's harvest begins.
Coto Brus's estimated harvest was 15,000 fanegas above 2019/20, and Pérez Zeledón's was rising too.
Pérez Zeledón Geshas won the washed category (Vista Paraíso, 90.63 points) and the honey and natural category (La Cusuka, 91.22) at the Taza de la Excelencia.
ICAFE split Brunca into two regions, Pérez Zeledón and Coto Brus.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Pérez Zeledón, Coto Brus and Buenos Aires are the cantons to look for. Coto Brus is higher and more humid and depends on coffee; Buenos Aires lies in the foothills of La Amistad International Park; Pérez Zeledón, the canton around San Isidro de El General, was among Brunca's first coffee areas.

records.name: Central Valley
records.summary: Where Costa Rican coffee began, around San José, Heredia and Alajuela.
records.lede: The Central Valley (Valle Central) surrounds San José, Heredia and Alajuela, on the central plateau where Costa Rican coffee growing began in 1779. It made about 15% of the crop in 2019/20, but its harvest has been shrinking, and in 2025 ICAFE folded the Tres Ríos region into it.

facts.label: of Costa Rica's crop in 2019/20
coffee first grown on the central plateau (Meseta Central)
where about 80% of its coffee grows (3,300–4,600 ft); the rest reaches 1,900 m (6,200 ft)

harvest.text: Picked from November to February. The valley has well-defined rainy and dry seasons.

cup.text: Café Britt describes a balanced cup with hints of chocolate and fruit and a subtle honey aroma; Royal Coffee calls the region's profile more citric and sweet.

feel.body: medium to full, depending on altitude

cup.prized: Cafe Imports says some of Costa Rica's best natural-process coffees (dried inside the whole cherry) come from here.

story.text: Coffee growing in Costa Rica began on the Meseta Central, the central plateau around San José.
The harvest came in 103,000 fanegas (Costa Rica's bushel-like harvest unit) below 2019/20, part of a downward trend over the last six harvests.
Hacienda Colima–Volcán Azul placed second among washed coffees at the national Taza de la Excelencia, with 90.09 points.
ICAFE merged Tres Ríos, a few kilometres east of the capital, into the Central Valley region.

records.name: Guanacaste
records.summary: Low farms across three provinces; soft acidity, round body.
records.lede: The Guanacaste coffee region spreads across parts of three provinces, Guanacaste, Puntarenas and Alajuela, and in Alajuela it centres on San Carlos and Sarapiquí. Its farms sit fairly low, at 600–1,300 m (2,000–4,300 ft), often under shade trees, and in 2025 ICAFE merged it into its Zona Norte (northern zone) region.

facts.label: where it grows (2,000–4,300 ft)
of Costa Rica's crop in 2019/20, with Orosi and Turrialba combined
average temperature (79 °F), the warmest region in 1Zpresso's guide

harvest.text: Picked from July to February.

cup.text: 1Zpresso's guide describes softer acidity, a moderate body and a round mouthfeel, sometimes with a salty edge and a bittersweet finish. Café Britt similarly notes a smooth body, light acidity and distinct bitter and salty notes.

sections.title: Now part of Zona Norte
body: In 2025 ICAFE folded Guanacaste into its Zona Norte region, so coffee from places like Nandayure now shares a region with places like San Carlos.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Wikipedia's table of the regions lists San Carlos, Sarapiquí, the Nicoya Peninsula and Puntarenas under Guanacaste.

records.name: Orosi
records.summary: Smallest harvest; a humid valley with chocolaty, elegant cups.
records.lede: Orosi is a valley in Cartago province where coffee is the leading industry, its hillsides lined with coffee and sugar cane. It makes the smallest harvest of Costa Rica's regions, and in 2025 ICAFE joined it to Turrialba; even together they remain the smallest.

facts.label: where it grows (3,300–4,600 ft)
of rain a year, May to November
harvest of any region, even after joining Turrialba in 2025

harvest.text: Picked from September to March by 1Zpresso's guide, though in 2020 ICAFE said picking in Orosi starts as early as July.

cup.text: 1Zpresso's guide says Orosi leans chocolaty, with an elegant acidity balancing its sweetness and body; Café Britt calls its coffees smooth and balanced.

sections.title: Growing it
body: The valley is humid, with about 2,500 mm of rain a year, and protected forest around it. 1Zpresso's guide links Orosi to larger beans and notes more than a century of coffee growing here.

sections.title: Now part of Turrialba
body: In 2025 ICAFE joined Orosi to the Turrialba region. Among its reasons, El Financiero reported, was that coffee from Turrialba, Orosi and Cachí shares similar traits.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Orosi is a district of Paraíso canton; Cachí is another name from the area.

records.name: Tarrazú
records.summary: Costa Rica's best-known region: high, sweet and brightly acidic.
records.lede: Tarrazú, in the mountains about 70 km south of San José, is Costa Rica's best-known coffee region and was its biggest in 2019/20, with about 40% of the crop. Most of it grows high enough to be graded SHB (Strictly Hard Bean, the top altitude grade). Locally the area is called Los Santos, and since 2025 that is also the name ICAFE, the national coffee institute, uses for the region.

facts.label: of Costa Rica's crop in 2019/20
where it grows (3,900–6,200 ft)
of Los Santos coffee land grew SHB beans (1,200–1,650 m · 3,900–5,400 ft) in 2019
protected origin name granted for three cantons

harvest.text: Picked from November to March. Rain falls from May to November and the dry season runs December to April; Café Britt says these clear seasons ripen the cherries evenly.

cup.text: Café Britt and a guide from grinder maker 1Zpresso both describe Tarrazú as tending toward chocolate, orange, vanilla and dried fruit; 1Zpresso adds a honey-like sweetness and jasmine-like aromatics.
cup.why: Announcing the 2019 protected name, the government credited the high altitude and late ripening for the coffee's very high acidity and very good body and aroma.
cup.prized: Competition lots: all three top coffees at the 2020 Taza de la Excelencia, Costa Rica's national quality contest, came from Tarrazú, two of them honey-processed (dried with some of the sticky fruit still on the seed).

story.text: Farmers began growing coffee in the high valley around San Marcos.
La Candelilla, in La Sabana de San Marcos, opened as Costa Rica's first micromill, a small mill a farm builds to process its own coffee.
Gesha production began in the region.
The government handed over a denomination of origin (a protected place name) covering the cantons of Tarrazú, Dota and León Cortés.
ICAFE renamed its region Los Santos, because only the council that runs the denomination may use the name Tarrazú.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Look for San Marcos de Tarrazú, the main town, and nearby Santa María (de Dota) and San Pablo, which also supply specialty coffee. The protected Tarrazú name covers three cantons (counties): Tarrazú, Dota and León Cortés. InterAmerican Coffee notes that this legal area is smaller than the area long sold as Tarrazú, so some coffee once labeled Tarrazú no longer qualifies.

sections.title: At harvest
body: Café Britt says the population of Los Santos nearly triples during the harvest, and that most farms grow their coffee under a mix of native and imported shade trees.

records.name: Tres Ríos
records.summary: The 'Bordeaux of Costa Rica', shrinking under urban growth.
records.lede: Tres Ríos sits a few kilometres east of San José, near the Irazú volcano, and has long been nicknamed the Bordeaux of Costa Rica. As the city spread over its farms, production fell, and in 2025 ICAFE folded it into the Central Valley region, though the Tres Ríos name can still be used to promote coffee.

facts.label: where it grows (3,900–5,400 ft)
merged into the Central Valley region
the volcano whose minerals enrich its soil

harvest.text: Picked from November to March.

cup.text: Cafe Imports describes a smooth, milder, easy-drinking profile with toffee sweetness and soft citrus. 1Zpresso's guide notes a refined, balanced acidity, a long finish and a fuller body.
cup.why: Its flavor is credited to fertile soil enriched with minerals from the Irazú volcano, balanced by rain and warm summers.
cup.watch: Urban growth has closed dozens of its coffee farms.

sections.title: Now part of the Central Valley
body: In June 2025 El Financiero reported that ICAFE had merged Tres Ríos into the Central Valley because it had become a small region: urban growth had replaced coffee plots and production had fallen. ICAFE's promotion manager, Andrés Piedra, said the Tres Ríos name can still be used in promotion.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Tres Ríos is in La Unión canton, Cartago province. Along with Tres Ríos itself, the communities of Concepción and San Ramón still grow coffee for the specialty market.

records.name: Turrialba
records.summary: Low, early-picking valley by an active volcano; gentle, light cups.
records.lede: Turrialba is a low region, at 500–1,400 m (1,600–4,600 ft), in a valley beside the active Turrialba volcano. It is among the first in Costa Rica to pick each year, from as early as July, and its coffee is known for a gentle, light cup. In 2025 ICAFE folded Orosi into it.

facts.label: where it grows (1,600–4,600 ft)
when picking can start, among the country's earliest
of Costa Rica's crop in 2019/20, with Orosi and Guanacaste combined

harvest.text: Picked from July to March, one of the earliest starts in Costa Rica.

cup.text: Café Britt describes mild acidity, a light body and a soft aroma, and 1Zpresso's guide a gentle, lighter cup with delicate aromatics.
cup.why: Café Britt says the active Turrialba volcano heavily shapes the flavors here.

story.text: ICAFE said picking would start from July in Turrialba and Orosi, as well as in the early-ripening Brunca region.
ICAFE merged Orosi into the Turrialba region; El Financiero noted that Turrialba's harvest had trended down over the previous six seasons.

sections.title: Growing it
body: Turrialba averages about 23 °C (73 °F), with roughly 2,800 mm of rain a year, on volcanic and alluvial (river-laid) soils, and 1Zpresso's guide says some of Costa Rica's earliest coffee farms were here. Royal Coffee says most coffee from Turrialba, Orosi and Guanacaste is graded HB or GHB (Hard Bean or Good Hard Bean), the grades for coffee grown below 1,200 m (3,900 ft).

records.name: West Valley
records.summary: Western slopes; orange, peach and honey; many competition winners.
records.lede: The West Valley (Valle Occidental) runs along the western slopes of Costa Rica's central mountains, on fertile volcanic soil, around towns like Naranjo and Grecia. It made about 20% of the country's crop in 2019/20, and Cafe Imports notes that a high share of Costa Rica's Cup of Excellence winners come from here.

facts.label: of Costa Rica's crop in 2019/20
where it grows (2,300–5,200 ft)
finalists at the 2020 Taza de la Excelencia, the national quality contest

harvest.text: Picked from October to February.

cup.text: Café Britt and 1Zpresso's guide describe West Valley coffees as ranging from orange and peach to honey and vanilla, and 1Zpresso adds chocolate-like notes. One roaster's red-honey lot from Naranjo (red honey leaves all the sticky fruit on the seed while it dries) is sold as bright, sweet and fruit-forward.
cup.prized: Cafe Imports notes a high share of the country's Cup of Excellence winners here, plenty of the Costa Rican varieties Villa Sarchi and Villalobos, and some newer, experimental ones such as SL28 and Gesha.

story.text: Villa Sarchi, a dwarf mutation of Bourbon, was found in north-western Alajuela province; it is still grown in small pockets here.
West Valley coffees made up 14 of the 26 finalists at the Taza de la Excelencia.
El Financiero reported that the urban growth behind Tres Ríos's decline is starting to be felt here too, in places like Grecia.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Naranjo, a canton in Alajuela province, is one West Valley name sold on bags; Grecia is another of the region's coffee towns.

records.name: Guji
records.summary: Southern Oromia's fruity naturals and washed lots, once sold as Sidamo.
records.lede: Guji is a zone of Oromia in southern Ethiopia, next door to Yirgacheffe and Sidama. It was long treated as part of Sidamo and has only fairly recently been recognised as a coffee area of its own, known for complex, fruity coffees, washed and natural.

facts.label: typical altitude (4,600–6,900 ft)
one Royal Coffee natural, from Deri Kidame, grew at 1,900–2,300 m (6,250–7,550 ft)
Uraga, Kercha, Hambela, Odo Shakiso, Adola and Bule Hora

harvest.text: Royal Coffee's Guji lots list October to January or November to February, depending on the lot.

cup.text: Coffee Hunter calls Guji complex, balanced and fruity, and 1Zpresso describes bright citrus and berry-like acidity with fruit-forward sweetness. Royal Coffee New York says its naturals tend to be fruit-forward with a medium body; in three Coffee Review write-ups of Guji coffees, cocoa nib showed up alongside the fruit each time.
cup.why: 1Zpresso credits fertile volcanic soils and big swings between day and night temperatures.
cup.prized: The Roasters Pack says the West Guji zone, home of the Kurume and Dega landraces, is known for some of Ethiopia's highest-quality coffee, with floral, citric cups.

sections.title: Reading the bag
body: Guji is a zone of Oromia, not part of the Sidama Region. Its coffee used to be sold in the exchange's Sidamo category, and some lots still carry both names, like Royal Coffee New York's “Ethiopia Natural Sidamo Guji G4”.
Woreda (district) names such as Hambela, Uraga, Kercha or Odo Shakiso often follow. Shakiso also has a washing station of that name, and Coffee Hunter photographs cherry sorting at Buku.

records.name: Harrar
records.summary: Eastern naturals: heavy, winey, blueberry and chocolate, more like Yemen.
records.lede: Harrar is the coffee of Ethiopia's dry eastern highlands, named for the old walled city of Harar. It is almost always natural (dried in the fruit) and tends to be heavy and winey, closer in style to Yemen's coffees than to Ethiopia's southern and western ones.

facts.label: almost always, dried inside the fruit
of the main regions Royal Coffee New York compares
longberry, shortberry and Mocha (peaberry)

harvest.text: Sources give one window for all of Ethiopia: about October to January (Cafe Imports, Achilles), or November to February (Royal Coffee New York). Cafe Imports expects shipments to arrive around April to June.

cup.text: 1Zpresso describes intense, winey fruit like blueberry and blackberry jam with a little spice and a heavy body, and Cafe Imports finds it distinctly chocolatey and nutty. Coffee Review says Harrars resemble Yemen's coffees more than southern or western Ethiopia's.
cup.why: 1Zpresso says the dry, cool climate suits natural processing, and Cafe Imports links the chocolate and nut tones to that drier climate.
cup.prized: The best show an intense blueberry or blackberry aroma, and roasters use it in espresso blends for its aromatics.
cup.watch: Drying in the fruit can tip into ferment: even a 93-point Harrar Coffee Review tasted in 2000 was noted as close to fermented.

story.text: The US trademark office turned down Ethiopia's “Harrar” application, part of a 2005–2007 push to register Harrar, Sidamo and Yirgacheffe in 34 countries.
The US office accepted Ethiopia's rebuttal on Harrar; by mid-2007 the three names held 28 registrations, including in Canada, the EU, Japan and the US.

sections.title: Reading the bag
body: Sweet Maria's speaks of a greater Harar or Hararghe region. Traders sort Harrar by bean: longberry, shortberry and Mocha, meaning peaberry, a cherry that grew one round seed instead of two.

records.name: Jimma
records.summary: Western zone known for naturals; home of Ethiopia's coffee research center.
records.lede: Jimma is a coffee zone in western Ethiopia's Oromia region, and the Limu coffee area sits inside it. It is best known for natural (dried-in-the-fruit) coffees, and the town of Jimma is home to the Jimma Agricultural Research Center, which released numbered selections like 74110.

facts.label: typical altitude (4,600–6,900 ft)
Jimma Agricultural Research Center founded (sources differ on the exact year)
release of 74110, 74112 and other early Jimma selections
districts Coffee Hunter groups under Limu and Jimma

harvest.text: Sources give one window for all of Ethiopia: about October to January (Cafe Imports, Achilles), or November to February (Royal Coffee New York). Cafe Imports expects shipments to arrive around April to June.

cup.text: 1Zpresso describes Jimma's naturals as tropical-fruited, with honey sweetness and wine-like aromatics, a full body and lively acidity.
cup.why: In a 2015 study by Jimma researchers, the Jimma site (1,753 m, 5,750 ft) gave the best natural coffee of three south-western sites, while the higher Gera site (1,940 m, 6,350 ft) gave the best washed coffee.

story.text: The Jimma Agricultural Research Center was founded to improve Ethiopian coffee and coordinate research nationally.
Selections 74110, 74112, 74140 and 74158 were released; a Royal Coffee New York Guji lot lists 74110 and 74112 today.

sections.title: Reading the bag
body: Coffee Hunter says the zone is politically defined as Jimma and puts Limu's woredas inside it, so bags may say Jimma, Limu or a woreda such as Gera or Goma. Cafe Imports spells it Djimma, and Sweet Maria's lists Agaro and Gera among western coffee areas.

records.name: Kaffa
records.summary: Southwestern forests where wild Arabica grows; the Gesha woreda is here.
records.lede: Kaffa (Keffa) is a forested zone in southwestern Ethiopia, often called the birthplace of Arabica: coffee still grows wild there, in deep forest at about 1,400–2,100 m. Coffee Hunter places the Gesha woreda (district), home of the Gesha variety, in this zone.

facts.label: where its forest coffee grows (4,600–6,900 ft)
Kafa forests named a UNESCO biosphere reserve
farm-gate coffee price in Kaffa, Bench Sheko and Sheka, October 2020 (Limu Seka, Gera and Gomma: 23–28)

harvest.text: Sources give one window for all of Ethiopia: about October to January (Cafe Imports, Achilles), or November to February (Royal Coffee New York). Cafe Imports expects shipments to arrive around April to June.

story.text: The traveller Paul Soleillet listed coffee among the main goods traded at Bonga, once the capital of the Kingdom of Kaffa.
The coffee that became the Gesha variety was collected from Ethiopian forests near a mountain usually written Gesha.
Building began on a National Coffee Museum in Bonga.
UNESCO named the Kafa Biosphere Reserve, protecting forest where wild Arabica grows.

sections.title: Reading the bag
body: You'll see Kaffa, Keffa or Kafa. Ethiocoffee groups Kaffa's coffee with Bench Maji's and Illubabor's as wild and semi-wild types. Older sources put the zone in the Southern Nations region (SNNPR); its main town, Bonga, is now the capital of the South West Ethiopia Peoples' Region, and a trading centre for coffee, honey and cardamom.

records.name: Limu
records.summary: Western washed coffees: sweet, clean and gentle, sometimes lemony.
records.lede: Limu is a coffee area in western Ethiopia's Oromia region, inside the zone politically defined as Jimma; its woredas (districts) include Limu Kossa and Limu Seka. It is best known for clean washed coffees with gentle acidity and a rounded sweetness.

facts.label: typical altitude (3,950–6,250 ft)
of the main regions Royal Coffee New York compares
farm-gate coffee price in Limu Seka, Gera and Gomma, October 2020

harvest.text: Sources give one window for all of Ethiopia: about October to January (Cafe Imports, Achilles), or November to February (Royal Coffee New York). Cafe Imports expects shipments to arrive around April to June.

cup.text: Coffee Hunter calls Limu sweet, smooth and clean with subtle acidity, and 1Zpresso adds floral and spicy undertones and a rounded sweetness. Algrano, a green-coffee marketplace, says it can taste very lemony.
cup.watch: Sources disagree on how it's processed: Coffee Hunter and 1Zpresso call Limu a washed-coffee area, while Royal Coffee New York says it is still mostly dried in the fruit, so check the process on the bag.

sections.title: Reading the bag
body: Coffee Hunter maps Limu and Jimma together, inside the Jimma zone, and lists Limu Kossa and Limu Seka among its woredas, so a bag may say Limu, Jimma or a woreda name.

records.name: Sidama
records.summary: Its own region since 2020; mostly washed, floral and citric.
records.lede: Sidama is a highland area of southern Ethiopia, in the Rift Valley, that became its own regional state in 2020; older bags call it Sidamo, the name Ethiopia trademarked. Most of its coffee is washed, and it tends toward citrus and florals.

facts.label: of its coffee is washed
typical altitude (4,900–7,200 ft)
voted yes in 2019 to make Sidama its own region
became Ethiopia's tenth regional state, on 18 June

harvest.text: Sources give one window for all of Ethiopia: about October to January (Cafe Imports, Achilles), or November to February (Royal Coffee New York). Cafe Imports expects shipments to arrive around April to June.

cup.text: 1Zpresso describes bright, citrus-led acidity and delicate sweetness, often with jasmine, bergamot and stone fruit; Wikipedia's overview singles out lemon, citrus and berries. Its naturals tend to be fruitier and fuller with softer acidity.
cup.why: 1Zpresso points to fertile volcanic soil, clear rainy seasons and large day–night temperature swings, and says its good water supply supports all the washing.
cup.prized: Sweet Maria's says areas once blended into bulk Sidama, such as Bensa and Chire, now stand out on their own.
cup.watch: Royal Coffee New York finds Sidama naturals fruit-forward and sweet but sometimes less delicate, and notes they must dry evenly to avoid defects.

story.text: The Sidama Coffee Farmers Cooperative Union was founded; Trade Aid called it Ethiopia's second-largest union in 2023.
The US trademark office turned down Ethiopia's “Sidamo” application; after a challenge, it was granted in February 2008.
In a November referendum, 98.5% of voters backed making Sidama a region of its own.
On 18 June Sidama left the Southern Nations region (SNNPR) and became Ethiopia's tenth regional state.

sections.title: Reading the bag
body: Sidamo is the older spelling and the old province name, and it is the one Ethiopia trademarked, so you'll see both. It has also been used loosely: Wikipedia lists Yirgacheffe and Guji as kinds of Sidamo, and Guji was sold in the exchange's Sidamo category. Today Guji is a zone of Oromia and Yirgacheffe is in Gedeo zone, both outside the Sidama Region.
Village and station names often follow the region: Sweet Maria's names Bensa and Chire, and Coffee Hunter shows the Bombe washing station.

records.name: Yirgacheffe
records.summary: Ethiopia's best-known washed coffee: floral, citric and tea-like.
records.lede: Yirgacheffe is a town and woreda (district) in Gedeo zone in southern Ethiopia, and on bags the name stands for a wider coffee area around it. It is the best-known of Ethiopia's washed coffees, famous for floral and citrus tones.

facts.label: typical altitude (6,250–7,200 ft)
districts Coffee Hunter groups under the Yirgacheffe name
Yirgacheffe's price rise by 2007, to $2 a pound, as its trademark drew attention

harvest.text: Sources give one window for all of Ethiopia: about October to January (Cafe Imports, Achilles), or November to February (Royal Coffee New York). Cafe Imports expects shipments to arrive around April to June.

cup.text: Yirgacheffe tends toward bright citrus and pronounced florals with a crisp, tea-like finish, say Coffee Hunter, 1Zpresso and Coffee Review. Cafe Imports finds its microregions differ: stone fruit and citrus in Adado, near-tropical fruit in Aricha, fruit tea in Kochere, toffee and almond in Chelchele.
cup.why: It is grown high, mostly at 1,900–2,200 m, and mostly washed, the method Royal Coffee New York links to its delicate, clean, floral cups.
cup.prized: Coffee Review calls a really fine Yirgacheffe extraordinary, yet it usually sells at everyday specialty prices.
cup.watch: Sweet Maria's finds the quality uneven, partly because coffee from neighbouring areas was often sold under the famous name.

story.text: The Yirgacheffe Coffee Farmers Cooperative Union was founded with 13 member unions; Royal Coffee New York says it has since grown to 28, with more than 38,000 farmers.
Ethiopia filed trademarks for Yirgacheffe, Sidamo and Harrar in 34 countries, and the US approved Yirgacheffe first.
The new Ethiopian Commodity Exchange (ECX) began selling most coffee pooled by region and grade, so lots could rarely be traced past the region.
From March, the exchange allowed washing stations to sell directly, which Cafe Imports expected to improve traceability.

sections.title: Reading the bag
body: Coffee Hunter lists eight woredas under the Yirgacheffe name, among them Kochere, Gedeb and Wenago, and Cafe Imports profiles microregions such as Adado, Aricha, Chelchele, Kochere and Konga. A label like “Yirgacheffe Aricha Gr1 Natural” reads region, place, grade, process.
Older sources treat Yirgacheffe as part of Sidamo, and 1Zpresso notes it was once part of the Sidama zone. It sits in Gedeo zone, outside the Sidama Region created in 2020.

records.name: Acatenango
records.summary: Shade-grown coffee on Fuego's ashy slopes, cooled by Pacific breezes.
records.lede: Acatenango is the valley among the Acatenango and Fuego volcanoes. Anacafé says coffee grows here under dense shade, up to about 2,000 m (6,500 ft), in coarse, sandy soil that Fuego's constant eruptions keep rich in minerals. Pacific breezes and clearly marked seasons let farms dry their coffee in the sun.

facts.label: temperatures (57–88 °F), the widest swing in Anacafé's figures
of rain a year (48–72 in)
a natural Geisha from Acatenango at the 2025 Cup of Excellence

harvest.text: Picked about December to March.

cup.text: Anacafé describes a marked acidity, a fragrant aroma, a balanced body and a clean, lingering finish; it names no specific flavors. Global Coffee Report's 2011 profile, written with Anacafé, also stresses the acidity and the long finish.

story.text: El Platanar y Anexos, a Caturra and Catuaí farm at 1,524 m (5,000 ft) in Acatenango, places 14th at the Cup of Excellence.
Two natural Geishas from Acatenango, from Los Jutes and La Cookies, place third and fourth among the competition's natural and honey exotics.
Two naturals from Chimaltenango, the department Acatenango belongs to, make the winners' list again.

records.name: Antigua
records.summary: A sunny volcano valley, now an EU-protected coffee name.
records.lede: Antigua is the valley around Guatemala's old colonial capital, ringed by the Agua, Fuego and Acatenango volcanoes. Anacafé, the national coffee association, describes it as sunny and low in humidity, with cool nights and the least rain of its eight regions. Its name was registered as a denomination of origin in Guatemala in 2011, and the EU protected it in October 2026.

facts.label: of rain a year (32–48 in), the least of the eight regions
humidity
denomination of origin registered in Guatemala
EU registers “Café Antigua” as a protected geographical indication

harvest.text: Picked about January to mid-March, by Anacafé-based guides. APCA, the growers' association, gives a wider window, November to April.

cup.text: Anacafé calls Antigua elegant and well balanced, with a rich aroma and a very sweet taste. The EU's 2026 description of Café Antigua lists honey, caramel, apple and toasted-nut aromas, a full body, and a lasting acidity that is neither sharp nor bitter.
cup.why: Coffee Review's Kenneth Davids notes that dry weather while the fruit ripens and is picked usually makes coffee sweeter, and Antigua gets the least rain of Anacafé's regions.
cup.prized: Sweetness and balance. Cafe Imports calls Antiguas sweet, smooth and good for blending.
cup.watch: Cafe Imports describes them as mild and on the lower-acid side.

story.text: The Antigua name gets its first trademark registration, according to a 2003 WIPO presentation.
Antigua's first certification program starts, by the same account.
Coffee Review notes that the growers' association does not count coffee from Fuego's Pacific-facing slopes, just outside the valley, as Antigua.
In December, Guatemala's registry certifies Antigua's denomination of origin as entry number 1 in its first book; the state holds the title.

On 8 October the EU registers “Café Antigua” as a protected geographical indication, on an application from the Asociación de Productores de Café Genuino Antigua, which says it began the process in 2021.

sections.title: Buying genuine Antigua
body: APCA, the Antigua growers' association, says it is made up of 40 farms, and points to a certificate of origin as the buyer's guarantee that a coffee is Genuine Antigua.
The EU protection covers green and roasted coffee, whole bean or ground, produced in Sacatepéquez department, and allows both Arabica and Robusta (Coffea canephora).

sections.title: How high is Antigua?
body: It depends who you ask. Anacafé puts the region at 1,520–1,710 m (5,000–5,600 ft); APCA says 1,400–2,000 m (4,600–6,600 ft); Cafe Imports says most farms sit at 1,300–1,600 m (4,300–5,200 ft).

sections.title: On the bag
body: Cup of Excellence lots from Sacatepéquez include Hacienda Carmona, a washed Bourbon grown at 1,783 m (5,850 ft) in Antigua Guatemala (2012), and Granja El Tempixque, a washed Catuaí from San Miguel Dueñas (2025), one of the department's municipalities.

records.name: Atitlán
records.summary: Smallholder coffee on the volcano slopes around Lake Atitlán.
records.lede: Atitlán's coffee grows around Lake Atitlán, about 90% of it on the slopes of three volcanoes, says Anacafé. Its soil is the richest in organic matter of Guatemala's five volcanic regions, and the lake's daily Xocomil winds shape the local climate. Much of the coffee comes from small Indigenous Kaqchikel and Tz'utujil growers.

facts.label: grown on the slopes of three volcanoes
of rain a year (72–92 in)
humidity

harvest.text: Picked about December to March.

cup.text: Anacafé describes Atitlán as very aromatic, with a bright citrus acidity and a full body. Cafe Imports adds nut and chocolate notes balanced by lemony acidity, with some florals.
cup.why: Cafe Imports links the nutty, chocolatey side to the windy, wet climate around the lake.

story.text: Coffee Review finds most Atitlán samples organic, from smallholder cooperatives often cut off by rough terrain.
Two Atitlán naturals place in the Cup of Excellence: a Ruiru 11 from San Lucas Tolimán and a Pacamara from Santiago Atitlán.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Look for municipalities such as Santiago Atitlán and San Lucas Tolimán. Finca Pampojila in San Lucas Tolimán placed again in 2026, listed under Sololá department, with a natural Ruiru 11.

records.name: Cobán
records.summary: Guatemala's rainforest region: rain, mist and fresh-fruit cups.
records.lede: Cobán is Guatemala's rainforest region, in the center of the country: cloudy, cool and wet all year. Anacafé says it has two seasons, rainy and rainier, and a fine mist locals call chipi-chipi hangs over hills of limestone and clay soil.

facts.label: of rain a year (120–160 in), second only to San Marcos
humidity, the highest in Anacafé's figures
temperatures (59–68 °F)

harvest.text: Picked about December to March.

cup.text: Anacafé describes a pleasant aroma, a fine, well-balanced body and distinct fresh-fruit notes. An older profile adapted from Anacafé material calls it medium-bodied, with light acidity.

story.text: German immigrants first plant coffee here at the end of the 19th century, says Global Coffee Report's 2011 profile.
A washed Centroamericano H1 from Finca Vinaros in Alta Verapaz, the department around Cobán, wins a Cup of Excellence place with 87.05 points.

sections.title: The weather
body: Coffee Review describes Cobán's weather as moist and Caribbean-influenced, and Perfect Daily Grind says the coffee grows mostly in mountains reached by tropical air from the Atlantic.

records.name: Fraijanes
records.summary: A high volcanic plateau dusted by ash from Pacaya.
records.lede: Fraijanes is a high plateau whose soil gets an occasional light dusting of ash from Pacaya, which Anacafé calls Guatemala's most active volcano. Morning cloud and dew clear quickly and the dry season is sunny, so coffee is dried in the sun. Fraijanes is also a municipality in Guatemala department, at about 1,585 m (5,200 ft).

facts.label: of rain a year (60–120 in)
temperatures (54–79 °F)
harvest, the earliest finish of the eight regions

harvest.text: Picked about December to February.

cup.text: Anacafé describes a bright, persistent acidity, plenty of aroma and a defined body, but names no specific flavors. In 2003 Coffee Review could find only one Fraijanes sample and called an Intelligentsia Fraijanes assertively acidic.

story.text: Coffee Review calls Fraijanes a very old, well-established high plateau with a sunny harvest season, but says few of its coffees reach the US.

Global Coffee Report describes Fraijanes as hemmed in by a growing city and facing labour shortages, contamination and crime, and profiles San Agustín Las Minas, a Rainforest Alliance farm that treats its own and the nearby city's wastewater, which would otherwise reach Lake Amatitlán untreated.

records.name: Huehuetenango
records.summary: The highest, driest of Guatemala's non-volcanic regions, and its Cup of Excellence powerhouse.
records.lede: Huehuetenango is Guatemala's mountainous northwest, on the Mexican border. Anacafé calls it the highest and driest of the country's three non-volcanic regions, kept free of frost by hot, dry winds from Mexico's Tehuantepec plain. It dominates the Cup of Excellence, the national competition and auction for the year's best lots: in 2026, farms there took 16 of the 27 winning places.

facts.label: Cup of Excellence winning places in 2026
top 2026 bid, for a lot of El Injerto's natural Geisha
soils, not volcanic ones
of rain a year (48–56 in)

harvest.text: Picked about January to April.

cup.text: Anacafé describes a fine, intense acidity, a full body and pleasant wine-like notes. Cafe Imports finds crisp apple-like (malic) and citrus acidity with toffee sweetness, and calls Huehue the most fruit-forward and complex of Guatemala's coffees.
cup.why: The dry Tehuantepec winds keep frost away, which lets cherries on high farms ripen slowly, 1Zpresso explains.
cup.prized: Roasters often prefer them to Antiguas, Coffee Review noted in 2003, calling the region an insider's favorite.
cup.watch: Natural (dried-in-the-fruit) lots vary more from lot to lot than washed ones, 1Zpresso notes.

story.text: Coffee Review calls Huehuetenango an insider's favorite; many of its samples come from small organic cooperatives.
El Injerto, Arturo Aguirre's farm, is already an eight-time Cup of Excellence winner, Global Coffee Report notes.
A washed Geisha from La Gran Manzana wins the washed-exotics category with 91.15 points; one lot sells for $143.10 a pound.
El Injerto's natural Geisha scores 91.86, the competition's highest, and one of its lots sells for $449.10 a pound.

sections.title: Where it's grown
body: Because the region is remote, nearly every producer processes their own coffee, and its many rivers and streams let mills sit almost anywhere, Anacafé says. Global Coffee Report notes the area was once a Mam Maya kingdom.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Lots often name a municipality rather than the department. 2025 Cup of Excellence winners came from La Libertad (home of El Injerto), San Pedro Necta, Cuilco and Unión Cantinil, and the same farms were listed under Huehuetenango in 2026.

records.name: Nuevo Oriente
records.summary: Smallholder coffee in the east, on old volcanic ground; chocolatey.
records.lede: Nuevo Oriente is a small region on Guatemala's eastern edge, bordering Honduras; Prensa Libre places it in Chiquimula department. It sits on a former volcanic range whose soil is metamorphic rock, balanced in minerals. Coffee has been grown here since the 1950s, almost all by small producers, in what was once one of the country's poorest, most isolated areas.

facts.label: when small farms began growing coffee here
of rain a year (72–80 in)
soil that holds water through the dry season

harvest.text: Picked about December to March.

cup.text: Anacafé calls Nuevo Oriente well balanced and full-bodied, with a chocolaty flavor. An importer's regional lot (StoneX) lists milk chocolate with orange and lemon acidity and a medium body.
cup.why: Cafe Imports links its full, balanced cup to cloudy, rainy weather with steady temperatures and little sun.

records.name: San Marcos
records.summary: The hottest, rainiest region, with delicate floral cups.
records.lede: San Marcos, in Guatemala's Pacific-facing mountains, is the warmest and wettest of Anacafé's eight regions, with up to 5,000 mm (200 in) of rain a year. The rains arrive earliest here, so coffee flowers first. Because rain at harvest time is unpredictable, much of the coffee is started in the sun and finished in a Guardiola, a mechanical dryer.

facts.label: of rain a year (200 in), the most of the eight regions
temperatures (70–81 °F), the warmest region
to flower in Guatemala, because the rains start earliest

harvest.text: Picked about December to March.

cup.text: Anacafé describes delicate floral notes in the aroma and the cup, a pronounced acidity and a good body. Global Coffee Report's 2011 profile, credited to Anacafé, says the same.
cup.watch: Coffee Review's Kenneth Davids found a 2003 San Marcos (a Green Mountain Dos Marías) assertively acidic.

story.text: Most San Marcos coffee reaching the US comes from one farm, Dos Marías, run by the Asturias family, Coffee Review reports.
Anacafé holds its 11th coffee competition for Quetzaltenango and San Marcos, with categories for the regional coffee and for processes such as honeys and naturals.

sections.title: How it's grown
body: Most farms have their own processing mills, Anacafé says. 1Zpresso links the region's fertile soil to the nearby Tajumulco volcano.

records.name: Agalta
records.summary: Eastern Honduras: family farms, tropical fruit, caramel and chocolate.
records.lede: Agalta is eastern Honduras, taking in Olancho, El Paraíso and parts of Francisco Morazán, says Coffeeness, and most of its farms are family-owned. Sources disagree on the weather: Perfect Daily Grind calls the climate more tropical, while Coffeeness describes a drier microclimate in a rain shadow, an area mountains shelter from rain.

facts.label: plus El Paraíso and parts of Francisco Morazán

cup.text: Perfect Daily Grind's 2017 guide describes diverse tropical fruit, a caramel and chocolate fragrance, a delicate but pronounced acidity and a sweet finish. Coffeeness finds it sweet and chocolate-led with a hint of spice and medium body, and says washed lots have a lively acidity and a crisp, clean finish.

harvest.text: IHCAFE's regional profile gives December to March; Coffee Hunter and a 2023 El Heraldo guide give the same months.

sections.title: IHCAFE's profile
body: IHCAFE's regional profile, as republished by RedHonduras, places Agalta in Olancho, Yoro, Atlántida and Colón, at 1,100–1,400 m (3,600–4,600 ft), 14–22 °C (57–72 °F) and 1,350–1,950 mm (53–77 in) of rain a year, with Bourbon, Caturra and Typica. It describes tropical fruit, a caramel and chocolate fragrance and a sweet aftertaste. Coffee Hunter also puts Agalta in the north and east; Coffeeness instead puts it in Olancho, El Paraíso and parts of Francisco Morazán.

records.name: Comayagua
records.summary: Central Honduras: bright, creamy cups and the country's top 2016 yields.
records.lede: The Comayagua region is central Honduras, covering Comayagua and Francisco Morazán, the department of the capital, Tegucigalpa. Coffeeness describes hot days, cool nights, moderate rain and well-balanced loamy soil, and heavy investment in processing equipment. IHCAFE, the national coffee institute, recorded the country's highest yields here in 2016.

facts.label: quintals (100 lb) of green coffee per manzana (1.72 acres) in 2016, the country's best yield
a washed Geisha from Francisco Morazán, third among 2026's Cup of Excellence exotics
what that Geisha sold for

cup.text: Perfect Daily Grind's 2017 guide describes a sweet, citrusy fragrance, bright acidity and a creamy, rich body. Coffeeness finds tropical fruit and balanced acidity, and says honey and washed lots give cleaner, more consistent cups.

story.text: Comayagua posts the country's highest average yield, 30.19 quintals of green coffee per manzana, by IHCAFE's count.
PDG's Comayagua profile cites José Abel Girón Dubón's Pacamara from Finca Las Botijas, washed champion of Project Origin's Best of Honduras auction at 91.34 points and $29.10 a pound.
El Pino's washed Geisha from Francisco Morazán scores 90.39 at the Cup of Excellence and sells for $84.60 a pound.

harvest.text: IHCAFE's regional profile gives December to March; Coffee Hunter and a 2023 El Heraldo guide give the same months.

sections.title: IHCAFE's profile
body: IHCAFE's regional profile, as republished by RedHonduras, gives 1,100–1,400 m (3,600–4,600 ft), 14–22 °C (57–72 °F) and 1,350–1,700 mm (53–67 in) of rain a year, with Bourbon, Caturra and Typica. It describes a sweet, citrusy fragrance, a vibrant acidity with citrus and sweet flavors, and a creamy body. El Heraldo's 2023 guide gives 1,100–1,700 m (3,600–5,600 ft) and adds Lempira.

records.name: Copán
records.summary: Western Honduras by Guatemala: chocolate, caramel and a creamy body.
records.lede: Copán is Honduras's western coffee region, taking in Copán, Ocotepeque and part of Santa Bárbara, along the borders with Guatemala and El Salvador. Its temperatures swing more than almost anywhere in the country, with lows of 11.5 °C (53 °F), and most of its coffee is grown in shade. It can be sold under the protected regional name Honduran Western Coffees (HWC).

facts.label: lows (53 °F); possibly the country's coolest region
Honduran Western Coffees, a protected regional name it shares with Opalaca
departments: Copán, Ocotepeque and part of Santa Bárbara

cup.text: Perfect Daily Grind's 2017 regional guide describes a sweet aroma, chocolate, caramel and citrus, a delicate acidity, a bold, creamy body and a long, balanced finish. Coffeeness finds chocolate and nut with medium body and acidity, and calls it ideal for espresso.
cup.why: Coffeeness credits the high elevations, which slow the ripening of the cherries.
cup.prized: Sasa Sestic, interviewed for the PDG guide, finds Copán coffees often work well in blends.

harvest.text: IHCAFE's regional profile gives November to March; Coffee Hunter and a 2023 El Heraldo guide give the same months.

sections.title: IHCAFE's profile
body: IHCAFE's regional profile, as republished by RedHonduras, gives 1,000–1,500 m (3,300–4,900 ft), 12–22 °C (54–72 °F) and 1,300–2,300 mm (51–91 in) of rain a year, with Bourbon, Caturra and Catuaí. It describes chocolate flavor, a round, balanced body and a long, pleasant aftertaste. El Heraldo's 2023 guide gives a wider 1,000–1,700 m (3,300–5,600 ft) and 16–24 °C (61–75 °F), and adds a sweet aroma.

records.name: El Paraíso
records.summary: By Nicaragua: Parainema country, and a 2017 Honduran price record.
records.lede: El Paraíso is southeastern Honduras, on the Nicaraguan border, and relatively warm at 16–22.5 °C (61–73 °F). It is known for Parainema, a rust-resistant variety that IHCAFE, the national coffee institute, released in 2004. In 2017 a Parainema from Finca El Laurel here won the Cup of Excellence and sold for $124.50 a pound, a Honduran record at the time.

facts.label: the 2017 Cup of Excellence winner, a Parainema: a Honduran record then
that lot's score, grown at 1,400 m (4,600 ft)
temperatures (61–73 °F), warm for Honduran coffee

cup.text: Perfect Daily Grind's 2017 guide describes sweet, citric, smooth cups with grape, mango and tropical fruit, a floral acidity and a creamy body; its winning Parainema showed green apple, jasmine, peach and blueberry. Coffeeness describes something gentler: nutty and brown-sugar sweet, medium-bodied, with low acidity.

story.text: IHCAFE releases Parainema, a rust-resistant selection from the Sarchimor line T5296.
Oscar Daniel Ramírez Valerio's Parainema from Finca El Laurel wins the Cup of Excellence with 91.81 points and sells for $124.50 a pound.
Laurel #3 places second in the Cup of Excellence's Parainema category with 89.47.
El Laurel places sixth among the Parainemas, with 87.68.

harvest.text: IHCAFE's regional profile gives December to March; Coffee Hunter and a 2023 El Heraldo guide give the same months.

sections.title: IHCAFE's profile
body: IHCAFE's regional profile, as republished by RedHonduras, gives 1,100–1,400 m (3,600–4,600 ft), 16–22 °C (61–72 °F) and 950–1,950 mm (37–77 in) of rain a year, with Catuaí and Caturra. It describes citrus flavors, a sweet fragrance, a smooth body and a lingering aftertaste. El Heraldo's 2023 guide gives 1,100–1,700 m (3,600–5,600 ft) and adds Pacas, Parainema and Lempira.

records.name: Montecillos
records.summary: Home of Café de Marcala, Honduras's first protected origin name.
records.lede: Montecillos lies in southwestern Honduras along the Salvadoran border, around the Montecillos mountains. Cold nights at altitude slow the ripening of the cherries, Perfect Daily Grind writes, and the region is home to Café de Marcala, Honduras's first denomination of origin, a legally protected place name.

facts.label: Honduran denomination of origin: Café de Marcala
top score of the 2025 Cup of Excellence, a washed Geisha from La Paz
top bid for that Geisha

cup.text: Perfect Daily Grind's 2017 guide describes citrus, peach, apricot and caramel, a velvety body and a sparkling acidity it calls tartaric (the acid found in grapes). Coffeeness finds sweet citrus with an apple-like acidity.
cup.why: PDG credits the altitude and cold nights, which let the cherries ripen more slowly.

story.text: A washed Geisha from La Salvaje in La Paz wins the exotic category of the Honduran Cup of Excellence with 91.59, the competition's top score.
La Paz places again, with a washed Geisha from the same producer, Fabio Antonio Caballero García, and a natural Parainema from Liquidambar.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Look for “Marcala” or “Café de Marcala”, the protected name, and for La Paz, a department Coffeeness places in Montecillos. Coffeeness also puts Intibucá and Lempira here, which PDG assigns to Opalaca.

sections.title: IHCAFE's profile
body: IHCAFE's regional profile, as republished by RedHonduras, places Montecillos in La Paz, Comayagua, southern Santa Bárbara and Intibucá, at 1,200–1,600 m (3,950–5,250 ft), 12–21 °C (54–70 °F) and 1,300–2,300 mm (51–91 in) of rain a year, with Bourbon, Catuaí, Caturra and Pacas. It describes fruity, sweet fragrances, a vibrant, bright acidity, orange and peach, and a velvety body. El Heraldo's 2023 guide gives 14–22 °C (57–72 °F) and 1,200–1,700 mm (47–67 in).

harvest.text: IHCAFE's regional profile gives December to April; Coffee Hunter and a 2023 El Heraldo guide give the same months.

records.name: Opalaca
records.summary: Fruit-forward mountain coffee and many Cup of Excellence winners.
records.lede: Opalaca covers much of Santa Bárbara, Intibucá and Lempira, and takes its name from the Opalaca mountains; Coffeeness describes a cool, humid climate with heavy rain. These three departments now supply most Cup of Excellence winners, the national competition and auction for the year's best lots: in 2026, 24 of the 30 winning places came from them.

facts.label: 2026 Cup of Excellence places from Santa Bárbara, Lempira and Intibucá
2025 Cup of Excellence places from Santa Bárbara alone
top 2026 bid, for a washed Geisha from El Pimporro in Intibucá

cup.text: Perfect Daily Grind's 2017 guide describes tropical fruit, grape and berry with a fine, delicate acidity; Sasa Sestic adds mango, florals and strong aromas. Coffeeness calls it wine-like and complex, with apple-like acidity and milk chocolate.
cup.prized: Geishas, Pacas and traditional Typicas. The 2026 Cup of Excellence's best traditional lots were washed Typicas from Lempira and washed Pacas from Santa Bárbara.

story.text: Jorge Lanza, a producer from Santa Bárbara, wins the Honduran Cup of Excellence.
Santa Bárbara farms take 22 of the 30 Cup of Excellence places, and a natural Typica from Finca Dariela in Lempira tops the traditional category with 90.50.
A washed Geisha from El Pimporro in Intibucá wins with 90.50 points and sells for up to $90 a pound; washed Typicas from Lempira top the traditional category.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Competition lists and many bags name the department: Santa Bárbara, Lempira or Intibucá. PDG splits Santa Bárbara between Opalaca and Copán, so a Santa Bárbara coffee could come from either region.

sections.title: IHCAFE's profile
body: IHCAFE's regional profile, as republished by RedHonduras, gives 1,100–1,600 m (3,600–5,250 ft), 19–21 °C (66–70 °F) and 1,350–1,900 mm (53–75 in) of rain a year, with Bourbon, Caturra, Catuaí and Typica. It describes an aromatic, balanced cup with a fine, delicate acidity, grape and blackberry, a smooth body and a sweet aftertaste. El Heraldo's 2023 guide gives 1,100–1,700 m (3,600–5,600 ft) and 16–22 °C (61–72 °F).

harvest.text: IHCAFE's regional profile gives November to February; Coffee Hunter and a 2023 El Heraldo guide give the same months.

records.name: Embu
records.summary: Mount Kenya's southeastern slopes: juicy, sweet, berry and caramel.
records.lede: Embu is a county on Mount Kenya's southeastern slopes, where many people work as coffee farmers. 1Zpresso describes its coffees as juicy and full, with bright fruit acidity and pronounced sweetness.

facts.label: typical altitude (4,900–6,550 ft)
average temperature
rain a year

harvest.text: 1Zpresso gives October to December. Across Kenya, some areas also pick a smaller fly crop in mid-year; Sweet Maria's says June to August.

cup.text: 1Zpresso describes bright fruit acidity and pronounced sweetness, with berry, citrus, floral, honey and caramel-like notes, juicy and full.

sections.title: Factories on the bag
body: Coffee Hunter's Kavutiri factory belongs to the Murue Farmers' Cooperative Society: 980 members in Runyenjes division at about 1,700 m (5,600 ft), whose cherry is pulped, fermented overnight in tiled tanks, washed in river water and dried on raised beds. Royal Coffee's Kathakwa factory gathers 1,050 smallholders at 1,600–1,700 m (5,250–5,600 ft) and picks from October to December.

records.name: Kiambu
records.summary: Estate country north of Nairobi: tropical fruit, bright and full.
records.lede: Kiambu is the county just north of Nairobi, and unlike most of Kenya, where cooperatives grow most coffee, it is dominated by large estates, many owned by multinational companies. Its coffee is mostly washed, and 1Zpresso finds vivid tropical fruit in it.

facts.label: typical altitude (4,900–6,900 ft)
large estates dominate here, unlike most of Kenya
rain a year

harvest.text: 1Zpresso gives September to December, a little earlier than the Mount Kenya counties. Across Kenya, some areas also pick a smaller fly crop in mid-year; Sweet Maria's says June to August.

cup.text: 1Zpresso describes vivid tropical fruit, bright acidity and a refreshing but full mouthfeel.
cup.watch: Royal Coffee says the big estates favour mechanised, higher-yield farming, which can come at the cost of cup quality.

sections.title: Estates on the bag
body: Kiambu lots often come from estates or small grower groups. Melbourne Coffee Merchants imports Muhathi Estate, 5 ha at 1,720 m (5,650 ft) in the Aberdare foothills near the Komothai river. Sample Coffee, a roaster, sells lots from the Ngewa-Komothai growers, about 30 producers at 1,600–2,000 m (5,250–6,550 ft) near the Gatamaiyo Forest Reserve, each with a small wet mill of their own.

records.name: Kirinyaga
records.summary: Mount Kenya's eastern slopes: floral, cranberry and blackcurrant, full-bodied.
records.lede: Kirinyaga is the county east of Nyeri, on Mount Kenya's eastern slopes, with volcanic soil and a mix of steep mountainsides and gentler hills. Its coffees tend to be floral and lively, with cranberry and blackcurrant notes and a full body.

facts.label: typical altitude (4,250–6,250 ft)
rain a year
Kerugoya, the largest town (5,079 ft); coffee and tea grow on the higher ground

harvest.text: 1Zpresso gives October to January. Across Kenya, some areas also pick a smaller fly crop in mid-year; Sweet Maria's says June to August.

cup.text: 1Zpresso describes floral aromas, cranberry and blackcurrant, lively acidity and a full body.
cup.why: Royal Coffee credits the volcanic soil close to Mount Kenya.

sections.title: Factories on the bag
body: The Rungeto Farmers' Cooperative Society runs the Karimikui, Kii and Kangoi factories. InterAmerican puts Karimikui's 1,400 farmers at 1,600–1,800 m (5,250–5,900 ft), with cherry pulped, fermented overnight, washed and dried on raised tables for 8–14 days. Driftaway sells a blend from the Kii and Kairu factories, run by Rungeto and by the far larger Baragwi society (16,892 members). Baragwi's Guama factory topped Coffee Review's 2016 list of 30 coffees with 97 points, Business Daily reported.

records.name: Murang'a
records.summary: Lush central-highland county of smallholders: floral, berry and blackcurrant.
records.lede: Murang'a is a lush county in Kenya's central highlands with volcanic soil, where Royal Coffee counts up to 100,000 smallholders and more small farms than estates. Its washed coffees tend toward florals, berries and blackcurrant with balanced acidity.

facts.label: typical altitude (4,900–6,250 ft)
smallholders, by Royal Coffee's 2026 count
rain a year

harvest.text: 1Zpresso gives October to December. Across Kenya, some areas also pick a smaller fly crop in mid-year; Sweet Maria's says June to August.

cup.text: 1Zpresso describes floral aromas with berry, citrus and blackcurrant, balanced acidity and a medium body, and says washing gives a clean, bright cup.
cup.why: Both 1Zpresso and Royal Coffee point to its fertile volcanic soil.

sections.title: Factories on the bag
body: InterAmerican's Kaganda factory, of the Kaganda Farmers Cooperative Society in Kahuro, has 1,500 members at 1,800–1,900 m (5,900–6,250 ft). Coffee Hunter lists Kirimahiga (New Kiriti society, 781 growers) and Kanjathi (Kangiri society, 1,300 growers) on the slopes of the Aberdare Range, with the main crop from October and a smaller fly crop from April.

records.name: Nyeri
records.summary: Kenya's most famous coffee county: bright citrus and blackcurrant.
records.lede: Nyeri is a county on the southwestern slopes of Mount Kenya, and Royal Coffee calls it Kenya's most famous specialty coffee region. Most of its coffee comes from smallholders, and it tends toward bright citrus acidity and blackcurrant-like fruit.

facts.label: typical altitude (5,250–6,550 ft)
rain a year
which Royal Coffee links to some of Kenya's best cups

harvest.text: 1Zpresso gives October to December. Across Kenya, some areas also pick a smaller fly crop in mid-year; Sweet Maria's says June to August.

cup.text: 1Zpresso describes bright citrus acidity and blackcurrant-like fruit with a subtle wine-like edge, complex and well balanced. Royal Coffee says Nyeri's red soil produces some of the best cup quality in Kenya.
cup.why: 1Zpresso points to its 1,600–2,000 m altitude and fertile, well-drained volcanic soil; Royal Coffee singles out the red soil.

sections.title: Selling it
body: In 2013/14 politicians in the Nyeri area stepped into how its coffee was marketed and limited its transport to control where it was sold, saying it was for the farmers; Sweet Maria's notes many questions since about whether farmers gained.

sections.title: Factories on the bag
body: Importers list Nyeri lots by factory (the Kenyan word for a wet mill) and the cooperative society that runs it. Royal Coffee's Gura factory belongs to the Othaya Farmers Cooperative Society: 500 members at 1,700–1,890 m (5,600–6,200 ft), picking from November to January. StoneX lists Gaturiri, of the Barichu society in Mathira East, and Melbourne Coffee Merchants imports Kiamabara, of the Mugaga society, whose 910 members farm at 1,600–1,900 m (5,250–6,250 ft).

records.name: Chiapas
records.summary: Mexico's biggest grower, on the Guatemalan border: full-bodied, chocolatey
records.lede: Mexico's southernmost coffee state straddles the Guatemalan border and grows about 40% of the country's coffee, at roughly 800–1,700 m (2,600–5,600 ft). Indigenous Mayan communities and their cooperatives are at the heart of coffee here.

facts.label: of Mexico's coffee (Coffee Review says about 41%)
growing altitude (2,600–5,600 ft)
the floor for coffee sold as Café Chiapas (2,600 ft)
the 2019 Cup of Excellence winner, a natural Geisha

harvest.text: Mexico picks from about November to March, with timing shifting by altitude; new-crop beans often reach roasters from spring onward.

cup.text: Coffeeness describes Chiapas coffee as full-bodied, with chocolatey sweetness and gentle acidity, and Soconusco lots as balanced with a bright, clean finish. Sweet Maria's finds some Chiapas lots resemble those from Guatemala's Huehuetenango, just across the border.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Coffeeness singles out the Soconusco area. Cooperatives named on Chiapas coffees include Majomut and Tzotzilotic Tzobolotic. Coffee had spread here, and to Oaxaca, by the mid-1800s.

sections.title: The protected name
body: Café Chiapas was requested by the state's coffee commission, COMCAFE. It covers coffee grown above 800 m (2,600 ft), which the declaration puts at about 75% of the state's coffee land, in twelve regions, among them Tapachula, Motozintla, Comitán, San Cristóbal de las Casas and Palenque. The rules name tall varieties (Typica, Maragogype, Bourbon, Mundo Novo) and short ones (Caturra, Garnica, Catuaí, Catimor, Pacamara), call for washed coffee dried at no more than 70 °C (158 °F), and describe high acidity, an intense aroma and a noticeable body. That is livelier than the gentle acidity Coffeeness describes.

story.text: Café Chiapas becomes a protected name (a denomination of origin) for coffee grown above 800 m (2,600 ft).
Finca Santa Cruz, at 1,680 m (5,500 ft) in the El Triunfo biosphere reserve, wins the Cup of Excellence with a natural Geisha scoring 93.04, from 248 entries.
The same farm wins both the washed category (91.36) and the natural and honey category (90.83).
Its natural Geisha tops the experimental category with 91.33 and draws the year's top bid, $94.70 a pound.

records.name: Oaxaca
records.summary: Sierra Madre coffee from small farms: bright, citrusy and floral
records.lede: Oaxaca's coffee grows in the Sierra Madre mountains at about 1,200–1,700 m (3,900–5,600 ft), almost all of it on small family farms. Pluma Hidalgo is its best-known area.

facts.label: growing altitude (3,900–5,600 ft)
its prized growing area
Café Pluma becomes a protected name, covering 30 municipalities
growers in 30-plus communities covered by the Pluma name

harvest.text: The Café Pluma rules describe a harvest of about six months, November to April, with altitude shifting when the fruit ripens.

cup.text: Coffeeness describes bright, citrusy cups with floral aromatics and a light body. Sweet Maria's ranks Oaxaca with Chiapas as Mexico's most interesting regions for quality, and says Oaxaca coffees taste distinct from those of Veracruz and Chiapas.
cup.why: Coffeeness credits Pacific breezes, mountain fog and volcanic, mineral-rich soils.

sections.title: Small farms
body: Almost all farms are small and family-owned, run with traditional, sustainable, organic methods, and the UCIRI cooperative is based here. Coffee had spread to Oaxaca by the mid-1800s.

sections.title: The protected name
body: Café Pluma, protected since February 2020, covers 30 municipalities in Oaxaca, among them Pluma Hidalgo, Santa Catarina Juquila, Santa María Huatulco and San Pedro Pochutla. Its rules call for shade-grown Arabica, mainly Typica and a local type called Pluma Hidalgo, picked ripe by hand, wet-processed the same day, fermented, washed and dried on patios to 12% moisture; dried-cherry (natural) coffee is also allowed. They describe a cup with pronounced acidity, a good aroma and a light body.

story.text: Café Pluma becomes a protected name for 30 municipalities of Oaxaca's Pluma region, a year after the application.
Tierra Amarilla, an experimental Bourbon and Typica from Heladio García España and Flor Eva Pérez Cueva, places sixth in its Cup of Excellence category.
Two Oaxacan lots place: El Mirador's honey Typica, Bourbon and Geisha (sixth among naturals and honeys) and Finca El Encino's washed Geisha (fourth in the experimental category).

records.name: Puebla
records.summary: Volcanic highlands that Coffeeness calls Mexico's coffee lab
records.lede: Puebla's coffee grows at about 1,200–1,800 m (3,900–5,900 ft) in a mild climate, on soils enriched by the region's volcanic peaks. Coffeeness calls it Mexico's coffee lab, with younger growers trying honey and natural processing and some experimental Geisha.

facts.label: growing altitude (3,900–5,900 ft)
processes younger growers are trying
among Mexico's coffee states by output, after Chiapas and Veracruz
El Milagro's washed Marsellesa and Colombia, 3rd in the washed category at the 2026 Cup of Excellence

harvest.text: Mexico picks from about November to March, with timing shifting by altitude; new-crop beans often reach roasters from spring onward.

cup.text: Coffeeness describes crisp acidity, clean citrus notes and a lighter body.

story.text: Los Manantiales' washed Marsellesa places third in the washed category (89.36), and an experimental Typica blend from El Río places second in its category (89.39).
El Milagro's washed Marsellesa and Colombia places third in the washed category (90.25), and Finca Los Naranjos' Marsellesa seventh in the experimental category.

records.name: Veracruz
records.summary: Mexico's oldest coffee region, on the Gulf: balanced, sweet, nutty
records.lede: Veracruz, on the Gulf Coast, is Mexico's oldest coffee region, with plantings documented by 1790; coffee grows here at about 1,000–1,600 m (3,300–5,200 ft). Mexico's specialty coffee revival began here in the 1990s.

facts.label: first documented coffee plantings in Mexico
growing altitude (3,300–5,200 ft)
the year Café Veracruz became a protected name
2025 Cup of Excellence places, far more than any other state

harvest.text: Mexico picks from about November to March, with timing shifting by altitude; new-crop beans often reach roasters from spring onward.

cup.text: Coffeeness describes balanced sweetness, gentle acidity and nutty flavors. Sweet Maria's has found some quality lots here and notes that Coatepec coffees are very different from Oaxaca's.
cup.why: Coffeeness credits its humid, subtropical microclimate.

story.text: Mexico's first documented coffee plantings centered on Veracruz.
Veracruz kick-started Mexico's specialty coffee revival.
Café Veracruz is declared a protected name (a denomination of origin) for coffee from the state.
Veracruz takes 23 of the 30 Cup of Excellence places; La Palma's Geisha wins the experimental category.
Huehuetepan's washed Gesha (91.22, $88.70 a pound) and El Izote's honey Gesha (91.03) win their categories, and the state takes 21 of 30 places.

sections.title: The protected name
body: Café Veracruz was requested by the Consejo Veracruzano del Café and covers green and roasted coffee from the state of Veracruz. The declaration credits volcanic soils, a humid climate, the altitude of the farms and a deep-rooted habit of fermenting freshly pulped coffee, and describes high acidity, an intense aroma, a spicy flavor and a noticeable body. That is a brighter picture than the gentle acidity Coffeeness describes.

records.name: Estelí
records.summary: One of five main departments, in Nicaragua's northern coffee highlands.
records.lede: Estelí is one of Nicaragua's five main coffee departments. Wikipedia places the heart of Nicaragua's coffee production in the northern central highlands, north and east of the town of Estelí.

facts.label: main coffee departments in Nicaragua
where Wikipedia centres Nicaragua's coffee production, in the northern highlands

harvest.text: Picked from October to March. No regional calendar was found, so this is Nicaragua's national window.

records.name: Jinotega
records.summary: Historically top quality; mild acidity, floral and yellow-fruit notes.
records.lede: Jinotega is one of Nicaragua's five main coffee departments, and with Matagalpa it has historically produced the country's best coffee. William Ortiz of the coffee company Caravela says its coffees often show mild acidity, floral notes and yellow-fruit flavors.

facts.label: main coffee departments in Nicaragua
source, with Matagalpa, of Nicaragua's best coffee

harvest.text: Picked from October to March. No regional calendar was found, so this is Nicaragua's national window.

cup.text: William Ortiz of Caravela says Jinotega coffees often have mild acidity, floral notes and yellow-fruit flavors.
cup.watch: Lower farms here face more disease and drying problems, and Nueva Segovia producer Silvio Sanchez finds their coffees generally less complex. Ortiz says good farm management can lift quality, and Caravela is investing in the area.

records.name: Madriz
records.summary: One of five main departments; cups differ from Nueva Segovia's.
records.lede: Madriz is one of Nicaragua's five main coffee departments, and its capital is Somoto. A 2021 guide notes that Madriz coffees generally have different flavor profiles from Nueva Segovia's.

facts.label: main coffee departments in Nicaragua
the department capital

harvest.text: Picked from October to March. No regional calendar was found, so this is Nicaragua's national window.

records.name: Matagalpa
records.summary: With Jinotega, historically the home of Nicaragua's best coffee.
records.lede: Matagalpa is one of Nicaragua's five main coffee departments. Historically it and Jinotega have produced the country's best coffee, and Wikipedia's history says that when most of Nicaragua's coffee grew in Managua department, Matagalpa produced the best beans.

facts.label: main coffee departments in Nicaragua
source, with Jinotega, of Nicaragua's best coffee

harvest.text: Picked from October to March. No regional calendar was found, so this is Nicaragua's national window.

sections.title: Today
body: A 2021 guide groups Matagalpa with Jinotega as lower-altitude areas that face more disease and drying problems, but where, Caravela's William Ortiz says, quality can rise with good farm management; Caravela is investing in both.

records.name: Nueva Segovia
records.summary: Highlands on the Honduran border; floral naturals, a 90-point lot.
records.lede: Nueva Segovia is one of Nicaragua's five main coffee departments, in the north on the border with Honduras. Two lots from here show its range: delicate, floral naturals from Finca Santa Teresa de Mogotón, grown above 1,500 m (4,900 ft), and a Centroamericano that scored 90.50 at the 2017 Cup of Excellence competition.

facts.label: Finca Santa Teresa de Mogotón, in La Unión (4,900 ft+)
a Centroamericano's score, second at the 2017 Cup of Excellence

harvest.text: Picked from October to March. No regional calendar was found, so this is Nicaragua's national window.

cup.text: Silvio Sanchez of Finca Santa Teresa de Mogotón calls his coffees very delicate and floral, unlike the usual Nicaraguan profile. The 2017 Cup of Excellence jury found cinnamon, peach, cherry and raspberry in Las Promesas de San Blas's Centroamericano, along with notes such as hazelnut, raisin, fig, pineapple and lime.
cup.why: Sanchez credits the altitude: farms this high are less affected by weather and heat than lower ones.

sections.title: Naturals and new varieties
body: At Santa Teresa de Mogotón, Sanchez focuses on natural-processed coffee (dried inside the whole cherry), which he says gives a sweet, distinctive profile.

In 2017 Gonzalo Adán Castillo Moreno's farm, Las Promesas de San Blas, placed second at Nicaragua's Cup of Excellence with a Centroamericano, an F1 hybrid (the first generation of a cross between two very different parents). Its 90.50 points earned it the Presidential Award, given to coffees scoring 90 or more.

records.name: Boquete
records.summary: Misty Barú slopes, home of Esmeralda's record-setting Gesha.
records.lede: Boquete is a highland district on the slopes of Volcán Barú, Panama's highest peak, in Chiriquí province. Its farms sit at about 1,200–1,800 m in a persistent mist off the Pacific, and Gesha is the main variety. The Peterson family's Hacienda La Esmeralda began selling Gesha here as a separate lot in the early 2000s, and its lots still set auction records.

facts.label: where coffee grows (3,900–5,900 ft)
typical temperatures (64–77 °F)
of rain a year at Los Naranjos, 2006–2014 (96 in)
Esmeralda's washed Gesha at Best of Panama (2025)

harvest.text: Panama picks from about December to March, says Sucafina; Achilles Coffee Roasters gives November–March. Both are Panama-wide dates, not Boquete's own. Rain in Boquete peaks from about May to November.

cup.text: Ozone Coffee describes Boquete Gesha as intensely jasmine-floral, with a bergamot-like complexity and a tea-like elegance; Coffeeness stresses its clarity and bright acidity.
cup.why: Sucafina credits bajareque, a fine mist carried over the mountains by northerly winds, which cools the farms and slows ripening so the cherries build more sugar.
cup.prized: Clean, floral Gesha: Esmeralda's 2025 washed lot scored 98 points.
cup.watch: Gesha is demanding to grow: it yields about half as much as Catuaí, and its cherries must be processed right after picking.
