story.text: European immigrants found coffee farms in Chiriquí, particularly around Boquete.
CATIE, the research centre in Costa Rica, distributes Gesha (accession T2722) across Panama, but most farmers plant only a few trees.
The Peterson family's all-Gesha lot from Hacienda La Esmeralda sells for more than US$20 a pound at Best of Panama, a record at the time.
Esmeralda's washed Gesha scores 98 points and sells for US$30,204 a kilo.
Esmeralda's own auction of 12 nanolots (lots of a few kilos) averages US$5,745 a kilo.

records.name: Renacimiento
records.summary: Remote district by Costa Rica: mellow, chocolatey and sweet.
records.lede: Renacimiento is a coffee district of Chiriquí near the Costa Rican border, with farms at about 1,100–1,700 m that catch humid Caribbean air. It is the least known of Panama's three main coffee regions because it is remote and short on mills and roads, though Sucafina says its growing conditions match the other two. Many of its producers are small-scale and Indigenous.

facts.label: where coffee grows (3,600–5,600 ft)
Río Sereno, the district seat (987 m · 3,238 ft)

harvest.text: Panama picks from about December to March, says Sucafina; Achilles Coffee Roasters gives November–March. Both are Panama-wide dates, not Renacimiento's own.

cup.text: Coffeeness describes Renacimiento coffee as more balanced, with mellow acidity, good body, and notes of milk chocolate and brown sugar.

records.name: Volcán
records.summary: Barú's western side: higher, sunnier, known for naturals and honeys.
records.lede: Volcán is the coffee area on the western side of Volcán Barú, across the mountain from Boquete, and is often grouped with nearby Cerro Punta. Farms climb to about 2,000 m and get more direct sun than misty Boquete, and its farms experiment widely with natural, honey and fermentation-led processing. The town is a farming hub where coffee grows alongside vegetables, flowers and dairy.

facts.label: top of the coffee lands (6,600 ft)
elevation of Volcán town (4,600 ft)
of rain a year in town, heaviest August–October (115 in)
of dry season, starting around mid-December

harvest.text: Panama picks from about December to March (Sucafina). In Volcán that lines up with the dry season, which starts around December 15 and lasts about four months.

cup.text: Coffeeness describes Volcán coffees as caramel, chocolate and nut with fruit underneath. It hears lemon and florals with a sweet aftertaste in the Typica, and a clear, lemony acidity in the Caturra.
cup.why: Coffeeness credits altitudes up to 2,000 m, which slow ripening, plus volcanic soil and more direct sun than Boquete gets.

records.name: Amazonas
records.summary: Peru's northeast: 15% of the crop and prize-winning natural Geishas
records.lede: Amazonas, in Peru's northeast, grows about 15% of the country's coffee, by USDA's count, across seven provinces at 900–2,100 m (3,000–6,900 ft). In the Cup of Excellence, Peru's national quality competition, it stands out for coffee dried in the fruit: all nine of its winning lots from 2023 to 2025 were naturals, dried inside the whole cherry, or honeys, dried with some of the sticky fruit left on.

facts.label: of Peru's crop (USDA, 2026)
where its coffee grows (3,000–6,900 ft)
of its Cup of Excellence winners, 2023–25, were naturals or honeys
exporting co-ops, third among regions (2026)

cup.text: Enigma's coffee guide describes bright, fruity Amazonas coffees with balanced acidity. US roaster Colipse lists honey, lemongrass and citrus.
cup.prized: Natural Geishas: seven of its nine Cup of Excellence winners from 2023 to 2025 were natural Geishas; the others were a natural Villa Sarchi and a honey Geisha.

story.text: Peru's farm census counted 42,744 ha of coffee in Amazonas, 10% of the national total.
Amazonas harvested 53,941 t, up 7.6% on 2021 and the fourth-largest crop among regions.
Three Amazonas naturals won Cup of Excellence places: two Geishas and a Villa Sarchi.
Three more natural Geishas placed, from Santa Teresa, El Gringo and Finca La Florida, which had also placed in 2024.

sections.title: Names on the bag
body: Colipse's washed lot comes from Yamón district in Utcubamba province, at 1,300–1,800 m (4,300–5,900 ft), grown from Typica, Bourbon and Castillo.

records.name: Ayacucho
records.summary: La Mar and Huanta provinces, topping out around 1,600 m
records.lede: Ayacucho grows coffee in the provinces of La Mar and Huanta, at 900–1,600 m (3,000–5,200 ft) by World of Coffee's figures, a lower ceiling than most Peruvian coffee regions. It held about 2.1% of Peru's coffee land in the 2012 farm census.

facts.label: of Peru's coffee land in the 2012 farm census
where its coffee grows (3,000–5,200 ft)

sections.title: Names on the bag
body: World of Coffee names La Mar and Huanta as Ayacucho's coffee provinces.

records.name: Cajamarca
records.summary: Jaén and San Ignacio: Peru's biggest crop and most competition wins
records.lede: Cajamarca, in Peru's north, grows more coffee than any other region by USDA's count: about 22% of the crop. Its coffee comes from provinces such as Jaén and San Ignacio, at 900–1,950 m (3,000–6,400 ft). Its farmers have won six of the nine Cup of Excellence Peru competitions, the national contest whose top lots sell at online auction, including every one from 2022 to 2025.

facts.label: of Peru's crop, the largest share (USDA, 2026)
where its coffee grows (3,000–6,400 ft)
Cup of Excellence Peru titles, 2017–2025
exporting co-ops, the most of any region (2026)

harvest.text: A German roaster lists June to September for its San Ignacio lot. Across Peru, picking runs from about April to September, starting earlier on lower farms.

cup.text: Herly Mego, a Cajamarca cupper quoted by PromPerú, Peru's export and tourism promotion agency, says San Ignacio's coffees run fruitier and more floral, with some chocolate and nuts, while warmer Jaén leans citrus. He finds the highest farms the most floral, with lots of honey and vanilla.
cup.why: Altitude, in Mego's account: low farms tend to give herbal, green-apple cups scoring around 85 points, middle farms chocolate and malt at 86–87, and the highest farms the most floral and intense coffees.
cup.prized: High washed Geishas. The jury's notes for the 2023 national winner, grown at 1,990 m (6,530 ft) in Jaén, include peach, jasmine, bergamot, black tea and honey.

story.text: Juan Heredia won the first Cup of Excellence Peru; his 328 kg lot sold for nearly US$71,000, a Peruvian auction record that still stood in 2024.
Grimanés Morales took the national title for Cajamarca.
Yoniser Mego Silva's washed Geisha from Alto Mirador in Jaén, grown at 1,990 m (6,530 ft), won with 90.74 points and sold for about US$80 a pound.
Miguel Padilla Chinguel won on his first entry, with a washed Caturra, Bourbon and Geisha lot from El Mirador farm in La Coipa, San Ignacio.
Ángel Manosalva Palomino's washed Geisha from La Catarata won with 90.64 points and US$80.10 a pound, in an auction that raised a record US$490,753.

sections.title: Names on the bag
body: Roasters' bags name Jaén and San Ignacio, the provinces World of Coffee lists for Cajamarca. Recent national winners came from Jaén (2023) and from La Coipa in San Ignacio (2024), and the 2023 winner belongs to the Cenfrocafé cooperative.

records.name: Cusco
records.summary: La Convención: three national titles and many washed Geishas
records.lede: Cusco, in Peru's south, grows its coffee in La Convención province and the Quillabamba area, at 900–2,000 m (3,000–6,600 ft). It won the Cup of Excellence Peru, the national quality competition, in 2018, 2020 and 2021. In 2025 its farms took 14 of the 30 winning places, more than any other region.

facts.label: Cup of Excellence winners in 2025, the most of any region
where its coffee grows (3,000–6,600 ft)
national titles: 2018, 2020 and 2021

cup.text: Enigma, a Cusco travel company, describes coffee from Quillabamba and La Convención as high in acidity, with floral aromas and complex flavors. US roaster Colipse lists floral and chocolate notes for Cusco.
cup.prized: Washed lots from its top farms: 12 of Cusco's 14 Cup of Excellence winners in 2025 were washed. Ten of the 14 included Geisha, and three were the variety SL-09.

story.text: Dwight Aguilar Masías's washed Geisha from Nueva Alianza won the second Cup of Excellence Peru with 91.08 points.
Hilda Leguía won the national title for Cusco.
Aguilar won again, Cusco's third title in four years.
Wilfredo Arias Candia's washed Geisha and Bourbon from Campo Verde placed second with 90.21 points and sold for up to US$72 a pound.
Cusco farms took 14 of the 30 winning places; the highest, Gilber Huayllas Huamán's washed SL-09 from Llaqta Pata, placed third.

sections.title: Names on the bag
body: Look for La Convención, the province World of Coffee names for Cusco, and Quillabamba, an area Sweet Maria's buyers have visited.

sections.title: The protected name
body: Café Machu Picchu–Huadquiña, granted by Indecopi, Peru's intellectual-property office, in March 2011, is one of Peru's two protected coffee names. It covers green Arabica from the hamlet of Huadquiña, a former hacienda in Santa Teresa district, La Convención. Peruvian press reports credit a microclimate shaped by the nearby Salkantay, Sacsarayoc and Humantay snow peaks, which slows ripening, and describe the coffee by its fragrance, flavor and dense body.

records.name: Huánuco
records.summary: Leoncio Prado province and Tingo María, in central Peru
records.lede: Huánuco, in central Peru, grows coffee in Leoncio Prado province, around Tingo María, at 900–2,000 m (3,000–6,600 ft), according to World of Coffee. It held about 4% of Peru's coffee land in the 2012 farm census. In 2025 a washed Geisha from Palma Pampa farm placed 28th in the Cup of Excellence, Peru's national quality competition, the region's only lot in that year's top 30.

story.text: Peru's farm census counted 16,819 ha of coffee in Huánuco, 4.0% of the national total.
Huánuco's regional government was among the backers of that year's Cup of Excellence Peru.
Alcidez Nicki Rodriguez Melgarejo's washed Geisha from Palma Pampa placed 28th with 87.19 points.

sections.title: Names on the bag
body: World of Coffee names Leoncio Prado province, with the town of Tingo María, as Huánuco's coffee area.

records.name: Junín
records.summary: Chanchamayo and Satipo, about a fifth of Peru's crop
records.lede: Junín, in central Peru, grows about 19% of the country's coffee, according to USDA, in the provinces of Chanchamayo and Satipo at 900–1,800 m (3,000–5,900 ft). Coffee took off in the Chanchamayo valley in the second half of the 1800s. USDA's 2022 report put Chanchamayo alone at about 16% of Peru's production, while noting that growth was shifting toward the northern highlands.

cup.text: Enigma's coffee guide says Junín's cups range from fruity to chocolatey, with a medium body. US roaster Colipse lists tropical fruit and caramel.
cup.prized: Naturals (dried inside the whole cherry) and honeys (dried with some sticky fruit left on) have done well. Two of Junín's three 2023 Cup of Excellence winners were naturals, one a Tupi; the third was a washed Geisha given an anaerobic ferment, in a closed vessel with little oxygen. In 2025 a honey Geisha placed ninth.

story.text: Coffee growing took off in the Chanchamayo valley, where early settlers included Germans, Austrians and Italians.
Guerrilla fighting damaged Chanchamayo's plantations and helped coffee leaf rust spread.
Peru's farm census counted 107,904 ha of coffee in Junín, 25.4% of the national total and more than any other region.
USDA reported Chanchamayo at about 16% of Peru's production, with growth shifting to the northern highlands.
Three Junín lots won Cup of Excellence places; the best, a natural blend of Geisha, Catimor and Caturra from Randu farm, placed fifth.

sections.title: Names on the bag
body: World of Coffee lists Chanchamayo and Satipo as Junín's coffee provinces.

records.name: Pasco
records.summary: Oxapampa province in central Peru; small in volume
records.lede: Pasco, in central Peru, grows coffee in Oxapampa province, at 900–2,000 m (3,000–6,600 ft) by World of Coffee's figures. It is small by volume: it held about 2.7% of Peru's coffee land in the 2012 farm census. In 2024 a washed Geisha from La Requia II farm scored 86.39 and sold through the Cup of Excellence's National Winner auction, which is for lots scoring 85 or more.

Peru's farm census counted 11,429 ha of coffee in Pasco, 2.7% of the national total.
Nancy Tania Andrade Gabancho's washed Geisha from La Requia II sold for US$13.20 a pound in the Cup of Excellence's National Winner auction.

body: World of Coffee names Oxapampa as Pasco's coffee province.

sections.title: The protected name
body: Café Villa Rica covers green Arabica from Villa Rica district in Oxapampa province, and has had a regulatory council since 2014. In 2025 Andina counted 2,600 growers on more than 1,500 ha, and about 49,500 kg exported under the name in 2024 and the first part of 2025. The registration rests on its quality, flavor, aroma and acidity.

records.name: Piura
records.summary: Huancabamba's semitropical valleys; small, with Geishas in the national top ten
records.lede: Piura, in Peru's north, is a small coffee region: it held about 1.1% of the country's coffee land in the 2012 farm census. World of Coffee places its coffee in the semitropical valleys of Huancabamba province, at 900–2,000 m (3,000–6,600 ft). Piura Geishas placed tenth in the Cup of Excellence, Peru's national quality competition, in both 2024 and 2025.

cup.text: Peruvian newspaper El Tiempo describes Piura's coffee as standing out for bright acidity, fruity notes and balanced sweetness. US roaster Colipse lists nutty, citrus and caramel.

story.text: Buyers from the Argentine café chain Café Martínez visited co-ops in Pacaipampa, San Miguel del Faique and Canchaque during the Ficafé 2023 fair.
Amaro Velasco Herrera's washed Geisha from El Naranjo placed tenth in the Cup of Excellence with 88.64 points.
Café Martínez began selling Piura coffee in its 18 shops and online.
Ronald Alejandro Baca Avila's natural Geisha from Seb placed tenth again for Piura, with 88.28 points.

sections.title: Names on the bag
body: World of Coffee names Huancabamba as Piura's coffee province. Café Martínez's buyers visited co-ops in Pacaipampa, San Miguel del Faique and Canchaque.

records.name: Puno
records.summary: Sandia province in the south; home of CECOVASA and Tunki
records.lede: Puno, in southern Peru, grows its coffee in Sandia province at 900–1,800 m (3,000–5,900 ft). The CECOVASA cooperative union, based in Juliaca, groups 10 smallholder cooperatives, eight of them in Sandia, serving about 5,000 families. In 2010 Puno's Tunki coffee was named the best specialty coffee at the SCAA fair in the United States, ahead of more than 120 entries.

cup.text: German coffee company Happy Coffee finds chocolate and nutty notes in Puno coffee, with a gently floral acidity, and says light roasts from the south can show papaya and orange. Enigma's coffee guide describes mild acidity, a medium body, and chocolate, caramel and ripe red fruit.
cup.prized: Bourbon: all three of Puno's 2023 Cup of Excellence winners were washed lots with Bourbon in them, and a Bourbon and Caturra blend from Candelaria farm placed fourth in 2018.

story.text: The CECOVASA cooperative union was founded, with its headquarters in Juliaca.
CECOVASA gained Fairtrade certification.
Tunki coffee from Puno was named the best specialty coffee at the SCAA fair in the United States.
Florencia Mamani Calcina's Bourbon and Caturra from Candelaria placed fourth in the Cup of Excellence.
Three Puno lots won Cup of Excellence places, and the awards were announced in Puno at the Ficafé coffee fair.

sections.title: Names on the bag
body: Look for Sandia, the coffee province, and CECOVASA, most of whose member cooperatives are in Sandia. Tunki is a Puno coffee, blended from smallholders' varieties and traded directly.

records.name: San Martín
records.summary: Moyobamba to Tocache: neck and neck with Cajamarca for volume
records.lede: San Martín is one of Peru's two biggest coffee regions. USDA puts it at about 20% of the crop, just behind Cajamarca, while ministry figures reported by the National Coffee Board (JNC) had it first in 2020 and 2021. World of Coffee places its coffee at 900–1,200 m (3,000–3,900 ft), the lowest top altitude of any Peruvian region it lists.

exporting co-ops (2026)

cup.text: Enigma's coffee guide describes pleasant acidity, a medium body and flavors of citrus, chocolate and nuts. US roaster Colipse lists chocolate, floral and citrus.

story.text: Peru's farm census counted 93,688 ha of coffee in San Martín, 22% of the national total, second only to Junín.
San Martín harvested about 89,800 t, the most of any region, by ministry figures reported by the JNC.
Its crop fell to 69,950 t, behind Cajamarca's 76,821 t.
Revista Economía reported 81,800 t, ahead of Cajamarca's 76,700 t.

sections.title: Names on the bag
body: The regional government's coffee project worked in five provinces: Moyobamba, Rioja, Lamas, El Dorado and Tocache.

records.name: Gakenke
records.summary: Rwanda's cool north: Ruli and Coko stations, floral and bright.
records.lede: Gakenke is a district in Rwanda's Northern Province, the country's coolest, whose northern edge is a chain of extinct volcanoes. The Dukunde Kawa cooperative runs washing stations at Ruli and Coko, and northern coffees tend to be floral with pronounced acidity.

facts.label: Dukunde Kawa washing stations: two at Ruli, one at Coko
the Northern Province is Rwanda's coolest all year

harvest.text: Sources give one window for all of Rwanda: about March to June (Achilles). Melbourne Coffee Merchants says April to July, and Visit Rwanda February to May.

cup.text: Melbourne Coffee Merchants, which buys its northern coffees in Gakenke, describes them as floral up front with pronounced acidity, often bright tropical fruit and a clean finish.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Look for Ruli or Coko, the Dukunde Kawa cooperative's station names.

records.name: Huye
records.summary: The south, where Maraba opened the first of Rwanda's new washing stations.
records.lede: Huye is a district in Rwanda's Southern Province, the country's rainiest coffee area, with Butare as its capital. In 2001 the Maraba cooperative opened Rwanda's first new washing station here, and southern coffees tend to be jammy and syrupy.

facts.label: Maraba cooperative opens its washing station here
washing stations built across Rwanda since
of Rwanda's coffee provinces: the Southern Province

harvest.text: Sources give one window for all of Rwanda: about March to June (Achilles). Melbourne Coffee Merchants says April to July, and Visit Rwanda February to May.

cup.text: Melbourne Coffee Merchants describes the southern coffees it buys, from Huye, Nyamagabe and Kamonyi, as jammy and juicy with a syrupy body and a long finish of raisin, brown sugar and chocolate.

story.text: Rwanda began reforming its coffee sector, after decades of state-set prices, the price collapse of the early 1990s and the 1994 genocide.
The Maraba cooperative opened its washing station in Huye, the first of more than 200 new stations.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Maraba is the best-documented name here; Melbourne Coffee Merchants lists the cooperative's stations as Cyarumbo, Sovu, Kabuye and Kibingo.

records.name: Karongi
records.summary: Lake Kivu's eastern shore; home of Gitesi: sweet, black tea, blackcurrant.
records.lede: Karongi is a district on the eastern shore of Lake Kivu in Rwanda's Western Province; its lakeside town, Kibuye, is the province's headquarters. Sweet Maria's has bought washed Bourbon from its Gitesi station for more than a decade.

facts.label: Kibuye, the district's lakeshore town (4,780 ft)
Sweet Maria's has bought from the Gitesi station

harvest.text: Sources give one window for all of Rwanda: about March to June (Achilles). Melbourne Coffee Merchants says April to July, and Visit Rwanda February to May.

cup.text: Sweet Maria's describes Gitesi as sweet at its core, with spiced, Darjeeling-like tea, blackcurrant and a hint of lemon: elegant as pour-over, spiced and chocolatey as espresso.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Gitesi is the station name to look for; Sweet Maria's visited it in 2014.

records.name: Nyamasheke
records.summary: Between Lake Kivu and Nyungwe park: volcanic soil, lake mist, Bourbon.
records.lede: Nyamasheke is a district in Rwanda's Western Province, between Lake Kivu and Nyungwe National Park. Coffee grows on volcanic soil in a warmer, misty lakeside climate, and the lots two importers buy here are washed Bourbon.

facts.label: farms supplying the Murundo station (5,600–6,900 ft)
typical plot of Murundo's ~300 small growers, about 300 trees each
Cup of Excellence award for Murundo's Kivu Belt coffee

harvest.text: Sources give one window for all of Rwanda: about March to June (Achilles). Melbourne Coffee Merchants says April to July, and Visit Rwanda February to May.

cup.text: Two importers' lots give a feel for it: Melbourne Coffee Merchants found Murundo's Kivu Belt juicy and sweet, with winey acidity, peach, orange blossom, hibiscus and pineapple, while Sweet Maria's tasted baking spice, black tea, dried apple and lemon in Gitwe.
cup.why: Melbourne Coffee Merchants credits nutrient-rich volcanic soil and the humid mist that forms over Lake Kivu, in an area hotter than Rwanda's north and south.

sections.title: At one washing station
body: At Murundo, which Melbourne Coffee Merchants buys from, cherries are pulped the same day, fermented dry for 8–12 hours, soaked for 20–26 hours with the water changed every 8 hours, then dried slowly: about 12 days under cover, then about three weeks on raised beds in the sun. Sweet Maria's also buys washed coffee from the Gitwe station in the district.

records.name: Rulindo
records.summary: Northern Province district; home of Tumba, fruity with black tea.
records.lede: Rulindo is a district in Rwanda's Northern Province, with its capital at Tare. Sweet Maria's buys washed Bourbon from its Tumba station and finds more fruit in it than in the other Rwandan lots it reviewed.

facts.label: the washing station Sweet Maria's buys from
the Northern Province is Rwanda's coolest all year

harvest.text: Sources give one window for all of Rwanda: about March to June (Achilles). Melbourne Coffee Merchants says April to July, and Visit Rwanda February to May.

cup.text: Sweet Maria's describes Tumba as very sweet, with pomegranate, berry tea, tamarind and black tea with lemon, turning to bittersweet chocolate when roasted darker. Melbourne Coffee Merchants calls northern Rwandan coffees floral and bright.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Tumba is the station name to look for.

records.name: Arabica
records.summary: The species behind Typica, Bourbon, Gesha and over half the world's coffee
records.lede: Arabica (Coffea arabica) is a species, not a variety: Typica, Bourbon, Gesha and the dozens of other varieties breeders and farmers have selected all belong to it. So if a bag's variety line just says “Arabica”, nothing is wrong. It tells you the species (so not Robusta), just not which variety.

facts.label: of world coffee: 105.9 of 189.7 million bags (USDA forecast, 2026/27)
years since Robusta and C. eugenioides crossed to form it
chromosomes, twice Robusta's 22
so its varieties grow true from seed

cup.text: Arabica is generally preferred for its sweeter taste. Next to it, Robusta tends toward lower acidity, more bitterness and a fuller, earthier, more woody cup, and Sweet Maria's says Robusta generally makes an inferior-tasting drink.
cup.why: Part of the gap is chemistry: WCR notes that Robusta has more caffeine and less sugar, and links its earthy aroma to compounds called pyrazines.
cup.prized: Within Arabica, WCR associates Ethiopia's landraces with very high cup quality, and Typica and Bourbon with standard to high quality.

story.text: Robusta and the wild C. eugenioides cross in the wild, and the hybrid, carrying a full set of chromosomes from each parent, becomes a new species: Arabica.

Seeds that had travelled from southwestern Ethiopia's forests to Yemen, then on to India, are shipped by the Dutch to Java; a Java plant sent to Amsterdam in 1706 starts the Typica line that later reached the Americas.
More than 60 scientists from 18 countries publish Arabica's genome, read from 40 wild and cultivated plants, in Nature Genetics.

sections.title: “Arabica” on the bag
body: A species is the broad botanical group; a variety is a named type inside it. WCR describes Arabica's varieties as distinct types that can all breed with one another, and its catalog lists dozens, from Bourbon to Centroamericano.
When a bag says only “Arabica”, it is naming the species rather than the variety. That's fine: you know you're not drinking Robusta, and the roaster simply hasn't said which Arabica variety it is.

sections.title: Why varieties stay true
body: Arabica self-pollinates: a tree's flowers can fertilize themselves. Because of that, Arabica varieties have long been grown from seed, and a stable variety keeps its traits from one generation to the next.

Robusta is the opposite. A Robusta tree can't fertilize its own flowers, so its seed is always a cross and farms are never genetically uniform; growers plant several clones instead. Arabica's own exception is the F1 hybrid, such as Centroamericano, whose seed doesn't breed true, so it is cloned.

sections.title: How it formed
body: Arabica is native to Ethiopia, where most of its genetic diversity is found. The 2024 genome study (Salojärvi and colleagues, Nature Genetics) dates the cross that created it to roughly 350,000–610,000 years ago. The date is uncertain: earlier estimates ranged from 20,000 to 1 million years, and a 2020 study put it at just 10,000–20,000 years.

A 2020 study argued that a single plant gave rise to the whole species, and the 2024 study found Arabica went through several population crashes (bottlenecks). The result is a crop with very low genetic diversity, which leaves it exposed to disease and climate risks.

family.parentsText: Coffea canephora (Robusta) × Coffea eugenioides, a natural cross
family.line: Allotetraploid: it carries a full chromosome set from each parent (2n = 44)

grownIn.text: Native to Ethiopia. Brazil is the biggest grower, with a forecast 47.5 million bags of Arabica in 2026/27.

records.name: Eugenioides
records.summary: Arabica's other parent, alongside Robusta
records.lede: Coffea eugenioides is a wild coffee from the mountains of East Africa and one of Arabica's two parents: hundreds of thousands of years ago it crossed with Robusta (C. canephora). Its beans carry far less caffeine than Robusta's, and since a Colombian farm began growing it for sale it has turned up in barista competitions.

facts.label: years ago it crossed with Robusta to make Arabica
caffeine in wild Kenyan beans, about a fifth of Robusta's 2.64% (2005 study)
where Finca Inmaculada in Colombia grows it (6,250–6,550 ft)

family.parentsText: Wild species; with Robusta, a parent of Arabica
family.line: Its chromosome set makes up one of Arabica's two genomes

cup.text: Sprudge describes it as naturally very sweet, with unusual notes like toasted marshmallow, lemon drops, sesame snaps and cereal milk, and says some feel it barely tastes like coffee. Competitors quoted by Barista Magazine called it unbelievably sweet, with candied strawberry and guava.
cup.prized: Sweetness: one World Brewers Cup champion used it to balance the acidity of a blend.
cup.watch: Yields are lower than Arabica's, and Intelligentsia's Geoff Watts says it has a very niche following.

story.text: It crosses naturally with Robusta, and the offspring becomes Arabica.
Diego Campos of Colombia wins the World Barista Championship with Finca Las Nubes' Eugenioides, and Andrea Allen places second with it in her blend.

grownIn.text: Wild in East Africa (Rwanda, Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania and DR Congo); grown for sale at Finca Inmaculada in Pichindé, Colombia, the farm that popularized it, and at Finca Las Nubes.

records.name: Excelsa
records.summary: Its own species again since 2025: tart fruit, chocolate and spice
records.lede: Excelsa is Coffea dewevrei, a coffee from Central Africa that botanists folded into Liberica in 2006 and, after a 2025 genomic study led by Kew, recognise again as a species of its own. It copes with heat and long dry spells, out-yields Liberica, and is gaining ground in Uganda, South Sudan and India.

facts.label: a Kew-led study names it a separate species, C. dewevrei
Ugandan farms growing it, mostly switched from Robusta (2023)
where it grows in India's coffee districts (1,650–3,950 ft)
caffeine in wild Excelsa beans, vs 2.64% for Robusta (2005 study)

sections.title: Why the name keeps changing
body: The 2025 study found that what had been called Liberica is three species: C. liberica in upper West Africa, C. dewevrei (Excelsa) in Central Africa, from Cameroon and the Congo to South Sudan and Uganda, and C. klainei in west-central Africa. Kew's Aaron Davis says the wild climates of Liberica and Excelsa are markedly different, and Excelsa has smaller fruits and seeds and thinner parchment than Liberica.

sections.title: “Libex”
body: A 2026 Kew study in Scientific Reports examined 113 samples from three continents and confirmed that many farmed trees mix the two species; in Sarawak, Malaysia, 40 of 45 samples carried Excelsa genes. Libex is reported to out-yield Liberica, with thinner pulp and parchment and smaller beans. Early tasters found it more balanced than Liberica, though the authors say a proper sensory study is still needed.

grownIn.text: Farmed in Uganda, South Sudan, India (Kodagu and Hassan) and Vietnam, and grown with Liberica in the Philippines; Sarawak's trees are often Liberica × Excelsa hybrids.

cup.text: Kew's Aaron Davis, writing for the SCA, says Excelsa leans toward tart fruit, chocolate and spice, and is sweet with medium body and acidity. India's South India Coffee Company calls well-processed Excelsa sweet and very fruity, with a fermented-fruit note and little acidity or bitterness.
cup.watch: Some lots taste medicinal, and early specialty buyers in India compared it to burnt rubber, so careful processing matters.

story.text: Excelsa is first recorded in the Congo (today's DR Congo), and in 1901 in the Central African Republic.
Plantations of 10,000–20,000 ha are set up in the Central African Republic; coffee wilt disease ruins them from the early 1940s.
Botanists fold it into Liberica as the variety C. liberica var. dewevrei.
A Kew-led genomic study of 55 plants splits it back out as C. dewevrei.
Kew proposes the name Coffea × libex for Liberica–Excelsa crosses found on farms.

records.name: Liberica
records.summary: A tall, thick-skinned species, best known as the Philippines' barako
records.lede: Coffea liberica is a tall coffee tree from West Africa that briefly stood second only to Arabica in the coffee trade of the late 1800s, after leaf rust hit Arabica plantations. Today it is a niche crop, best known as kapeng barako in the Philippines. A 2025 genetic study narrowed the species: Excelsa, long lumped in with it, now counts as its own.

facts.label: West African countries where it grows wild, after the 2025 split
estimated world output of Liberica and Excelsa together (2025)
tree height (66 ft); pickers use ladders
when planters took it up as leaf rust ravaged Arabica

cup.text: Kew's Aaron Davis, writing for the SCA, says Liberica tends to be dominated by tropical fruit, and is sweet with medium body and acidity; well processed, it has been praised as sweet and mild with little bitterness. Philippine barako is known for a strong flavor and an aniseed-like fragrance.
cup.watch: It has an old image problem: in the late 1800s drinkers were unsure of its flavor and traders disliked it, and its thick pulp made processing hard.

story.text: Spanish friars bring coffee to the Philippines, first planting it around Lipa, Batangas, later the home of barako.
Planters start growing it as leaf rust devastates Arabica in Ceylon; by the late 1800s it is the trade's second species after Arabica.
Leaf rust reaches the Philippines, then one of the world's top four coffee producers, and the industry collapses.
By the turn of the century it has fallen out of favour almost everywhere, as Robusta gains ground.
A Kew-led genomic study splits it into three species, leaving C. liberica itself to upper West Africa.

grownIn.text: Grown on a small scale in the Philippines (Batangas and Cavite, mostly for the local market), Malaysia (Johor) and Indonesia (Java, West Kalimantan and Sumatra's Jambi peatlands).

sections.title: A crop for hot lowlands?
body: Its wild range is now Sierra Leone, Liberia, Côte d'Ivoire, Ghana and Nigeria. Kew's researchers see Liberica and Excelsa as candidates for hot, wet lowlands where Arabica struggles; one Sarawak farm grows Liberica at 500 m (1,650 ft). The second Borneo Coffee Symposium, in Kuching, put both on its cupping tables, and the first Liberica brewing competition has been held.
Many farmed “Liberica” trees carry Excelsa genes too: in a 2026 study, 40 of 45 samples from Sarawak did.

records.name: Racemosa
records.summary: Low-caffeine, drought-hardy wild coffee from southeastern Africa's lowland forests
records.lede: Coffea racemosa is a small-beaned wild coffee from central and southern Mozambique, eastern Zimbabwe and northern KwaZulu-Natal in South Africa, where it grows in hot, seasonally dry lowland forest. Herbarium records call it “Inhambane coffee”, and settlers there drank it; one South African farm now grows it for specialty roasters.

facts.label: where it mostly grows wild (2,000 ft), in coastal and lowland forest
mean yearly temperature where it grows (73 °F), with 807 mm (32 in) of rain
caffeine in its beans, vs 2.64% for Robusta (2005 study)
Coffee Review score for a washed South African lot (2020)

cup.text: Kew's 2021 study found its flavor clearly different from Arabica's, with tasting panels noting blackcurrant, spiced wine, star anise and liquorice. Coffee Review found a 2020 lot richly bittersweet, with tangerine zest and quince, and a 2025 lot herbal and spicy, with cedar and cocoa: more subtle than flashy.
cup.watch: The tiny beans are hard to roast: all four of Kew's tasting panels struggled, and Global Coffee Report says its flavor and scores have varied widely.

plant.yield: very low: about 12 g of green coffee per 7-year-old tree in 2021

story.text: Breeders cross it with Arabica, hoping for resistance to the coffee leaf miner; the work leads to the cultivar Siriema.
Coffee Review scores a washed lot from Charles Denison's Elephant Coast Estate 92.
Kew and partners in Mozambique and South Africa publish a study of its climate, farming and flavor.
A London roaster's lot from the same estate scores 89.

sections.title: Who grows it
body: Charles Denison farms it at Hluhluwe in KwaZulu-Natal as Cultivar Coffee; bags name Elephant Coast Estate. In 2021 he had about 1,500–2,000 producing trees on 1.5 ha. A project on Mozambique's Ibo Island was dedicated to the species but has likely stalled after storm damage and unrest. Kew's authors see a niche market for it, held back by low yields and small beans.

grownIn.text: Native to Mozambique, eastern Zimbabwe and northern KwaZulu-Natal; farmed on a small scale in South Africa and probably on a few farms in southern Mozambique.

records.name: Robusta
records.summary: The hardy, high-caffeine species behind about 44% of the world's coffee
records.lede: Robusta (Coffea canephora) is the world's second big coffee species, native to the forests of central and western Africa. It generally yields more, has fewer pest and disease problems and needs a warmer climate than Arabica, and its share of world coffee has climbed since the early 1990s.

facts.label: forecast for 2026/27, about 44% of world coffee (USDA)
from Vietnam, the biggest grower (2026/27 forecast)
mean annual temperature it needs, vs ~19 °C for Arabica
caffeine, Robusta vs Arabica

cup.text: WCR says Robusta is often lower in acidity and higher in bitterness, with a fuller body and an earthy aroma. In espresso blends it is used for body and crema.
cup.why: WCR links the earthy aroma to compounds called pyrazines, and notes Robusta has more caffeine and less sugar than Arabica.
cup.prized: WCR notes that, handled and processed with care, Robusta can serve specialty markets.

story.text: The first documented Robusta farming, in Congo, from plants of the Lomami River area.
Botanist Louis Pierre names the species.
Seed from Congo goes via Brussels to Java, where the first systematic Robusta breeding is done.
Robusta reaches Espírito Santo, Brazil, where the subtype “koillou” becomes “conilon”.
Robusta's share of world coffee rises from about 25% to about 40%.

sections.title: Where it grows
body: Wild Robusta grows in humid forest understory from Guinea to Uganda and Angola, mostly at 50–1,500 m (165–4,920 ft). Today it is farmed in about 20 warm, humid countries, and just six (Vietnam, Brazil, Indonesia, Uganda, India and Côte d'Ivoire) grow 95% of it.
Leaf rust ravaged Arabica in Southeast Asia in the late 1800s, and in the early 1900s Java's growers took Robusta up quickly for its yield and apparent rust resistance.

sections.title: Why farms are never uniform
body: A Robusta tree can't fertilize its own flowers, unlike Arabica, so it needs pollen from a different plant. Farmers plant several clones together, and because some clones can't fertilize each other, matching their flowering times matters.

family.parentsText: Wild species; two broad groups, Guinean (west-central Africa) and Congolese (central Africa, the most widespread)
family.line: Diploid (22 chromosomes) and cross-pollinating; one of Arabica's two parents

grownIn.text: Six countries grow 95% of the world's Robusta; Vietnam leads and Brazil, where it's called conilon, is second.

records.name: Stenophylla
records.summary: Heat-tolerant West African wild coffee that tastes like Arabica
records.lede: Coffea stenophylla is a wild coffee from Guinea, Sierra Leone and Côte d'Ivoire that was once widely farmed in Upper West Africa and then almost forgotten. A 2021 study found it grows at a mean annual temperature 6.2–6.8 °C warmer than Arabica, yet blind tasters mostly took it for Arabica.

facts.label: mean annual temperature it grows at; Arabica needs ~19 °C
of judges in a blind test thought it was Arabica
score from a London panel (80 counts as specialty)
the last wild sighting before its 2018 rediscovery

cup.text: Tasters in the 2021 study found natural sweetness, medium-high acidity, fruitiness and good body, with notes including peach, blackcurrant, mandarin, honey, light black tea, jasmine, chocolate and caramel.

story.text: Stenophylla's last sighting in the wild for more than 60 years.
In December, researchers find a single plant at their main site in Sierra Leone, then a healthy population in another forest.
Davis and colleagues publish its heat tolerance and Arabica-like flavor in Nature Plants; a community nursery is set up in Sierra Leone the same year.
About 5,600 seedlings are planted in eight trial plots, and Sierra Leone's government confirms the plants are growing well.
A Kew study finds theacrine in its beans, the first record of this alkaloid in coffee beans; the first harvest from the trial plots is expected.

sections.title: Bringing it back
body: A five-year project, led by the University of Greenwich and Kew with Coffee Culture Sierra Leone and Welthungerhilfe and supported by Sucafina, aims to restart production in Sierra Leone. About 80% of its young plants survived a 2024 heatwave of 59 straight days at 40 °C (104 °F) or more. More than 5,000 more plants were in production for 2025. As of February 2025, seeds and seedlings weren't being released, and exporting plants would need the government's approval.
In a 2025 chemistry study, its beans resembled Arabica in caffeine, sugar and citric acid, though not in every compound, which may help explain why tasters find it Arabica-like.

sections.title: Where it grows
body: It grows wild in hot lowlands at about 400 m (1,300 ft). It is on the IUCN Red List of threatened species, and in a separate CIRAD test it and two other wild species tasted in 2020 all appeared resistant to leaf rust.

grownIn.text: Native to Guinea, Sierra Leone and Côte d'Ivoire; now in trial plots in Sierra Leone, where Kew and its partners hope to restart production.

records.summary: A 1970s Ethiopian research pick, bred to fight coffee berry disease.
records.lede: One of the first numbered selections from Ethiopia's Jimma Agricultural Research Center (JARC): a single mother tree picked in the Metu-Bishari forest of Illubabor, in the west. It was chosen to resist coffee berry disease, a fungal disease first reported in Ethiopia in 1971, and to yield well, and it was released in 1978/79. Lots named 74110 are common at Ethiopia's Cup of Excellence, often next to its sibling 74112.

In a trial of seven early selections at three research stations in the southwest, 74158 had the top cup score, and 74110, 74112 and 74140 were statistically level with it.

records.summary: A natural Catimor × Pacamara cross from Guatemala, released in 2014.
records.lede: Found around 1980 by the farmer Francisco Manchamé in Chiquimula, Guatemala, and thought to be a natural cross between a Catimor and Pacamara. Anacafé, Guatemala's national coffee association, selected it and released it in 2014; World Coffee Research calls it very high-yielding and rust-resistant, with good quality above 1,300 m (4,250 ft).

sections.title: Growing it
body: WCR warns it isn't uniform: plants aren't stable from one generation to the next. It ripens late, gives a high outturn (green coffee per kilo of cherry), first bears in its second year, and is recommended above 1,200 m (3,950 ft) near the equator and above 900 m (2,950 ft) at 5–15° latitude.

records.name: Andungsari
records.summary: ICCRI's dwarf Catimor selection from East Java, released in 1999.
records.lede: A dwarf Catimor-type variety selected by the Indonesian Coffee and Cocoa Research Institute (ICCRI) in East Java. Selection of Andungsari 1 began in 1982, and after about 17 years of trials Indonesia's agriculture ministry released it in 1999. It yields well but needs full sun and generous inputs, and Royal Coffee lists it as susceptible to leaf rust.

grownIn.text: Indonesia: Java, including its Sunda (western) and central regions, and a little in Aceh, Sumatra.

story.text: ICCRI selected Andungsari 1 in East Java and began about 17 years of trials.
Indonesia's Ministry of Agriculture released it as a commercial variety.
ICCRI released Komasti, an improved Catimor that Sweet Maria's describes as 'Composite Andungsari 3'.

sections.title: In the cup
body: There's little published tasting detail. Sweet Maria's Thompson says it has a nice cup in his experience, Sucafina calls its cup profile delicious, and Single O credits it with sweetness, while saying Sigarar Utang brings more intensity and mouthfeel.

sections.title: Not the same as Komasti
body: Royal Coffee lists Komasti as its own ICCRI variety: its name means 'Andungsari Component Three', it is made of six genotypes, and it has leaf rust resistance the original Andungsari lacks. Sweet Maria's records its name as 'Composite Andungsari 3'.

records.name: Arara
records.summary: Brazil's popular yellow-fruited, rust-resistant variety, released by Procafé in 2012.
records.lede: A compact, yellow-fruited Brazilian variety that grew from a natural cross spotted among Obatã trees in Paraná. Fundação Procafé, a Brazilian coffee research foundation, studied it from the late 1990s and released it in 2012. Known for strong rust resistance, high yields and a late harvest, it grew popular through the 2010s; Ozone reports that about 60% of Procafé's seed requests were for Arara.

family.parentsText: Obatã × Yellow Catuaí (a natural cross; some sources name Yellow Icatu as the second parent)
family.line: Selected from plants found among Obatã trees in Paraná and developed by Fundação Procafé over more than 15 years.

grownIn.text: Brazil, especially Minas Gerais.

cup.text: Sucafina found lots with a classic Brazilian Bourbon pulped-natural profile (skin removed, dried with some fruit on): sweet and chocolatey, with honey and molasses. Ozone describes a sweet cup with good body and restrained acidity, with caramel, nuts and ripe fruit.
cup.prized: Competition scores: Sucafina notes scores in the low 90s, and Ozone reports a 92.50 that won the 2019 BSCA Aroma contest for Fazenda Sertãozinho in Botelhos, Minas Gerais.
cup.watch: Sucafina says farmers sometimes pick it too early, because its signs of ripeness differ from other varieties'.

story.text: First selected in Paraná from a natural cross among Obatã trees.
Fundação Procafé began studying it closely and brought it into its breeding work.
Released commercially.
An Arara from Fazenda Sertãozinho scored 92.50 to win the BSCA Aroma competition.

sections.title: Growing it
body: Sucafina advises keeping it to 20–30% of a farm's producing area, and notes that newer Brazilian varieties like it often need pruning and renewing sooner. Aegro reports that its cherries cling to the branch, so fewer drop before harvest, and that it does poorly in lowlands.

records.name: Ateng
records.summary: Sumatra's catch-all name for short Catimor trees, from Aceh Tengah.
records.lede: Less a single variety than a local label: on Sumatra and other Indonesian islands, 'Ateng' is the common name for Catimor-type trees (Caturra × Timor Hybrid). The name is short for Aceh Tengah, the Sumatran regency around Lake Takengon, and Sweet Maria's traces the original selection to one productive dwarf tree on an Aceh farm. 'Ateng Super' and 'Ateng Jeluk' (or Jaluk) are usually other names for the same thing.

facts.label: what the name usually means
the Sumatran regency it's named for
picked for low trees that are easy to harvest
where it's usually grown, thanks to its disease resistance

family.parentsText: A Catimor (Caturra × Timor Hybrid) selection
family.line: Sweet Maria's traces it to a single productive dwarf tree on a farm in Silih Nara district, Aceh, whose seed spread among farmers.

grownIn.text: Widely planted on Sumatra and other Indonesian islands.

sections.title: Why the bag names blur
body: Sample Coffee says the various Ateng names usually all mean Catimor plants, so treat 'Ateng' on a bag as an umbrella term, not a precise pedigree. Royal Coffee adds that Ateng is sometimes confused with Sigarar Utang, which genetic testing places close to it, and Sweet Maria's calls Sigarar Utang an improved Ateng selection.

sections.title: Reputation
body: The author of Royal Coffee's guide to Indonesian varieties says Ateng is planted widely for its disease resistance but isn't considered high quality.

records.name: Blue Mountain
records.summary: Jamaica's Typica strain, and separately, a protected Jamaican coffee name.
records.lede: Blue Mountain means two different things. As a variety, it's Jamaica's own strain of Typica, which has been planted in many other countries, including Kenya. As a label, Jamaica Blue Mountain is a protected name: only coffee from Jamaica's Blue Mountains that the country's regulator certifies may carry it.

facts.label: World Coffee Research lists Blue Mountain as another name for it
(3,500–5,000 ft) where Jamaica's farms sit, per Coffee Review
grown in western Kenya, says Coffee Hunter
of Jamaica Blue Mountain coffee goes to Japan (Jamaican embassy figure)

cup.text: Coffee Review's Miguel Meza (2010) found fresh, well-handled Jamaican lots excellent: balanced and sweet, with full body, good acidity and hazelnut and savory notes, though not very bright, fruity or floral.
cup.watch: Meza thought much Jamaica Blue Mountain isn't worth the hype: coffee is pulped in the mountains but dried near sea level in Kingston, problems can arise if it goes down before all the fruit is off, and storage in hot port towns can fade it.

story.text: Governor Sir Nicholas Lawes introduces coffee to Jamaica near Castleton, north of Kingston, from a plant given by Martinique's governor.
World Coffee Research gives 1730 as the year the English brought Typica from Martinique to Jamaica.
Blue Mountain is planted in western Kenya, according to Coffee Hunter.
On 9 January, 60% of that year's harvest ships to Japan; Japan marked the date as Blue Mountain Coffee Day from 2019.

sections.title: The region and the label
body: The name covers coffee from the parishes of Saint Andrew, Saint Thomas, Portland and Saint Mary, in the Blue Mountains between Kingston and Port Antonio. Only coffee certified by the Jamaica Agricultural Commodities Regulatory Authority, formerly the Coffee Industry Board, may be called Jamaica Blue Mountain, and the name is a registered trademark in the US, EU and UK.
Jamaican coffee from outside the Blue Mountains is sold as Jamaica High Mountain, grown at 460–910 m (1,500–3,000 ft), or lower down as Jamaica Supreme or Low Mountain.

sections.title: The variety abroad
body: Coffee Review calls Jamaica Blue Mountain Jamaica's own Typica strain and says it has been planted in many parts of the world. Coffee Hunter says it has grown in western Kenya since 1913, resists coffee berry disease (a fungus that attacks the cherries) and copes with high altitude, but can't adapt to every climate. A Blue Mountain-variety coffee from Kenya is a different thing from certified Jamaica Blue Mountain.

family.parentsText: A local Typica strain
family.line: Jamaica's Typica line; World Coffee Research treats Blue Mountain as a name for Typica.

grownIn.text: Jamaica, and planted abroad, including western Kenya.

records.summary: A tall Bourbon selection that's a Rwandan and Burundian staple.
records.lede: A Bourbon selection made in East Africa from a population probably named for Mayagüez, Puerto Rico, where the US Department of Agriculture kept a coffee collection that had received Bourbon from Central America. The population reached the Mulungu collection in what's now the DR Congo in the 1930s and Rwanda in the early 1950s. It's now common in Rwanda and Burundi.

sections.title: BM139 and BM71
body: Once the Mayagüez population reached East Africa, breeders picked mother trees from it for new releases. World Coffee Research says two of them, Bourbon Mayagüez 71 and 139, perform very similarly in the field. It rates BM71's cup potential good, a step below BM139's very good, and says BM71 suits medium altitudes. The Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) is listed as breeder of both.

World Coffee Research recommends it for specialty coffee in Brazil and notes it has out-cupped traditional varieties, Bourbon among them, at lower elevations. In 2021 a Catiguá MG2 won Brazil's Arabica 'Coffee of the Year' prize, announced at the Semana Internacional do Café.

story.text: A Catiguá MG2 from Fazenda Santiago in Patos de Minas won the Arabica 'Coffee of the Year' prize, announced at the Semana Internacional do Café.
A WCR study across 23 sites found its rust resistance excellent in some places but less consistent elsewhere.

sections.title: Growing it
body: WCR lists it as late-ripening, with medium fertilizer needs, susceptible to nematodes (tiny root worms), and planted at 4,000–5,000 trees per hectare. EPAMIG's own description calls its ripening intermediate and its fruit red, and says it adapts widely to different environments.

records.name: Catimor
records.summary: Caturra × Timor Hybrid: high-yielding, rust-resistant, often doubted in the cup.
records.lede: Not one variety but a family of them: short, heavy-bearing trees bred by crossing Caturra with the Timor Hybrid, whose Robusta genes fight leaf rust. Catimors spread from the 1970s across Latin America, Africa and Asia, and in specialty coffee the name came to stand for high yields and ordinary cups.

facts.label: first Catimor lines reach Brazil and Costa Rica
countries growing Catimors, by a 2002 Cenicafé count
WCR's cup-quality rating at high altitude for T8667, Central America's Catimor
compact trees, from the Caturra side

cup.text: Its reputation is poor. Ozone Coffee says some Catimors have been linked to a heavier body with earthy, woody or herbal notes; Coffee Hunter describes acidity with some bitterness, astringency (a drying feel) and a slightly salty aftertaste; Sweet Maria's says its cup is sometimes inferior.
cup.why: Sweet Maria's puts it down to the Robusta genes from the Timor Hybrid. Ozone adds that careless picking and processing make the earthy notes worse, and Coffee Project New York says big, unshaded commodity farms in Yunnan, China, deepened its image problem.
cup.prized: Grown and handled well it can surprise: Ozone points to a Peruvian study where Catimors scored 82.5–87.4, with natural and anaerobic lots doing best, and a Brazilian study found a Catimor line, UFV 390-52, cupping at 88.
cup.watch: Bitterness and astringency, or earthy, woody flavors when picking and processing are careless.

story.text: At Portugal's coffee rust center (CIFC), Red Caturra is crossed with Timor Hybrid selections 832/1 and 832/2; sources date the first crosses anywhere from 1959 to the late 1960s.
The CIFC hybrids HW26 and H46 go to Brazil and Costa Rica; in Brazil they get the name Catimor.
CATIE, the research center in Costa Rica, receives fifth-generation seed of the line T8667 from Brazil's Federal University of Viçosa.
T8667 seed spreads across Central America, and national programs pick their own versions: Costa Rica 95, Lempira, Catisic.
Rust starts infecting once-resistant Catimors, notably Lempira and Costa Rica 95.

sections.title: One name, many varieties
body: World Coffee Research stresses that Catimor isn't a distinct variety but a group of many with similar parents. The national Catimors of Central America and Mexico, such as Costa Rica 95, Lempira, Catisic, IHCAFE 90 and Oro Azteca, come from Caturra × Timor Hybrid 832/1; Colombia's Variedad Colombia came from Caturra × a different Timor Hybrid line, 1343.
In Africa, Catimor 129 (called Nyika in Malawi) was released in Malawi in 2006 and also resists coffee berry disease; Papua New Guinea selected and released six Catimor lines.

sections.title: Growing it
body: WCR rates T8667 for the warmest zones and acidic soils at low to medium altitude; in Peru the recommended range is 800–1,400 m (2,600–4,600 ft). Catimors bear heavily and need a lot of fertilizer, and Sweet Maria's says they can wear themselves out in 5 to 10 years.

records.lede: A cross of Mundo Novo and yellow Caturra made in 1949 at Brazil's Instituto Agronômico (IAC) in Campinas, first called H-2077 and released in Brazil in 1972. Its compact size lets farms pack in thousands of trees per hectare, and it helped drive Central America's shift to full-sun coffee in the 1970s and 1980s. It comes in red- and yellow-fruited types.

sections.title: Growing it
body: Studies in Honduras and Costa Rica found no significant yield difference between Catuaí and Caturra. It needs plenty of fertiliser and is susceptible to nematodes (tiny root worms) and coffee berry disease, though that disease isn't present in Central America. Mexico developed a similar variety, Garnica, around 1960–61.
Brazilian breeders have kept using it: Arara is a cross of Obatã and Yellow Catuaí, and Catucaí is a natural cross of Icatu and Catuaí.

records.lede: A Brazilian variety that grew from a natural cross between Icatu and Catuaí, first selected in 1988 by breeders at the Brazilian Coffee Institute (IBC). Its cherries ripen red or yellow, following the Catuaí parent, and it inherits Robusta genes through Icatu. Barista Hustle says it resists leaf rust and Ascochyta, a fungal leaf disease, well.

cup.text: The 2017 Cup of Excellence jury in Nicaragua called its prize lot balanced, with cinnamon, peach, cherry and hazelnut. Ozone Coffee says the variety can make clean, sweet cups with bright acidity.

cup.watch: It needs very heavy feeding, can struggle to root in its first two years, and is susceptible to nematodes (tiny root worms).

story.text: CATIE, CIRAD and PROMECAFE, a network of Central America's national coffee institutes, start the breeding program behind the region's F1 hybrids.
Centroamericano is released to Central American farmers; about 1,000 hectares were planted by 2017.
Gonzalo Castillo's lot from Las Promesas de San Blas in Nueva Segovia places second at Nicaragua's Cup of Excellence with 90.50 points.
CATIE begins supplying Centroamericano, Milenio and Esperanza plants to about 200 coffee-growing families in the Trifinio region of Guatemala, Honduras and El Salvador.

sections.title: Growing it
body: WCR describes a compact plant with large beans and very high yields that bears its first crop in year two. It is highly resistant to leaf rust and tolerates coffee berry disease, but nematodes can harm it, and it should not get too much nitrogen.
In a Nicaraguan trial of nine F1 hybrids, it showed no rust lesions and was among the two most promising for yield and stability.

records.summary: Bourbon brought to Kenya by French Spiritan missionaries in 1893.
records.lede: French Mission is the name for the Bourbon coffee that Spiritan missionaries planted in Kenya. In 1893 they sowed Bourbon seed from La Réunion at their mission at Bura in the Taita Hills, and in 1899 moved seedlings to the St Austin mission near Nairobi, which handed seed out to settlers. Kenya's K7 was selected from it.

sections.title: A name to read carefully
body: Because the seed came straight from La Réunion, French Mission is widely treated as another name for Bourbon. But SL34, long said to come from a French Mission tree on Loresho Estate in Kabete, tests as Typica-related, so World Coffee Research says that account may be wrong. Sweet Maria's goes further and calls "French Mission" mostly a marketing term.

records.name: Gesha 1931
records.summary: Gesha Village's Panama-like selection from Ethiopia's wild Gori Gesha forest
records.lede: Gesha 1931 is a name Gesha Village, a farm in southwestern Ethiopia's Bench Maji zone, uses for one of its own Gesha selections. The farm picked it out of the varied wild coffee from around the Gori Gesha forest, keeping the plants whose shape, beans and cup came closest to Panama's Geisha. Roasters say the number is the year a British expedition first collected Gesha there.

cup.text: Roasters tend to describe it as floral and tea-like. La Cabra found jasmine, stone fruit and a black-tea finish in a natural from the Oma plot; Sey called a washed Oma lot intensely floral and tea-like in clarity; and Coffee Review's top-rated 2024 natural showed wisteria, bergamot, dried mango and cocoa nib.

story.text: Roasters date the first collection of Gesha in this area, by British researchers, to 1931, and the selection is named for that year.
Adam Overton and Rachel Samuel lease 471 ha in Bench Maji; seed they gathered with Willem Boot from the Gori Gesha forest's wild trees is planted there.
Coffee Review scores two natural Gesha 1931 lots from the farm 94 and 95.
A natural Gesha 1931 from the Oma plot scores 96 and is No. 29 on Coffee Review's Top 30 of the year.

sections.title: Reading the bag
body: Gesha Village sells by plot and by selection. Roasters list three selections from the farm: Gesha 1931, Gori Gesha, and Illubabor Forest 1974, a disease-resistant selection named for the 1974 expedition that collected it. Plot names such as Oma, Surma and Gaylee are among the farm's eight blocks, named after nearby villages and sites.

sections.title: Gesha 1931 or Gori Gesha?
body: Both come from the same wild population. Sey says research and genetic testing point to the Gori Gesha forest as where Panama's Gesha was first collected, and that two groups were identified there: Gori Gesha and Gesha 1931, the plants most like Panama's Geisha. Roasters disagree on how Gesha 1931 relates to the Panama line: Intelligentsia calls it the original Gesha and the Panama line's forebear, while Rosso calls it a descendant of the Panamanian strain. No published genetic test comparing them was found.

records.name: Gori Gesha
records.summary: Seed from the Ethiopian forest that likely gave Gesha its name.
records.lede: Coffee selected from wild trees in the Gori Gesha forest of southwestern Ethiopia, the forest Gesha's name is thought to come from. Gesha Village, an estate about 20 km away in the Bench Maji zone, gathered seed there with Gesha specialist Willem Boot and planted it on the farm it leased in 2011.

sections.title: Gori Gesha and Panama Gesha
body: The famous Panama Gesha comes from one accession: seed collected in Ethiopia's forests in the 1930s, grown at the Lyamungu research station in Tanzania, and logged at CATIE in Costa Rica as T2722 in 1953. World Coffee Research found that line distinct and uniform, and notes that several genetically different coffees have been called Gesha.
Gesha Village's Gori Gesha is a separate selection, taken straight from wild trees in the forest.

records.name: Icatu
records.summary: Brazil's tall Arabica with Robusta genes, bred at IAC from 1950.
records.lede: A tall, productive Brazilian variety from the Instituto Agronômico de Campinas (IAC) that carries genes from Robusta. Breeders crossed a Robusta with doubled chromosomes (which made a fertile cross with Arabica possible) with Bourbon, then crossed the offspring back to Mundo Novo over several generations; Daily Coffee News calls it the world's first artificial, commercial Arabica × Robusta hybrid. So its Robusta genes came from a deliberate cross, not from the Timor Hybrid, the natural Arabica × Robusta hybrid widely used in Arabica breeding.

sections.title: Its children
body: Icatu is a parent of later Brazilian varieties: Catucaí came from a natural cross of Icatu and Catuaí, and EPAMIG's MGS Aranãs crosses a Catimor with Icatu IAC H3851-2.

sections.title: Growing it
body: In a 1995–2004 Embrapa trial in Acre state, the Icatu lines showed no rust while Mundo Novo did. A 2008 paper on the trial notes, citing earlier Brazilian work, that Icatu doesn't handle dry spells the way Robusta does, even with a good root system.

World Coffee Research rates its cup potential very low and says it's now susceptible to rust in Honduras, yet IHCAFE 90 lots have placed in the country's Cup of Excellence, in 2017 and again in 2026.

It's highly susceptible to ojo de gallo, a leaf-spot disease, and is now confirmed susceptible to leaf rust in Honduras. Coffeeness lists it in Copán, Comayagua, Agalta and El Paraíso.

story.text: IAPAR began the crossing program that led to IPR 107.
The selected third-generation (F3) progenies were planted out for testing.
Released to Brazilian farmers.
A WCR study of 29 varieties at 23 sites named it among the top performers for stable rust resistance.

sections.title: Growing it
body: Its breeders recommend it for semi-dense to super-dense plantings in Paraná, with plants 0.5–0.7 m apart in rows 2.5–3 m apart. Over four harvests in Paraná it out-yielded both IAPAR 59 and Catuaí Vermelho IAC 81.

World Coffee Research lists it as needing a lot of fertilizer and as susceptible to nematodes (tiny root worms). Its mother parent, IAPAR 59, is itself a Sarchimor: Villa Sarchi CIFC 971/10 × Timor Hybrid CIFC 832/2.

sections.title: In the cup
body: Its breeders rated its cup equal to or better than Mundo Novo's, and WCR rates its quality potential at high altitude as very good.

records.name: Ja'adi
records.summary: A Haraaz name for curly-leaved, tightly clustered Yemeni trees.
records.lede: Ja'adi comes from the Arabic ja'd, curly or rough; farmers link it to wavy leaf edges or to cherries packed in tight clusters. In a 2022 survey it was specific to Sanaa governorate, especially Haraaz, and most sampled trees (83%) were in the New-Yemen (Yemenia) group. Like other Yemeni names, it's a local label rather than a defined variety.

facts.label: of sampled Ja'adi trees (15 of 18) were New-Yemen types
of names cited in Haraaz, the most there
(5,600–8,550 ft) where Ozone Coffee says Haraaz coffee grows

cup.text: Ozone Coffee, which sells a single-farm Ja'adi from East Haraaz, describes dried fruit like dates, figs and raisins, warm spices such as cardamom and clove, and a dark-chocolate and molasses base. That's one roaster's view, and because the name covers mixed genetics, lots can differ.
cup.watch: Ozone warns that dark roasting tends to burn off its spice.

sections.title: Growing it
body: Ozone Coffee describes Haraaz farms on hand-built stone terraces with under 400 mm of rain a year, fed with manure and ground stone rather than chemical fertiliser. Almost all Yemeni coffee, Ja'adi included, is natural-processed: whole cherries dried in the husk, on rooftops and, more and more, on raised beds.
The beans tend to be small, hard and often irregular, and there is no working seed sector, so verified Ja'adi seedlings are hard to get.

family.parentsText: A farmers' name; most sampled trees were New-Yemen types, with a few Typica/Bourbon and SL34

grownIn.text: Sanaa governorate, concentrated in Haraaz.

records.name: Jackson
records.summary: An Indian rust-tolerant selection that became common in Rwanda and Burundi.
records.lede: Jackson traces to trees a Mr. Jackson found resisting leaf rust on his farm in Mysore, India, in the early 1900s. In the 1920s seedlings went to research stations in Kenya and Tanzania, and today it's common in Rwanda and Burundi. Its rust tolerance has since been lost, and genetic tests place it in the Bourbon group.

facts.label: from very vigorous, tall trees
WCR's rating for its cup potential up high
where it does best near the equator (3,950 ft)
the genetic group tests place it in

cup.text: Sample Coffee's Burundi lots featuring Jackson have been described with strawberry and orange, or with rich chocolate, green grape and soft florals. Those are notes on single lots, not a variety-wide profile.

plant.altitude: above 1,200 m (3,950 ft) near the equator

story.text: Mr. Jackson spots rust-tolerant trees on his farm in Mysore, India.
Seedlings go to research stations in Kenya and Tanzania.
It reaches Rwanda, possibly through the Mulungu collection in today's DR Congo (set up in the 1930s) or with Kenyan settler farmers in the 1940s.

sections.title: The family
body: Jackson, Kent, Coorg and Mysore all come from the same part of India and are likely late descendants of the seeds Baba Budan brought from Yemen to India in 1670. The Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) is listed as the breeder of today's Jackson 2/1257.

family.parentsText: Farmer selection from rust-tolerant trees in Mysore, India (Bourbon-related)

grownIn.text: Common in Rwanda and Burundi.

records.name: Java
records.summary: An Ethiopian landrace once mistaken for Typica, later brought to Central America.
records.lede: Named for the Indonesian island, but World Coffee Research says DNA fingerprinting indicates it's a selection from an Ethiopian landrace population called Abyssinia, not the Typica it was once taken for. The Dutch took it from Ethiopia to Java in the early 1800s; it was later selected in Cameroon for tolerance of coffee berry disease and brought to Central America in 1991.

facts.label: CIRAD breeder Benoit Bertrand brought it to Costa Rica
Panama recognized it officially, first in Central America
of coffee berry disease, but susceptible to leaf rust
fertilizer needs, a fit for smallholders

story.text: The Dutch take it from Ethiopia to the island of Java.
It reaches Cameroon through the seed company Vilmorin, where breeder Pierre Bouharmont notes partial tolerance of coffee berry disease.
Released in Cameroon after about 20 years of selection.
CIRAD brings it to Costa Rica for smallholders; seed goes to other Central American countries but isn't released there.
Panama becomes the first Central American country to recognize it officially.

sections.title: Growing it
body: A tall tree with bronze new leaves and large beans, first cropping in its third year. World Coffee Research rates its quality potential very good at high altitude, above 1,600 m (5,250 ft) near the equator, and presents it as a hardier alternative to Gesha for small farmers.

sections.title: Java and AB3
body: World Coffee Research lists another Ethiopian selection grown on Java separately: AB3, picked in Ethiopia by P. J. S. Cramer and brought to Indonesia in 1928, released in 1995 and grown on a small scale on Java's state plantations.

family.parentsText: A selection from the Ethiopian landrace population Abyssinia, by DNA fingerprinting; once thought to be a Typica
family.line: Taken from Ethiopia to Java, later selected in Cameroon

grownIn.text: Java (Indonesia), Cameroon and Central America, including Costa Rica and Panama

plant.altitude: high: above 1,600 m (5,250 ft) near the equator

records.name: K7
records.summary: A 1930s Kenyan selection that tolerates coffee berry disease.
records.lede: K7 is a Kenyan selection from French Mission coffee. World Coffee Research credits it to R.H. Walker and says it was released in 1936 after five generations of selection by Scott Agricultural Laboratories. It tolerates coffee berry disease (CBD), a fungal disease of the cherries, and is found mainly in Kenya and Tanzania, where breeders have used it widely.

facts.label: released in Kenya
WCR's rating for coffee berry disease
(3,300–5,250 ft) where it does best near the equator
beans on tall trees with medium yield

cup.text: 1Zpresso's Kenya guide describes floral aromas with citrus and berry flavors, delicate sweetness, bright acidity and a full mouthfeel. WCR rates its cup potential up high as good.

plant.altitude: 1,000–1,600 m (3,300–5,250 ft) near the equator

sections.title: Rust and berry disease
body: World Coffee Research rates it susceptible to leaf rust, but a 2014 review of Kenyan varieties says K7 resists some rust races and partly resists CBD, and 1Zpresso calls its rust resistance moderate. 1Zpresso suits it to mid and lower altitudes.
You can spot it by its spreading young side branches, while older main branches tend to droop.

family.parentsText: Selection from French Mission (Bourbon-like)
family.line: Credited to R.H. Walker; refined over five generations at Scott Labs.

grownIn.text: Mainly Kenya and Tanzania.

records.name: Kent
records.summary: India's early rust-tolerant selection, parent of S795 and KP423.
records.lede: Kent is an old Indian Arabica that World Coffee Research traces to a single tree Mr. L.P. Kent selected on his Doddengooda Estate in Mysore in 1911. It's known as the first coffee selected for tolerance to leaf rust, a tolerance that has since broken down. Its descendants, such as S795 in India and Indonesia and KP423 in Tanzania and Uganda, are now more common than Kent itself.

facts.label: selection date per WCR; India's Coffee Board says the 1920s
taken to Tanzania and other parts of East Africa
Indian planters favoured it for being less prone to rust
the most popular Indian Arabica selection of the 1940s, developed from Kents

cup.text: Homegrounds describes a mild, naturally sweet cup with low acidity and medium body, often with nutty or spicy notes, and My Coffee Explorer says Indian Kents tend toward chocolate, nuts and mild fruit. India's Coffee Board still credits it with exceptional cup quality.

story.text: Kent is believed to descend from the first Bourbon-type seeds Baba Budan brought from Yemen to India.
L.P. Kent selects a single tree on Doddengooda Estate in Mysore, the start of Kent and the varieties bred from it.
Kent reaches Tanzania, where Lyamungu Research Station starts a selection program on it.
India releases S795 (S.288 × Kents) in 1945–46, and Tanzania releases the Kent selection KP423.

sections.title: Which family?
body: Sources disagree. World Coffee Research calls Kent a Bourbon-related population and puts its offspring KP423 in the Bourbon group, while Royal Coffee and Homegrounds call it a Typica. WCR also says Jackson, Kent, Coorg and Mysore all come from the same part of India and likely descend from Baba Budan's seeds.

sections.title: Where it's grown
body: India's Coffee Board says Kent is now grown in only a few areas, listing it among the main varieties of the Nilgiris. Royal Coffee calls it an older variety still sometimes found in Kenya, and Tanzania's Acacia Hills farm, at 1,750–1,950 m (5,750–6,400 ft), still grows some Kent.

family.parentsText: A single-tree selection from Mysore, India
family.line: A planter's selection; WCR calls the population Bourbon-related, others call it Typica.

grownIn.text: A few Indian areas, and as an older variety in Kenya and Tanzania.

records.name: Kurume
records.summary: A small-cherried local Ethiopian landrace from around Yirgacheffe.
records.lede: A regional Ethiopian landrace (a local type farmers have kept, not a research release) from the Yirgacheffe area. It's named after a native tree with small fruit, and is known for small cherries and a generous crop. It's common in the Gedeo and Guji zones, often grown alongside other local types such as Wolisho and Dega.

facts.label: and a big crop most years
the zones where it's commonly grown
in the top 30 at Cup of Excellence Ethiopia 2021, both from Oromia
