family.parentsText: A landrace kept by farmers; no known parents
family.line: From Ethiopia's wild coffee, with seed selected locally by farmers; named after a native tree

grownIn.text: Ethiopia: Gedeo (around Yirgacheffe) and Guji; also named on lots from Gera, in Jimma

plant.yield: good, regular crops of small cherries

records.name: Laurina
records.summary: A dwarf, Christmas-tree-shaped Bourbon mutant from La Réunion.
records.lede: Laurina, also called Bourbon Pointu, is a dwarf mutant of Bourbon generally thought to have been selected from a field on La Réunion, then called Bourbon island, in the early 1800s. Its trees grow in a pyramid, like a Christmas tree. A 2009 scientific review says its beans are known for excellent cup quality, but calls the exact story of its origin ambiguous and debated.

facts.label: selected on La Réunion, by the usual account
and pyramid-shaped, like a Christmas tree
cup quality, per a 2009 review in Euphytica

sections.title: The shape
body: A CIRAD study found that Bourbon and Bourbon Pointu branch off the trunk at about the same angle, around 50°. The Christmas-tree shape comes instead from the Laurina mutation changing how the top of the main stem grows compared with the side branches.

sections.title: The low-caffeine claim
body: Laurina is often sold as naturally low in caffeine. One decaf-focused newsletter puts it at 0.2–0.8% caffeine by weight, against 1.2–1.8% for most Arabica, but it cites no study, so treat that figure as unconfirmed.

family.parentsText: Bourbon (natural dwarf mutant)
family.line: Selected on La Réunion; the details of its origin are debated.

grownIn.text: First selected on La Réunion, the former Bourbon island.

records.name: Lempira
records.summary: Honduras's Catimor, once rust-resistant, now confirmed susceptible there.
records.lede: A Catimor that IHCAFE, Honduras's national coffee institute, selected from the Central American line T8667. Farmers planted it for higher yields and rust resistance, but a new rust race has since got through, and World Coffee Research now lists it as confirmed susceptible in Honduras.

facts.label: WCR's cup-quality rating at high altitude
to leaf rust in Honduras, confirmed by scientific evaluation
Lempira among the varieties of Honduras's Cup of Excellence winners

story.text: CATIE in Costa Rica receives the Catimor line T8667, which IHCAFE later selected Lempira from.
Rust starts infecting Lempira, one of the cases WCR singles out of resistance breaking down.
Lempira is among the varieties of the winning lots at Honduras's Cup of Excellence, where every winning lot scored at least 86.

sections.title: Its reputation
body: WCR rates its quality potential at high altitude as low and calls it highly similar to Costa Rica 95. Competition results are kinder: Lempira was among the varieties of the 2017 Honduras Cup of Excellence winners, a year when winning lots scored 86 to 91.81.

sections.title: Where it grows
body: Coffeeness names Lempira among the varieties of El Paraíso, Montecillos and Agalta. WCR recommends it for the warmest zones and for acidic, aluminium-rich soils.

family.parentsText: Timor Hybrid CIFC 832/1 × Caturra (selected from T8667)
family.line: Pedigree selection by PROMECAFE and IHCAFE in Honduras.

grownIn.text: Honduras, including El Paraíso, Montecillos and Agalta.

plant.rust: rated intermediate, but now confirmed susceptible in Honduras
plant.altitude: low to medium: 1,000–1,600 m (3,300–5,250 ft) near the equator

records.name: Limani
records.summary: Puerto Rico's compact, rust-resistant Sarchimor, released to farmers in 1994.
records.lede: A compact, rust-resistant variety grown in Puerto Rico, from a cross of the Timor Hybrid and Villa Sarchi. Brazil's Instituto Agronômico de Campinas sent the seed to the island's Agricultural Experiment Station in 1982, and after trials it went to farmers in 1994. World Coffee Research warns that plants sold as Limani often don't match the original.

facts.label: released to Puerto Rican farmers
a dwarf tree, planted 5,000–6,000 to the hectare
(3,300 ft+), where WCR says true Limani does well
its first crop after planting

family.parentsText: Timor Hybrid 832/2 × Villa Sarchi
family.line: A pedigree selection made by Puerto Rico's Agricultural Experiment Station from a Brazilian population of this Sarchimor cross.

grownIn.text: Released in Puerto Rico, where it is still important to the island's coffee.

plant.altitude: above 1,000 m (3,300 ft)

story.text: Brazil's IAC supplied Limani, along with another variety, Fronton, to Puerto Rico's Agricultural Experiment Station.
After trials showed rust resistance and high yield potential, it was released to farmers.

sections.title: The name problem
body: WCR calls true Limani elusive: because the seed has been hard to trace, plants sold under the name often don't match the original reference material.

On the island it has proved itself. A 2021 University of Puerto Rico thesis notes that the experiment station found it outperformed Bourbon, Caturra and Pacas there, and that it remains important to Puerto Rican production for its performance and rust resistance.

sections.title: Growing it
body: WCR lists it as needing a lot of fertilizer, ripening at an average pace, and giving a high outturn, meaning a lot of green coffee from each kilo of cherry.

records.name: Maragogipe
records.summary: A Typica mutation with giant beans, found in Brazil in 1870.
records.lede: A natural mutation of Typica found near the town of Maragogipe, Brazil, in 1870, caused by a single dominant gene. It's known for its very large beans, sometimes called elephant beans, and it's one of the two parents of Pacamara.

facts.label: beans, WCR's yardstick for the biggest size
from tall trees with big leaves and long gaps between leaf pairs
WCR's rating for its cup potential up high
where it does best near the equator (5,250 ft)

cup.text: Coffee Hunter describes a mild, smooth cup with gentle, sweet acidity, a fresh oaky note and a dark, syrupy body. World Coffee Research rates its cup good to very good in Central America.
cup.watch: Yields are so low that World Coffee Research calls Pacamara, its big-bean offspring, the better option for farmers.

plant.altitude: high: above 1,600 m (5,250 ft) near the equator

sections.title: Growing it
body: Besides leaf rust, it's susceptible to coffee berry disease and nematodes (tiny root worms). It needs little fertiliser and turns a high share of cherry weight into green coffee. Coffee Hunter says it matures slowly and is most common in Brazil, Guatemala and Mexico.

family.parentsText: Typica (natural mutation)
family.line: A single dominant gene mutation found near Maragogipe, Brazil.

grownIn.text: Most common in Brazil, Guatemala and Mexico, says Coffee Hunter.

records.name: Marsellesa
records.summary: A high-yielding Nicaraguan Sarchimor that WCR notes for high acidity.
records.lede: A Sarchimor selected in Nicaragua for rust resistance by CIRAD and ECOM and released in 2009. World Coffee Research describes a high-yielding plant adapted to medium altitudes, with notably high acidity in the cup.

facts.label: released, after selection in Nicaragua
WCR's cup-quality rating at high altitude
acidity in the cup, WCR notes

cup.text: WCR notes notably high acidity. The importer Coffee Hunter describes a fruity, floral fragrance, a medium, balanced acidity and a medium body, like Caturra but sweeter.
cup.prized: The Costa Rican consultant Jorge Ramírez Rojas told Perfect Daily Grind that Marsellesa and Obatã cup even better than Caturra and Catuaí.

sections.title: Growing it
body: WCR lists it as susceptible to nematodes and tolerant of coffee berry disease, with a high outturn (green coffee per kilo of cherry) and heavy feeding needs. Coffee Hunter says it matures and grows faster than Caturra and Catuaí, holds its cherries in heavy rain, and does best up to 1,300 m (4,250 ft).

family.parentsText: Timor Hybrid CIFC 832/2 × Villa Sarchi CIFC 971/10
family.line: Pedigree selection for rust resistance in Nicaragua by CIRAD-ECOM.

grownIn.text: Selected in Nicaragua.

records.name: Mibirizi
records.summary: Probably Rwanda's oldest coffee, a Typica type with top cup ratings.
records.lede: Probably the oldest coffee variety in Rwanda, and still important to smallholders there and in Burundi. A Belgian coffee historian wrote that Germany's colonial administration brought it from Guatemala in the 1910s, and in the 1920s it went to Catholic missions, including one at Mibirizi in western Rwanda. Genetic tests tie it to the Typica group.

story.text: Germany's colonial administration brings coffee from Guatemala to Rwanda, where it's called "Guatemala"; it was probably Typica, since Guatemala then grew only Typica.
The coffee is handed out to Rwanda's Catholic missions, including the one at Mibirizi, whose well-kept trees later supplied seed to the Mulungu collection in today's DR Congo.
Several Mibirizi lines are compared at the Rubona research station near Huye; it's unclear whether any reached farmers.

sections.title: The family
body: Its history is poorly documented. World Coffee Research says Mibirizi plants were probably mixed with French Mission plants from Kenya, which are Bourbon-type, but recent genetic tests confirm a link to the Typica group.

family.parentsText: Typica-like, possibly mixed with French Mission (Bourbon)
family.line: Probably Typica from Guatemala, kept at Rwandan missions.

grownIn.text: Smallholder farms in Rwanda and Burundi.

records.name: Milenio
records.summary: Sarchimor × Rume Sudan F1 hybrid; a 2023 lot scored 93
records.lede: A first-generation (F1) hybrid from the same parents as Centroamericano: the rust-resistant Sarchimor T5296 and the Ethiopian landrace Rume Sudan. It came from the first wave of Central American hybrids, and WCR rates it very high-yielding and rust-resistant, though its plants are not uniform.

Coffee Review scores a 100% Milenio lot from Finca Las Lajas 93 points.
CATIE starts supplying Milenio, with Centroamericano and Esperanza, to smallholders in the Trifinio region.

records.name: Monte Claro
records.summary: A rust-tolerant Venezuelan Arabica bred by INIA in Táchira state.
records.lede: An Arabica variety bred in Venezuela by the national agricultural research institute, INIA, in Táchira state, over roughly 40 years of work; its name was registered with Venezuela's national seed commission in 2013. It is valued for tolerating leaf rust and other diseases, and in 2023 Reuters reported that a Monte Claro took first place among 186 samples at a Caracas coffee show, scoring 90.11 points.

A Monte Claro won first place among 186 samples at a Caracas exhibition, scoring 90.11, enough to count as specialty coffee.

sections.title: On the record
body: World Coffee Research lists Monte Claro among the varieties on its 2023 poster of its variety catalog. Reuters reported in 2023 that coffee experts praise its flavor and yield.

records.name: Mundo Maya
records.summary: ECOM–CIRAD F1 hybrid with the top yields in Nicaraguan trials
records.lede: A first-generation (F1) hybrid of the rust-resistant Sarchimor T5296 and a wild Ethiopian accession, ET01, selected in Nicaragua by the coffee trader ECOM and the French research institute CIRAD. In a multi-site Nicaraguan trial it gave the highest yield of eleven coffees, more than 56% above Marsellesa, with no rust lesions.

facts.label: yield over Marsellesa in Nicaraguan trials
lesions seen on it in those trials

for very good quality, says WCR (4,265 ft+)

cup.text: In the Nicaraguan trial it scored 79.5 on the SCA scale (the industry's 100-point cupping score), between Caturra at 76.3 and Starmaya and Centroamericano at about 80.5, and not clearly different from the rest. WCR rates its quality very good above 1,300 m.

sections.title: Growing it
body: WCR describes a compact plant with large beans that yields very well if planted in healthy soil and suits agroforestry (coffee grown under trees). It resists some root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne) but not Pratylenchus, another root worm, and should be propagated only as clones.

family.parentsText: T5296 (a Sarchimor) × wild Ethiopian accession ET01 (CATIE collection)
family.line: Selected by ECOM and CIRAD in Nicaragua; propagated as clones

grownIn.text: Selected and trialled in Nicaragua; CIRAD says it is being tested in more than 15 countries.

plant.altitude: very good quality above 1,300 m (4,265 ft)

records.name: Mundo Novo
records.summary: Brazil's tall, vigorous natural cross of Bourbon and Typica.
records.lede: A natural cross of Bourbon and Typica found in Brazil's São Paulo state, discovered in 1943 and handed to Brazilian farmers from 1952. It's tall, vigorous and productive, can be harvested by machine, and is important in Brazil and elsewhere in South America, though rare in Central America. Crossed with Caturra, it gave Catuaí.

cup.text: Coffee Hunter's notes are mixed: some describe it as sweet and full-bodied with low acidity, while others say it often lacks sweetness and can turn bitter, and that good fertilising helps.
cup.watch: It can taste short on sweetness or bitter, says Coffee Hunter.

plant.altitude: high: above 1,600 m (5,250 ft) near the equator

story.text: The natural cross is found at Mineiros do Tietê, São Paulo; selection from seed sown at Novo Mundo, today Urupês, gives rise to the variety.
Brazilian farmers start receiving it; it reaches Costa Rica the same year but isn't widely planted there.
Introduced to Guatemala, and to Honduras by CATIE in 1974.
Brazil's Instituto Agronômico (IAC) starts releasing new selections.

sections.title: Growing it
body: It's very vigorous, responds well to pruning, needs plenty of fertiliser, and ripens late for a traditional variety. It's susceptible to the major coffee diseases. Coffee Hunter says the Typica parent was the Sumatra type.

family.parentsText: Bourbon × Typica (natural cross)
family.line: Found in São Paulo state; selected by IAC.

grownIn.text: Mainly Brazil and elsewhere in South America, including Peru; also Malawi.

Both parents reached La Cumplida farm in Matagalpa in 1991; CIRAD developed the hybrid in Nicaragua with the ECOM Group, and the plants are cloned in a tissue-culture lab in Sébaco.

records.name: Obatã
records.summary: Brazil's rust-resistant Sarchimor, released in 2000 and now grown in Costa Rica.
records.lede: A high-yielding Sarchimor bred by Brazil's Instituto Agronômico (IAC) in Campinas and released in 2000; Costa Rica's coffee institute brought it in for commercial release in 2014. It has large beans and a good rating for cup potential from World Coffee Research, and some lots have impressed: one from Sítio Novo Canaã scored 94 points in a cupping at Brazil's Fazenda Ambiental Fortaleza, the farm's highest score to that point.

bean size

cup.text: Felipe Croce of Fazenda Ambiental Fortaleza describes an Obatã lot with high acidity, a big body, strong sweetness and a floral side, and says that at a blind cupping it gave off a burst of floral aroma when ground. The Danish roaster Stillers lists chocolate, caramel and honey, among other notes, for a red-honey Obatã from Costa Rica's Central Valley.
cup.prized: Obatã reached the final rounds of Brazil's BSCA quality contest in 2004 and 2006, Revista Cultivar reported.
cup.watch: Croce found only 18–22 Brix (a sugar reading) at visual ripeness in Obatã and similar hybrids, against 26–35 for pure Arabica.

story.text: IAC registers IAC 1669, the first-generation hybrid of a 1967 Villa Sarchi × Timor Hybrid CIFC 832/2 cross made in Portugal; Obatã's code, IAC 1669-20, carries that number.
IAC releases Obatã in Brazil.
It reaches the final rounds of the BSCA quality contest in both years.
Costa Rica's coffee institute (ICAFE) releases it for commercial planting.

sections.title: Growing it
body: WCR rates it high-yielding with intermediate rust resistance, late ripening and heavy feeding needs. Five Elephant's story describes it as disease-resistant and well suited to São Paulo and southern Minas Gerais.
It's also a parent: Arara, a newer Brazilian variety, is Yellow Catuaí × Obatã.

family.parentsText: Timor Hybrid CIFC 832/2 × Villa Sarchi CIFC 971/10
family.line: Pedigree selection by IAC in Campinas, Brazil.

grownIn.text: Brazil, and Costa Rica since 2014, including the Central Valley.

plant.altitude: low to medium: 1,000–1,600 m (3,300–5,250 ft) near the equator; 700–1,300 m (2,300–4,250 ft) at 5–15° latitude

records.name: Orange Bourbon
records.summary: Sold as an orange-cherried Bourbon; one DNA test found Pink Bourbon.
records.lede: Sold as a Bourbon whose cherries ripen orange; importer Sucafina credits it with Bourbon's fine cup at high altitude, and its weakness to major diseases. In 2023 an importer had one 'Orange Bourbon' DNA-tested alongside four Pink Bourbons, and it carried Pink Bourbon's markers, which point to an Ethiopian landrace. That was a single sample, from Colombia or Costa Rica.

facts.label: samples in a 2023 DNA test; it carried Pink Bourbon markers
ripe cherries

family.parentsText: Named as a Bourbon; the one sample DNA-tested (2023) carried the markers of Pink Bourbon, an Ethiopian landrace
family.line: Unclear; may overlap with Pink Bourbon

grownIn.text: The tested sample came from a producer in Colombia or Costa Rica; the sources found don't say where else it's grown

plant.rust: susceptible to major diseases, like other Bourbons (Sucafina)

records.name: Oro Azteca
records.summary: Mexico's Catimor, released in 1995 for warm zones and acidic soils.
records.lede: A Catimor that INIFAP, Mexico's national agricultural research institute, released in 1995 after pedigree selection from a Caturra × Timor Hybrid cross. It's high-yielding and suited to warm zones and acidic soils, and World Coffee Research rates its cup potential at high altitude as good, where it rates T8667, a key Catimor line in Central American breeding, low.

facts.label: released in Mexico by INIFAP
WCR's cup-quality rating at high altitude
(2,000–4,250 ft) where Coffee Hunter says it does best in Mexico

cup.text: The importer Coffee Hunter describes a pleasant fragrance, medium intensity, a long aftertaste and a lean toward high acidity.

sections.title: Growing it
body: Coffee Hunter says it suits Chiapas, Oaxaca, Puebla and Veracruz and that it came out of about 15 years of research. WCR recommends it for the warmest zones and for acidic, aluminium-rich soils, and lists it as susceptible to ojo de gallo, a leaf-spot disease.

family.parentsText: Timor Hybrid CIFC 832/1 × Caturra
family.line: Pedigree selection by INIFAP in Mexico.

grownIn.text: Mexico: Chiapas, Oaxaca, Puebla and Veracruz.

plant.altitude: low to medium: 1,000–1,600 m (3,300–5,250 ft) near the equator; 700–1,300 m (2,300–4,250 ft) at 5–15° latitude

records.name: Pacas
records.summary: El Salvador's dwarf Bourbon mutation, found on a Pacas family farm in 1949.
records.lede: A natural dwarf mutation of Bourbon found in 1949 on a farm owned by the Pacas family in El Salvador's Santa Ana region. Like Caturra and Villa Sarchi, it carries a single-gene change that keeps the plant compact, so farms can plant it closer together and harvest more fruit per hectare. It's about a quarter of El Salvador's coffee and one parent of Pacamara.

facts.label: of El Salvador's coffee, per WCR
compact trees, planted 5,000–6,000 per hectare
WCR's rating for its cup potential up high
very highly susceptible to leaf rust

cup.text: Coffee Hunter describes a cup much like Bourbon's but slightly less sweet, with good body. World Coffee Research calls its quality standard in Central America.

plant.altitude: high: above 1,600 m (5,250 ft) near the equator

story.text: Found on the Pacas family's farm in Santa Ana, El Salvador.
El Salvador's coffee research institute, ISIC, begins selecting the best plants generation by generation.
Honduras's coffee institute, IHCAFE, introduces it to Honduras.

sections.title: Growing it
body: Besides leaf rust, it's susceptible to coffee berry disease and nematodes (tiny root worms). Coffee Hunter adds that it handles wind, sun and drought. Seed is available from Procafé in El Salvador.

family.parentsText: Bourbon (natural dwarf mutation)

grownIn.text: Mainly El Salvador; also Honduras.

records.name: Pache
records.summary: A compact Typica mutation from Guatemalan farms.
records.lede: Pache is a natural mutation of Typica found on farms in Guatemala; Sample Coffee names El Brito, Santa Cruz Naranjo and Santa Rosa. Achilles Coffee Roasters dates it to the 1940s and describes a fairly short, compact plant. It's grown mainly in Guatemala, with some in El Salvador and Honduras.

facts.label: natural mutation, found in Guatemala
(3,450–5,500 ft) where Coffee Hunter says it grows well
Sample Coffee calls it highly susceptible to rust and berry disease

cup.text: Usually described as gentle. Coffee Hunter calls it mild or even plain, and Achilles Coffee Roasters describes a balanced, delicate cup that can lean sweet, nutty, fruity or floral. Sample Coffee's Guatemalan lots featuring Pache have listed green apple, pear and plum.
cup.watch: Coffee Hunter's word is "plain": it's subtle rather than vivid.

sections.title: Pache Colis and Pache Enano
body: Coffee Hunter describes Pache Colis, found in Mataquescuintla, Guatemala, where Caturra and Pache grew side by side: a short plant, 0.8–1.25 m (2.6–4.1 ft) tall, with very large berries, sturdy leaves and partial resistance to phoma, a fungal disease. Pache Enano is an especially small Guatemalan plant.

family.parentsText: Typica (natural mutation)

grownIn.text: Mainly Guatemala, also El Salvador and Honduras.

records.name: Papayo
records.summary: A long-cherried Huila coffee whose roots are still disputed.
records.lede: A rare coffee from Huila, Colombia, named because its long, pointed cherries reminded growers of papaya. It was first taken for a Caturra mutation. Importer Sucafina says World Coffee Research testing shows a close relationship to Ethiopian landraces, but a 2025 test by Cenicafé, Colombia's coffee research center, found it 80–97% similar to part of Castillo, so its origin is still open.

facts.label: (4,600–6,550 ft) where most reported lots grow
its DNA match to a component of Castillo in Cenicafé's 2025 test
Jack Simpson won the World Barista Championship with a Papayo in his milk course

cup.text: Ozone, a London roaster, sums up Papayo lots as tropical (mango, pineapple, papaya) and stone-fruity, with jasmine or hibiscus and black tea; some washed ones lean to chocolate and caramel.

sections.title: What the DNA says
body: Sucafina reports that World Coffee Research testing shows a close relationship to Ethiopian landrace material, without a date or details.

Cenicafé's 2025 annual report compared Papayo with 92 accessions in the Colombian coffee collection using 41 genetic markers and found 80–97% similarity to a component of Castillo; Ozone notes that's not a full lineage. World Coffee Research hasn't confirmed whether Papayo and Ombligón are the same variety.

family.parentsText: Unresolved: once thought a Caturra mutation; tests point to Ethiopian landrace material or to part of Castillo
family.line: Found on farms in Huila; origin unconfirmed

grownIn.text: Mainly Huila, especially around Acevedo and Pitalito; smaller plantings in Cauca, Tolima and Quindío

records.name: Parainema
records.summary: Honduras's Sarchimor that set a Cup of Excellence price record.
records.lede: A Sarchimor selected in Honduras by IHCAFE, the national coffee institute, from the line T5296 and released in 2004. World Coffee Research rates it very high-yielding and highly rust-resistant, and it has done well in competition: Parainemas won Honduras's Cup of Excellence in 2015 and 2017, and the 2017 winner sold for a then-record $124.50 a pound.

facts.label: released by IHCAFE
2017 Honduras Cup of Excellence winner, then a record for any CoE coffee
points for that lot
winning lots in the 2026 Honduras Cup of Excellence's own Parainema category

cup.text: Perfect Daily Grind reported the 2017 Honduran winner as vibrant and lingering with a velvety mouthfeel, and its acidity as refined, crisp and citric. That's one lot, though; WCR rates the variety's quality potential at high altitude as good.
cup.prized: Its competition record: Cup of Excellence wins in Honduras in 2015 and 2017, and in 2026 a category of its own, topped by a natural from La Loma in Santa Bárbara at 89.14 points.
cup.watch: Not every farm suits it: a grower in Chiapas told Perfect Daily Grind it didn't adapt to his farm's excess humidity.

story.text: IHCAFE starts developing it.
IHCAFE releases Parainema, a pedigree selection of T5296.
Oscar Daniel Ramírez Valerio's washed Parainema from Finca El Laurel, El Paraíso, wins the Honduras Cup of Excellence and sells for $124.50 a pound.
The Honduras Cup of Excellence gives Parainema its own category, Parainema Catracha, with ten winning lots.

sections.title: Growing it
body: WCR lists it as resistant to some root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne, worms that attack roots) but not to Pratylenchus, another nematode group, and tolerant of coffee berry disease. It suits low to medium altitudes and needs plenty of fertilizer.

IHCAFE technicians caution that rust resistance in improved varieties isn't permanent, Bloomberg Línea reported in 2022; the same report said producers in Matagalpa, Nicaragua, had started planting it.

family.parentsText: Selection of T5296 (Villa Sarchi × Timor Hybrid CIFC 832/2)
family.line: Pedigree selection by IHCAFE in Honduras.

grownIn.text: Honduras, where 7 of the 10 winners in the 2026 Cup of Excellence's Parainema category came from Santa Bárbara; Matagalpa farmers in Nicaragua had begun planting it by late 2022.

plant.altitude: low to medium: 1,000–1,600 m (3,300–5,250 ft) near the equator; 700–1,300 m (2,300–4,250 ft) at 5–15° latitude

records.name: Paraíso
records.summary: EPAMIG's yellow-fruited, rust-resistant dwarf for Brazil's mountain coffee farms.
records.lede: A short, yellow-fruited Brazilian variety, Paraíso MG H 419-1, from a cross of Yellow Catuaí and the Timor Hybrid. Work on it began at the Federal University of Viçosa and continued at the São Sebastião do Paraíso research station of EPAMIG, Minas Gerais's agricultural research company. EPAMIG recommends it for mountain coffee farming, and its lots have won top places at the Cerrado Mineiro region's coffee awards.

facts.label: ripe cherries
average (60 kg bags) over 106 farm harvests, statistically level with Catuaí
points, winning the natural category of the 8th Cerrado coffee awards
a short tree, planted 0.5–0.6 m apart in the row

family.parentsText: Yellow Catuaí IAC 30 × Timor Hybrid UFV 445-46
family.line: From plant 3 of cross H 419, begun at the Federal University of Viçosa and selected at EPAMIG's São Sebastião do Paraíso station.

grownIn.text: Minas Gerais, Brazil, including the Cerrado Mineiro, where its lots have won regional awards.

sections.title: On the farm
body: In a study of commercial fields published in 2021, farmers named rust resistance and vigour as its strengths. Their main complaint (44% of farmers) was that ripe cherries cling hard to the branch at picking; some also reported slow early growth and plants toppling over. Ripening was intermediate to late, and most farmers still sprayed fungicides.
Minas Gerais's state news agency has reported that it isn't adapted to machine harvesting, though it is a reference for cup quality.

sections.title: Awards
body: A Paraíso from Fazenda Londrina in Coromandel won the natural category of the 8th Prêmio de Cafés do Cerrado with 90.33 points. At the 9th edition, announced in November 2021, Paraíso lots placed first and third in the pulped-natural category (skin removed, dried with some fruit left on), with EPAMIG's MGS Paraíso 2 in second.

records.name: Ruiru 11
records.summary: Kenya's compact, disease-resistant hybrid of 1985, made by hand-pollination
records.lede: Kenya's answer to the 1968 coffee berry disease (CBD) epidemic, which cost the country about half its crop. Released in 1985, it is not one plant line but a composite: a mix of sibling first-generation (F1) hybrids from Catimor mother trees hand-pollinated by a complex male parent bred from K7, SL28, N39, Rume Sudan and others.

facts.label: released by Kenya's coffee research station at Ruiru
a mix of F1 hybrid siblings, not one line
so it can be planted far more densely than SL trees
its first crop

cup.text: Royal Coffee says it has a poor reputation with specialty cuppers, who expect the flavor and sweetness of Kenya's SL varieties, and Sweet Maria's calls it disease-resistant but poor in quality.
cup.prized: Growers value it for its productivity and its resistance to CBD and leaf rust.
cup.watch: Sucafina's Kenyan team says it must be picked at a near-purple ripeness to do well in the cup. Some in the trade wonder whether Kenya's blackcurrant character has faded as farms moved from SL trees to Ruiru 11; Sucafina doesn't confirm it.

story.text: A coffee berry disease epidemic costs Kenya about half its production.
The Ruiru research station starts breeding for CBD resistance in a compact tree.
Ruiru 11 is released; it stays Kenya's most widely distributed variety into the early 2020s.
Batian, a tall variety drawn from lines behind Ruiru 11's male parent, is released.

sections.title: How the seed is made
body: Breeders hand-pollinate the Catimor mother trees with pollen from the male-parent lines, then hand farmers the resulting F1 seed as one mixed variety. Hand pollination is slow, and WCR says it has made it hard to grow enough seed to meet demand.
Some Kenyan farmers graft it onto SL rootstock, so the SL trees' wide root system makes up for Ruiru 11's shallower roots.

family.parentsText: Catimor (mother) × multi-cross male parent from K7, SL28, N39, Rume Sudan and others
family.line: Hand-pollinated F1 seed released as a composite by the Coffee Research Foundation, now part of KALRO

grownIn.text: Kenya's most widely distributed variety from the 1980s to the early 2020s.

plant.rust: tolerant to leaf rust; resistant to coffee berry disease

records.name: Rume Sudan
records.summary: An old South Sudanese landrace prized by breeders and baristas.
records.lede: An old landrace first grown on the Boma plateau of South Sudan. It yields too little for most farms, but breeders have used it for disease resistance: World Coffee Research credits it, with other parents, for the coffee berry disease resistance in Kenya's Ruiru 11, and it's in Batian's family tree too. Saša Šestić won the 2015 World Barista Championship with a Sudan Rume from Colombia.

facts.label: South Sudan, where it was first grown
a carbonic-macerated Sudan Rume from Colombia won the World Barista Championship
why few farms grow it commercially
of Kenya's disease-resistant Ruiru 11 and Batian

family.parentsText: A landrace from South Sudan; no known parents
family.line: Kept mainly by breeders as a source of disease resistance

grownIn.text: First grown on South Sudan's Boma plateau; rare commercially, though a Colombian lot won the 2015 World Barista Championship

plant.rust: more resistant to leaf rust and coffee berry disease than Bourbon or Typica, says Sucafina

records.name: S795
records.summary: India's 1940s Arabica with Liberica genes, also Indonesia's 'Jember'.
records.lede: One of India's most widely grown Arabicas, released in 1945–46 by the Coffee Board of India's research station at Balehonnur and later spread across Indonesia, where it is often called 'Jember' or 'Lini S'. Its rust resistance comes from Liberica genes and from Kent, not from the Timor Hybrid: its parent S288 was selected from a natural Arabica × Liberica hybrid, and its other parent, Kent, was prized for rust tolerance.

facts.label: released in India as Selection 3
top lots at Indonesia's first Cup of Excellence, in 2021, contained it
of coffee in a 2009-harvest survey on Flores, the most of any variety
a vigorous tree with bronze young leaves

family.parentsText: S288 × Kent; S288 is an Indian line selected from S26, a natural Arabica × Liberica hybrid
family.line: Bred by R.L. Narasimhaswamy at the Balehonnur Coffee Research Station, then improved by mass selection for yield, rust tolerance, and bean and cup quality.

grownIn.text: Widely grown in India and Indonesia; Sweet Maria's calls it one of the main varieties on Sulawesi, and it led a 2009 variety survey on Flores.

plant.rust: susceptible in India; highly resistant in WCR's 15-country trial
plant.altitude: above 1,200 m (3,950 ft) near the equator; above 900 m (2,950 ft) at 5–15° latitude

cup.text: In a 2009-harvest study on Flores, tasters most often ranked S795 their favourite, describing a balanced cup with strong sweet tones. Single O tastes maple syrup, caramel and brown sugar in it.
cup.watch: In Coffee Review's 2001 tasting of Indian coffees, three washed S795 samples scored 77–81: mostly sweet but plain, and two went flat as they cooled.

story.text: India released S288, the Liberica-carrying parent line, as Selection 1.
S795 was released as Selection 3.
Its introduction to Indonesia began through the Jember research station in East Java.
Twelve of the top 26 coffees at Indonesia's first Cup of Excellence contained S795.

sections.title: The rust story
body: WCR rates S795 susceptible to rust in India, where most of it grows, yet highly resistant across its trial at 23 sites in 15 countries. The difference is the fungus: India has the world's largest concentration of rust races (strains), and a variety that resists rust in one place may not in another. Sweet Maria's likewise reports that it had some rust resistance but has widely lost it.
Its resistance genes still matter: Oil Slick Coffee notes that researchers have used the SH3 gene from S795 to pass on highly effective rust resistance.

sections.title: Many names
body: In Indonesia it is called Jember, after the research station that supplied it, or Lini S. Sweet Maria's notes that some say 'Jember' really refers to its parent S288, which has turned up on Sulawesi but not Sumatra.

records.name: Sarchimor
records.summary: Villa Sarchi × Timor Hybrid: the rust-resistant family behind Parainema.
records.lede: The other big Timor Hybrid family: compact Villa Sarchi crossed with the Timor Hybrid in Portugal in 1967. Like Catimor it's a group, not one variety, and its offspring include Honduras's Parainema, Nicaragua's Marsellesa and Brazil's Obatã.

facts.label: first cross, the hybrid H361, made at CIFC in Portugal
the name its population got at CATIE in Turrialba, Costa Rica
WCR's cup-quality rating at high altitude for T5296

cup.text: Opinions split. Sweet Maria's finds the cup can show green or herbal flavors, while the Costa Rican consultant Jorge Ramírez Rojas told Perfect Daily Grind that its base is similar to Caturra and Catuaí, and Coffee Hunter says it cups well at low and medium altitudes.
cup.why: Perfect Daily Grind notes that cup quality depends heavily on altitude and conditions, and that in poorer settings the Timor Hybrid side shows more.
cup.prized: Some newer Sarchimors have won quality awards, says the Chiapas grower Tomás Edelmann; a Parainema set a Cup of Excellence price record in Honduras in 2017.
cup.watch: Green or herbal flavors.

story.text: CIFC crosses Timor Hybrid CIFC 832/2 with compact Villa Sarchi; the hybrid, H361, is nicknamed Sarchimor.
H361 goes into field trials, and Brazil's IAC registers the first-generation hybrid of the same 1967 cross as IAC 1669.
PROMECAFE, a Central American research cooperative, forms to fight leaf rust.
National selections arrive: Obatã in Brazil (2000), Parainema in Honduras (2004) and Marsellesa in Nicaragua (2009).
A washed Parainema wins Honduras's Cup of Excellence and sells for a record $124.50 a pound.

sections.title: The family
body: Selections from T5296 include Parainema (Honduras), Cuscatleco (El Salvador), Limani (Puerto Rico), and Obatã, Tupi and IAPAR 59 (Brazil). Marsellesa, picked in Nicaragua, comes from the same Timor Hybrid 832/2 × Villa Sarchi cross. CATIE in Costa Rica handed the material on to breeding programs across Latin America.
It also feeds the newer F1 hybrids (first-generation crosses) made with Ethiopian landraces: Centroamericano is Rume Sudan × T5296.

sections.title: Growing it
body: WCR describes T5296 as well-adapted to medium altitudes but not uniform: its plants aren't stable from one generation to the next, so it isn't recommended to farmers as is. A grower and a consultant interviewed by Perfect Daily Grind say Sarchimors are vigorous, with big leaves and beans, but need a lot of fertilizer.

family.parentsText: Villa Sarchi × Timor Hybrid CIFC 832/2 (CIFC hybrid H361)
family.line: Crossed at CIFC in Portugal in 1967, then selected by national programs across the Americas.

grownIn.text: Selected and grown across Central America, Mexico, Brazil and Puerto Rico.

plant.altitude: low to medium: 1,000–1,600 m (3,300–5,250 ft) near the equator

records.name: Sidra
records.summary: Ecuador's competition favorite: sold as Typica × Bourbon, possibly Ethiopian.
records.lede: A coffee from Pichincha, in northern Ecuador, long described as a cross of Typica and Bourbon. Reported DNA tests point instead to Ethiopian landrace roots, though that evidence is second-hand and unpublished. It became a competition star after Jooyeon Jeon won the 2019 World Barista Championship with a Sidra from La Palma y El Tucán in Colombia.

facts.label: Jooyeon Jeon won the World Barista Championship with Sidra
(5,400–5,900 ft) where it's usually grown
La Palma y El Tucán in Colombia planted its first Sidra trees, about 1,800 of them
and highly susceptible to coffee berry disease, say growers

cup.text: Importer Cole Torode describes ripe stone fruit, citrus, orange blossom and white grape; a former La Palma y El Tucán producer finds honey, malt and red apple with mild citrus acidity. Jonathan Ramírez, Ecuador's 2018 barista champion, points to an unusual menthol note.

sections.title: What the DNA says
body: Sidra was first reported as a Typica × Bourbon cross, and importers still describe it that way, but no test is cited for it. Some farmers and roasters had samples tested and were told it resembles Ethiopian heirloom coffees; other tests reportedly gave different parents. None of these results has been published in detail.

Perfect Daily Grind's Spanish edition reports that World Coffee Research found Sidra to be fully landrace; its English edition quotes World Coffee Research as saying Sidra may lack a clear identity and could be several varieties sold under one name. One unproven story traces it to a since-closed Nestlé breeding station in Pichincha that worked with Ethiopian and Bourbon coffees.

family.parentsText: Sold as Typica × Bourbon; reported DNA tests point to Ethiopian landrace roots (second-hand, unpublished)
family.line: Origin unconfirmed; possibly a former Nestlé research station in Pichincha

grownIn.text: Mainly Ecuador (Pichincha, Loja, Imbabura and others) and Colombia; also planted in Honduras, Peru and Panama

records.name: Sigarar Utang
records.summary: North Sumatra's fast-cropping farm selection; the name means 'repay the debt'.
records.lede: A Timor Hybrid-based variety from North Sumatra whose Batak name means 'repay the debt', a nod to how quickly and heavily it crops. Local farmers say it was found in 1988 on a farm in Lintongnihuta district, and Indonesia's agriculture ministry endorsed it in 2005. Its exact parentage is murky: Royal Coffee says the information around it is full of misinformation.

facts.label: when farmers say it was found, in North Sumatra
endorsed by Indonesia's agriculture ministry
to mature, and high-yielding
fruiting, says Single O

family.parentsText: Arabica × Timor Hybrid selection 831, as usually reported; genetic testing suggests the Arabica was a Typica (Blawan Pasumah)
family.line: A farmer's field selection, not a breeding-program cross; other accounts name Caturra or Bourbon as the Arabica parent.

grownIn.text: Indonesia: selected in Humbang Hasundutan, North Sumatra, and found across Sumatra and Java, per Single O.

plant.yield: high; crops quickly, and year-round per Single O

story.text: Found on Opung Opan's farm in Batu Gajah hamlet, Lintongnihuta district, according to local farmers.
ICCRI reportedly introduced it more widely.
Indonesia's Ministry of Agriculture endorsed it.

sections.title: A tangled pedigree
body: Royal Coffee gives it as Arabica × Timor Hybrid selection 831, but notes genetic testing suggests a Typica called Blawan Pasumah crossed with the Timor Hybrid, and that it clusters closely with Ateng. Single O lists Caturra × Timor Hybrid 831, and Sweet Maria's records it as an improved Ateng selection with Bourbon in it, while doubting such details for a farmer's selection.

sections.title: On bags
body: It turns up blended with Andungsari, for example in a washed lot from the Frinsa collective in West Java and a lot from Kerinci in Sumatra. Single O finds it more intense, with more mouthfeel, than Andungsari.

records.name: SL14
records.summary: A late-1930s Kenyan selection from a drought-resistant tree.
records.lede: SL14 is one of the selections Kenya's Scott Agricultural Laboratories made in the late 1930s, taken from a single tree labelled "Drought Resistant II". Royal Coffee says it matters in both Kenya and Uganda, and that genetic tests place it in the Typica group, unlike the Bourbon-related SL28.

facts.label: selected by Scott Agricultural Laboratories
the genetic group tests place it in
where Royal Coffee says it's important

sections.title: Scott Labs
body: Selections made at Scott Labs from 1935 to 1939 got the SL prefix, and Sweet Maria's says 42 trees of various origins were studied for yield, quality, drought and disease resistance. The lab's founding date varies by source: Sweet Maria's says 1903, named after Dr Henry Scott of the Church of Scotland mission at Kikuyu, while World Coffee Research says 1922.

family.parentsText: Single-tree selection from a tree labelled "Drought Resistant II"

grownIn.text: Kenya and Uganda.

records.name: Selection 9
records.summary: India's Tafarikela × Timor Hybrid, known for its cup but rust-prone.
records.lede: An Indian variety from the Central Coffee Research Institute (CCRI) that crosses Tafarikela, an Ethiopian Arabica, with the Timor Hybrid. Counter Culture calls it known for its cup quality but susceptible to rust, and names it, with Chandragiri, one of India's two most popular varieties in cultivation. A Selection 9 lot won the Fine Cup Award at the Flavour of India competition in 2002.

facts.label: its Ethiopian parent, credited with the cup
won the Fine Cup Award at Flavour of India
with drooping branches
and suited to different coffee zones

family.parentsText: Tafarikela × Timor Hybrid (via Selection 8, India's pure-line Timor Hybrid selection)
family.line: Developed by CCRI in the 1970s, using a Timor Hybrid introduced to India in 1961.

grownIn.text: India, across its different coffee zones.

cup.text: Coffee Review notes that Indian coffees from Selection 9 can show more floral and fruity delicacy than India's usual clean, straightforward cup, with more emphasis on flowers and clean fruit.
cup.why: Sucafina credits its Ethiopian parent, Tafarikela, for the cup quality.

story.text: The Timor Hybrid was introduced to India; a pure-line selection of it became Selection 8, Selection 9's parent.
CCRI developed the Tafarikela × Timor Hybrid cross.
A Selection 9 lot won the Fine Cup Award at the Flavour of India competition.
Poabs Estates' organic SLN-9 won Best Specialty Arabica at the 12th Flavour of India awards.

records.name: Starmaya
records.summary: The first F1 coffee hybrid that can be grown from seed
records.lede: A first-generation (F1) hybrid of the rust-resistant Marsellesa and a male-sterile plant (one that makes no pollen) found among Ethiopian coffees in CATIE's gene bank in Costa Rica. Because the mother can't pollinate itself, the seed it sets is hybrid seed, so Starmaya can be grown from seed instead of costly lab clones.

facts.label: the only F1 coffee hybrid seed growers can multiply this way
cost per seed, about half a lab-made hybrid plantlet
green coffee per plant vs Caturra and Marsellesa in trials
of trees can come out off-type

cup.text: WCR notes notably high acidity. PT's Coffee described a red-honey lot from Costa Rica as fruit-forward, with marmalade, grape and semi-sweet chocolate and a creamy body.

feel.body: fuller than Caturra in trial cuppings

cup.why: In Nicaraguan trials from 710 to 1,250 m (2,330–4,100 ft) it out-scored Caturra at every site, 79.2–83.1 points against 72.5–78.9, and did best at the highest site; the breeders note that both the plant and the place shape the cup.
cup.watch: It resists rust less well than its Marsellesa parent: in one commercial field 8% of Starmaya plants showed rust spores, against 1% of Marsellesa.

story.text: CIRAD researchers spot a male-sterile plant while screening Ethiopian coffees in CATIE's gene bank in Costa Rica.
The first half-hectare seed garden goes in, in Nicaragua: 1,600 sterile mother trees and 400 Marsellesa pollen donors.
ECOM names the variety and starts farm trials; World Coffee Research calls it a major breakthrough.
CIRAD announces Starmaya can now be supplied as seed, at about half the cost of lab propagation.

sections.title: Why seed matters
body: Most F1 coffee hybrids lose their traits if grown from their own seed, so they are cloned in labs, which WCR says can cost double what seed-grown plants do. A Starmaya seed garden yields about half a million seeds per hectare, at roughly half the price of a lab-made hybrid plantlet.
The trade-off is uniformity: WCR says about 15% of planted trees may come out different from the standard, and the breeders counted 16% off-types in Starmaya fields.

family.parentsText: Male-sterile Ethiopian plant CIR-SM01 (mother) × Marsellesa (pollen)
family.line: Hybrid seed from a seed garden where sterile mothers are pollinated by Marsellesa; bred by CIRAD with ECOM

grownIn.text: Bred and trialled at ECOM's La Cumplida farm in Nicaragua; lots also come from Costa Rica's Naranjo area, and trial plants went to Vietnam and Cameroon.

plant.rust: resistant, but less so than Marsellesa
plant.altitude: medium: 900–1,300 m (2,950–4,265 ft) at Central America's latitudes

records.name: Tabi
records.summary: Colombia's tall rust-resistant variety, from Typica, Bourbon and Timor Hybrid.
records.lede: A rust-resistant variety that Cenicafé, Colombia's coffee research center, released in 2002. Unlike the short Castillo and Colombia varieties, Tabi is a tall tree with long branches, like the Typica and Bourbon in its family. Its name means "good" in the Guambiano language.

facts.label: released by Cenicafé
a tall tree with long branches
the Timor Hybrid line in its parents
its SCA scores in a 2023 Cenicafé study, best of the three varieties tested

cup.text: In a 2023 Cenicafé fermentation study, Tabi out-cupped Castillo and Colombia, scoring 82.7–83.2 on the SCA's 100-point scale. The importer Coffee Hunter says it normally gives very good cups.
cup.why: The retailer Japanese Coffee Co. credits its Typica and Bourbon genes.

story.text: Cenicafé releases Tabi as a tall, rust-resistant variety.
Cenicafé's variety guide lists Tabi as one of only four varieties with seed certified by Colombia's farm authority (ICA), with Castillo, the regional Castillos and Cenicafé 1.

family.parentsText: Typica × Timor Hybrid CIFC 1343 and Bourbon × Timor Hybrid CIFC 1343
family.line: Bred by Cenicafé from crosses of tall Typica and Bourbon with the Timor Hybrid.
family.type: Neither Catimor nor Sarchimor: Timor Hybrid crossed with tall Typica and Bourbon

grownIn.text: Bred for Colombia, where its seed is certified.

records.name: Tekisic
records.summary: El Salvador's improved Bourbon, selected over nearly 30 years.
records.lede: Tekisic is a Bourbon selection made by El Salvador's coffee research institute, ISIC, which started selecting in 1949 and released it in 1977. The name joins tekiti, a Nahuatl word for "work", with ISIC. It ripens early, rates very good for cup quality at high altitude, and out-yields unselected Bourbon between 900 and 1,500 m (2,950–4,900 ft).

facts.label: released after nearly 30 years of selection
WCR's rating for its cup potential up high
of El Salvador's coffee is Tekisic or unselected Bourbon
ripening, on tall trees

plant.altitude: high: above 1,600 m (5,250 ft) near the equator

sections.title: How it was made
body: ISIC used mass selection: it picked the best plants, pooled their seed to grow the next generation, and repeated. Tekisic isn't resistant to the major coffee diseases, leaf rust included. It's widespread in El Salvador and economically important in Guatemala.

family.parentsText: Bourbon (mass selection)
family.line: Selected by ISIC, El Salvador, 1949–1977.

grownIn.text: Widespread in El Salvador; important in Guatemala.

records.name: Timor Hybrid
records.summary: A natural Arabica × Robusta cross that gave coffee rust resistance.
records.lede: A coffee tree that appeared on the island of Timor in the 1920s from a natural cross of Arabica and Robusta. Its Robusta genes let it resist leaf rust, a fungus that strips coffee leaves, so breeders spent much of the 20th century crossing it into new varieties, including the Catimors and Sarchimors.

facts.label: first rust-resistant tree found, in a Typica plantation
Timor farmers start planting it
the two selections behind the Catimor and Sarchimor families
the line Colombia's breeders used, received in 1960

cup.text: Its offspring carry a poor reputation: World Coffee Research says varieties carrying Robusta genes, as its offspring do, have traditionally been linked with lower cup quality. A 2015 Brazilian study was kinder: its trial, mostly Timor Hybrid plants and their offspring, averaged about 82 points, above the 80-point specialty line, and one Timor Hybrid plant was described as chocolatey.
cup.why: The importer Coffee Hunter blames its Robusta (Coffea canephora) genes for the weaker cups of its offspring.

story.text: A rust-resistant tree turns up in a Typica plantation on Timor that had been planted in 1917; it's taken to be a natural Arabica × Robusta cross.
Seeds from that tree start small plantations on the island.
Seeds go to research centers around the world, among them Portugal's coffee rust center (CIFC), which shares its selections with breeding programs.
World Coffee Research warns that the Timor Hybrid's rust resistance is showing signs of breaking down.
Researchers report new rust races in Timor-Leste that infect both key selections, CIFC 832/1 and 832/2.

sections.title: Why breeders wanted it
body: Besides leaf rust, breeders have used it to add resistance to coffee berry disease, root-knot nematodes (tiny worms that attack roots) and bacterial blight.

That resistance is wearing thin. Some once-resistant varieties, notably Lempira in Honduras and Costa Rica 95, began catching rust in the early 2000s, and because most rust-resistant varieties share this one parent, World Coffee Research says most experts expect them to lose their resistance in the near to medium term.

sections.title: In Timor-Leste today
body: Many of the farms where the original type grows were abandoned after Indonesia's 1975 invasion and now grow semi-wild, says Slow Food, which places it in the Ermera area. Most of Timor-Leste's plantations today are Timor Hybrid offspring crossed back to traditional Arabica.

family.parentsText: Arabica × Robusta (Coffea canephora), a spontaneous cross found in a Typica plantation
family.line: Not bred: a natural cross on Timor. Breeders later picked lines such as CIFC 832/1, 832/2 and 1343 and crossed them into Arabica varieties.
family.type: Founder of both the Catimor and Sarchimor families

grownIn.text: Found in what is now Timor-Leste; seeds also went to other Indonesian islands from the late 1950s.

records.name: Tufahi
records.summary: A Yemeni name meaning apple, for apple-shaped cherries.
records.lede: Tufahi comes from the Arabic word for apple, and Yemeni farmers use it for trees with apple-shaped cherries. It was the third most-cited coffee name in a 2022 survey of 148 Yemeni farms. Like Udaini, it covers trees from all three of Yemen's genetic groups, so it's a local name rather than a defined variety.

facts.label: of names farmers cited in the 2022 survey
of sampled Tufahi trees were New-Yemen (Yemenia) types
the rest were Typica/Bourbon (23%) or SL34 (21%) types

sections.title: Where the name points
body: With Udaini, Tufahi was the main name in Ibb, Dhamar and Raymah, and it made up 17% of names cited in Haraaz. Tufahi trees from Al Mahwit and Sanaa were mainly New-Yemen, while those from Ibb and Dhamar were mainly SL34 and Typica/Bourbon types.

family.parentsText: A farmers' name, not a genetic line: New-Yemen, Typica/Bourbon and SL34 trees all go by it

grownIn.text: Named across Yemen, especially Ibb, Dhamar and Raymah.

records.name: Tupi
records.summary: An early-ripening, rust-resistant Brazilian Sarchimor from IAC.
records.lede: A Sarchimor from Brazil's Instituto Agronômico (IAC), one of the selections Brazil made from the Villa Sarchi × Timor Hybrid cross. A 2012 article on IAC's history describes it as rust-resistant and early-ripening.

facts.label: its full IAC code
ripening
to leaf rust

cup.text: Felipe Croce of Brazil's Fazenda Ambiental Fortaleza says Tupi has a distinctive taste that often recalls bell pepper. A grower in Chiapas, Mexico, told Perfect Daily Grind it does well there, especially as a natural (dried inside the whole cherry) or honey (dried with some of the sticky fruit left on the seed).
cup.watch: A bell-pepper note, says Croce.

sections.title: Not the same as IAC 125 RN
body: IAC 125 RN, once called Tupi RN IAC 1669-13 and also known as IBC 12, is a separate selection from the same IAC 1669 hybrid. It was registered in 2012 and bred for resistance to the root-knot nematode Meloidogyne exigua as well as rust, and a 2012 Revista Cultivar piece on IAC's history lists Tupi IAC 1669-33 and IAC 125 RN as separate cultivars.

family.parentsText: Villa Sarchi × Timor Hybrid CIFC 832/2 (IAC's hybrid 1669)
family.line: Selected by IAC in Brazil from its Sarchimor population.

grownIn.text: Brazil, and farms such as Finca Hamburgo in Chiapas, Mexico.

records.name: Typica Mejorado
records.summary: An “improved Typica” grown in Ecuador, introduced there alongside Sidra.
records.lede: Its name is Spanish for “improved Typica”. It's one of Ecuador's newer specialty varieties, grown there alongside Gesha, and Olger Rogel is reported to have introduced it to Ecuador, as he did Sidra.

facts.label: where it's grown as a newer specialty variety
reported to have introduced it, and Sidra, to Ecuador

family.parentsText: Parentage not documented in the sources found; the Typica link rests on the name
family.line: Introduced in Ecuador; origin undocumented

grownIn.text: Ecuador

records.name: Udaini
records.summary: Yemen's most common coffee name, but not one genetic variety.
records.lede: Udaini is the name Yemeni farmers use most for their coffee trees: a third of all names cited in a 2022 survey of 148 farms. The study says it's named after a region, Al Udaini. DNA tests found Udaini trees in all three of Yemen's genetic groups, so the name tells you about local tradition more than about the plant.

facts.label: of names farmers cited in the 2022 survey, the most of any
of sampled Udaini trees were New-Yemen (Yemenia) types
the rest were Typica/Bourbon (19%) or SL34 (14%) types

sections.title: Where the name points
body: Region says more than the name. Udaini trees from Al Mahwit and Sanaa were mainly New-Yemen, while those from Ibb and Dhamar were mainly SL34 and Typica/Bourbon types. In Ibb, farmers named only Udaini and Tufahi.
The few written descriptions make Udaini a tall tree, and Ozone Coffee says farmers link it with flat, elongated leaves, but the study's authors say the tall-versus-compact split isn't clear-cut.

family.parentsText: A farmers' name, not a genetic line: New-Yemen, Typica/Bourbon and SL34 trees all go by it

grownIn.text: Named across Yemen's coffee governorates, including Ibb, Dhamar, Raymah, Sanaa and Al Mahwit.

records.name: Villa Sarchi
records.summary: Costa Rica's wind-tolerant dwarf Bourbon, a parent of Sarchimor.
records.lede: A natural dwarf mutation of Bourbon found in the northwest of Costa Rica's Alajuela province in the 1950s or 1960s, then improved by local growers through selection. It's suited to the very highest farms and tolerates strong winds. Crossed with Timor Hybrid in Portugal from 1967, it gave the Sarchimor group of rust-resistant varieties.

facts.label: compact trees, planted 5,000–6,000 per hectare
and suited to the highest-altitude farms
bean size, a notch under Caturra's
its cross with Timor Hybrid (hybrid H361)

cup.text: Coffee Hunter describes elegant acidity, intense berry notes and a lot of sweetness. World Coffee Research rates its cup potential up high as good.

plant.altitude: high: above 1,600 m (5,250 ft) near the equator

story.text: Found as a dwarf Bourbon mutation in northwestern Alajuela, Costa Rica.
Portugal's coffee rust research center (CIFC) starts crossing compact plants with rust-resistant Timor Hybrid; Timor Hybrid CIFC 832/2 × Villa Sarchi becomes hybrid H361, Sarchimor.
Honduras's coffee institute, IHCAFE, introduces it to Honduras.
Brazil registers IAC 125 RN, a Villa Sarchi × Timor Hybrid cross selected at IAC.

sections.title: Names
body: World Coffee Research lists La Luisa and Villalobos Bourbon as other names for it. Cafe Imports, though, lists Villalobos as a separate Costa Rican variety, so a bag that says Villalobos may or may not be this plant. It's rarely grown outside Costa Rica; Cafe Imports says the West Valley grows a lot of it.

family.parentsText: Bourbon (natural dwarf mutation)
family.line: Improved by Costa Rican growers through pedigree selection.

grownIn.text: Mainly Costa Rica, especially the West Valley; introduced to Honduras in 1974.

records.name: Villalobos
records.summary: A Costa Rican variety whose identity sources don't agree on.
records.lede: Villalobos is a coffee grown in Costa Rica. Importer Cafe Imports calls it specific to Costa Rica and says the West Valley grows a lot of it. Its identity is muddled: Costa Rica's coffee institute, ICAFE, calls it a subtype of Typica and Cafe Imports' glossary a dwarf Typica mutation, while World Coffee Research lists "Villalobos Bourbon" as another name for Villa Sarchi, a dwarf Bourbon mutation.

facts.label: Costa Rica's coffee institute calls it a subtype of Typica

WCR treats "Villalobos Bourbon" as another name for it

family.parentsText: Unclear: WCR files "Villalobos Bourbon" under Villa Sarchi, a Bourbon mutation

grownIn.text: Costa Rica, especially the West Valley.

records.name: Wolisho
records.summary: A big-cherried, shade-loving local landrace from Ethiopia's Gedeo zone.
records.lede: A regional Ethiopian landrace (a local type farmers have kept for generations) named after a tree native to Gedeo, the zone around Yirgacheffe. It's a large tree with long leaves and big cherries, usually grown under semi-forest shade, and often on the same farms as Kurume and Dega.

crop from year to year
drought-tolerant and at home in shade

family.parentsText: A landrace kept by farmers; no known parents
family.line: Grown for centuries in Ethiopia's highlands, especially Gedeo

grownIn.text: Ethiopia: Yirgacheffe (Gedeo), Sidama and Guji

plant.stature: large canopy, long branches and leaves

records.name: Wush Wush
records.summary: A southwest Ethiopian landrace that found a second home in Colombia.
records.lede: An Ethiopian landrace first found around Wushwush, in the southwestern highlands, and isolated on a farm there. It reached South America in the 1990s and is now grown mostly in Colombia and Panama. A 2012 study also lists a cultivar named Wushwush among 23 that Ethiopia's agricultural research institute developed to resist coffee berry disease.

family.parentsText: An Ethiopian landrace from the Wushwush area; no known parents
family.line: Isolated on a farm in Wushwush, southwest Ethiopia

grownIn.text: Mostly Colombia and Panama today; first found in southwest Ethiopia

records.name: Yellow Bourbon
records.summary: Yellow-fruited Bourbon that turned up in São Paulo around 1930.
records.lede: Bourbon whose ripe cherries are yellow instead of red. Ozone Coffee says it's believed to have first appeared around 1930 on a Red Bourbon farm near Pederneiras, in Brazil's São Paulo state, and that by 1942 researchers at Brazil's Instituto Agronômico (IAC) had shown a single genetic factor, which they named xanthocarpa, controls the yellow color.

facts.label: first seen near Pederneiras, São Paulo
xanthocarpa, controls the yellow fruit (IAC, 1942)
origin: a Red Bourbon mutation, or a cross with a yellow Typica

sections.title: Where it came from
body: Two explanations are still open: it may be a mutation of Red Bourbon, or a natural cross between Red Bourbon and Amarelo de Botucatu, a yellow-fruited Typica. The 1942 work at Campinas was led by Carlos Arnaldo Krug.

family.parentsText: Red Bourbon (mutation), or Red Bourbon × Amarelo de Botucatu
family.line: Origin unresolved.

grownIn.text: Associated above all with Brazil.

records.name: Yemenia
records.summary: A genetic group of Arabica found so far only in Yemen.
records.lede: Yemenia is the name Qima Coffee and plant scientist Christophe Montagnon of RD2 Vision gave in 2020 to a group of Yemeni coffee trees whose DNA matched no known cultivated variety and no sampled Ethiopian coffee. Scientists call it the New-Yemen group, and Qima says the name means "the Yemeni mother" in Arabic. It's a genetic group, not one defined variety: trees in it go by several local names.

facts.label: no cultivated variety or sampled Ethiopian coffee belongs to it
announced by Qima Coffee and RD2 Vision
winning lots at Qima's 2020 auction were Yemenia
points for several Yemenia lots in a blind 2020 jury cupping

cup.text: Early descriptions come from the 2020 competition jury. German roaster Raphael Braune heard berry notes like SL28, the sweetness of a Yellow Bourbon and aromatic complexity like Gesha's. These are judges' impressions of particular lots, not a side-by-side trial of the group.

story.text: A genetic study led by World Coffee Research found Yemen's coffee is a sub-group of Ethiopian Arabica and, as a whole, less diverse.
Qima Coffee and RD2 Vision announce Yemenia after DNA fingerprinting 137 Arabica samples; 15 of the 20 winning lots at that September's auction are Yemenia.
A paper in Genetic Resources and Crop Evolution describes the New-Yemen cluster as unique to Yemen and unrelated to any known cultivated variety or Ethiopian sample.
A follow-up survey of 148 Yemeni farms finds that local variety names don't reliably match the trees' genetics.

sections.title: A group, not a name on a bag
body: In the 2022 survey, most trees farmers called Dawairi (86%), Jaadi (83%) and Udaini (67%) tested as New-Yemen. But some trees under those same names were Typica/Bourbon or SL34 types, and overall the names showed no significant link to genetics. A bag that says Udaini doesn't guarantee Yemenia.

Region was a better clue than the name: Udaini and Tufahi trees from Al Mahwit and Sanaa were mainly New-Yemen, while those from Ibb and Dhamar were mainly SL34 and Typica/Bourbon types. The study's authors recommend proper variety trials as the next step for Yemen's seed sector.

sections.title: Why breeders care
body: Yemen's coffee has grown for centuries in hot, dry, full sun, unlike Ethiopia's shaded forests, and World Coffee Research asks whether Yemeni trees could help scientists learn more about heat and drought tolerance. Global Coffee Report (2025) puts rainfall in Yemen's coffee regions at about 200–350 mm a year, against the roughly 1,000 mm coffee usually needs.

family.parentsText: A genetic group (the New-Yemen cluster), not a bred variety
family.line: Found by DNA fingerprinting; it may still overlap with Ethiopian coffee that hasn't been collected or tested yet.

grownIn.text: Found only in Yemen so far.
